lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.answer: Read one line → Parse that line → Use id → Next line
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.explanation: 1) StringIO provides a stream, such as a file containing multiple JSON lines. 2) ``for line in stream:`` reads one line at a time. 3) Each line is converted into a dictionary using ``json.loads``. 4) Since only the ID of the current row is used directly, a full list of rows is not created beforehand.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.project_context: This ties into understanding code that inspects large JSONL files containing cards and nodes without loading the entire file into memory.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.reading_goal_internal: `for line in stream:`이 JSONL 레코드를 한 줄씩 처리하게 하는 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `for` iterates through an iterable, retrieving elements one by one and executing the block repeatedly.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: In JSONL, we verify that a single loop variable represents a record string and check whether that line is parsed immediately.
concept_explanation.key_point: `for line in stream:` The structure processes records one line at a time rather than converting the entire file into a list all at once.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: A `for` loop does not always use less memory simply because it is a `for` loop. If you collect every row into a list again inside the loop, the benefits of streaming are reduced.

teaching_example.code:
import json
from io import StringIO
stream = StringIO('{"n": 1}\n{"n": 2}\n')
for line in stream:
    print(json.loads(line)['n'])
teaching_example.walkthrough: In each iteration, it reads and parses only one line and prints 1 and 2 in sequence.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) StringIO provides a stream, such as a file containing multiple JSON lines. 2) ``for line in stream:`` reads one line at a time. 3) Each line is converted into a dictionary using ``json.loads``. 4) Since only the ID of the current row is used directly, a full list of rows is not created beforehand.
answer_explanation.why_correct: `for line in stream:` The structure processes records one line at a time rather than converting the entire file into a list all at once.

common_wrong_choice.choice: Combine all lines and call `json.loads` only once
common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Since JSONL treats each line as an independent JSON record, this code calls `json.loads` on every line.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Verify that each iteration of the loop corresponds to a single JSONL record.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Read JSONL streaming as a repetition of **obtain one line → parse one record → process it immediately**.

lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.title: Reading the delimiter keyword argument that enables TSV reading
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.reading_goal: `delimiter='\t'` The keyword argument defines the column boundaries in the TSV file.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.code:
import csv
from io import StringIO
f = StringIO('title\tlevel\nJSONL\t6\n')
reader = csv.DictReader(f, delimiter='\t')
row = next(reader)
print(row['title'])
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.question: What does `delimiter='\t'` do?
choices: Use the tab character as the column separator.
Add a tab character after every value.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.answer: Use the tab character as the column separator.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.explanation: 1) StringIO contains tab-separated TSV text. 2) When calling ``csv.DictReader``, ``delimiter='\t'`` is passed as a keyword argument. 3) `DictReader` uses tabs as column delimiters. 4) Each row is read as a dictionary with header names as keys.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.project_context: This connects to understanding the configuration difference when reading CSV and TSV learning data with the same `DictReader` API.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.reading_goal_internal: `delimiter='\t'` keyword argument가 TSV의 컬럼 경계를 정하는 의미를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: A keyword argument specifies the name of the argument to clearly indicate which setting value is being passed.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Read the name `delimiter` and the fact that `\t` is a tab character together.
concept_explanation.key_point: `delimiter='\t'` This specifies that DictReader should use tabs instead of commas as column delimiters.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: `\t` Do not interpret “`\t`” as two characters: a backslash followed by a “t.” In Python strings, “” is a tab character.

teaching_example.code:
import csv
from io import StringIO
f = StringIO('name\tscore\nA\t3\n')
reader = csv.DictReader(f, delimiter='\t')
print(next(reader)['score'])
teaching_example.walkthrough: `delimiter='\t'` Therefore, the name and score columns are separated by tabs.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) StringIO contains tab-separated TSV text. 2) When calling ``csv.DictReader``, ``delimiter='\t'`` is passed as a keyword argument. 3) `DictReader` uses tabs as column delimiters. 4) Each row is read as a dictionary with header names as keys.
answer_explanation.why_correct: `delimiter='\t'` This specifies that DictReader should use tabs instead of commas as column delimiters.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: DictReader simply reads lines based on specified delimiters; it does not perform JSON conversion.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Read the role of the setting specified by the keyword.

answer_explanation.takeaway: In TSV, ``delimiter='\t'`` determines **where to split columns**.

lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.title: Separate the stem and suffix of “Path” when reading filenames
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.reading_goal: Accurately read the parts returned by `p.suffix` and `p.stem` from the filename.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.code:
from pathlib import Path
p = Path('report.jsonl')
print(p.stem, p.suffix)
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.question: Which option is closest to the output?
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.explanation: 1) `Path('report.jsonl')` creates a path object. 2) `p.stem` reads the filename portion excluding the final extension. 3) `p.suffix` reads the final extension `.jsonl`. 4) It prints both values.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.project_context: This applies when branching based on the `.json`/`.jsonl` format of card data files or when generating result filenames.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.reading_goal_internal: `p.suffix`와 `p.stem`이 파일명에서 반환하는 부분을 정확히 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: Attribute access uses the `.` followed by a name after an object to access the attributes or functions provided by that object.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Distinguish between the full path and the filename element, and identify which parts are represented by `stem` and `suffix`, respectively.
concept_explanation.key_point: `p.suffix` ``report.jsonl`` returns ``.jsonl``, and ``p.stem`` returns ``report``.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that `suffix` returns only `jsonl` without the period, but `Path.suffix` includes the leading period as well.

teaching_example.code:
from pathlib import Path
p = Path('archive.tar.gz')
print(p.stem, p.suffix)
teaching_example.walkthrough: Since only the final suffix is used as the basis, the stem is `archive.tar`, and the suffix is `.gz`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) `Path('report.jsonl')` creates a path object. 2) `p.stem` reads the filename portion excluding the final extension. 3) `p.suffix` reads the final extension `.jsonl`. 4) It prints both values.
answer_explanation.why_correct: `p.suffix` ``report.jsonl`` returns ``.jsonl``, and ``p.stem`` returns ``report``.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: `Path.suffix` includes the period in the file extension.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Distinguish which parts of the original filename are the stem and which are the suffix.

answer_explanation.takeaway: `stem` "`suffix`" refers to the name excluding the final file extension, while "" refers to the name including the final file extension.

lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.title: Converting Relative Paths to Absolute Paths Using `Path.resolve()`
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.reading_goal: Read the difference between `resolve()` interpreting a relative path as an absolute `Path` and checking whether the file exists.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.code:
from pathlib import Path
path = Path('data/items.json').resolve()
print(path.is_absolute())
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.question: Which of the following is the closest description of the result of `Path('data/items.json').resolve()`?
choices: This is an absolute path relative to the current working directory; the existence of the file must be verified separately.
A dictionary containing the contents of the items.json file
A True value indicating that the file definitely exists
As a result of changing the current working directory
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.answer: This is an absolute path relative to the current working directory; the existence of the file must be verified separately.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.explanation: 1) Create a relative path. 2) `resolve()` calculates the absolute path relative to the current working directory. 3) Store the result. 4) Calculating the absolute path does not guarantee that the file exists.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.project_context: When debugging issues where relative paths vary depending on the execution location, this helps distinguish between the actual interpretation path and whether a file exists.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.reading_goal_internal: `resolve()`가 상대 Path를 현재 작업 폴더 기준의 절대 Path로 바꾸어 반환하며, 이 결과 자체가 파일 존재를 증명하지는 않는다는 점을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `Path.resolve()` is a method call that interprets a Path as an absolute path and returns a new Path result.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: First, check whether the original `Path` is a relative path, and then read how the result of the ``resolve()`` call becomes an absolute path relative to which reference point.
concept_explanation.key_point: With the default `strict=False` setting, paths that do not exist can be interpreted as absolute paths whenever possible; therefore, a successful `resolve` result does not guarantee that the file exists.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: `resolve()` It’s easy to assume that it reads the file contents or even performs the `exists()` check on your behalf.

teaching_example.code:
from pathlib import Path
config = Path('config/app.json').resolve()
print(config.is_absolute())
teaching_example.walkthrough: Calling `resolve` on a relative path returns an absolute path relative to the current working directory.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) ``data/items.json`` is a relative path. 2) ``resolve()`` interprets this as an absolute path relative to the current working directory. 3) The returned path is stored in ``path``. 4) ``is_absolute()`` only checks whether the path is absolute; it does not verify whether the file actually exists.
answer_explanation.why_correct: `resolve()` The key is path resolution, since reading the file’s contents or verifying its existence are separate tasks.

common_wrong_choice.choice: A True value indicating that the file definitely exists
common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Calculating absolute paths and checking for file existence are two separate questions.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: `resolve()` It separates the return type from the role of existence checks, such as ``exists()``.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Read `resolve()` as **"resolves a relative path → returns an absolute path"**, and **check for existence separately**.

lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.title: Reading the `timeout=10` keyword argument
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.reading_goal: `timeout=10`" within an HTTP call is interpreted as a keyword argument that passes a value to a specific parameter.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.code:
import requests

response = requests.get("https://example.com", timeout=10)
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.question: Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of `timeout=10` from the perspective of Python call syntax?
choices: Pass the value 10 as a keyword argument to the `timeout` parameter.
Select the tenth character of the URL.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.answer: Pass the value 10 as a keyword argument to the `timeout` parameter.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.explanation: The call begins with `requests.get(`. The URL is the first positional argument. `timeout=10` is the second argument, where the parameter name is specified directly. This is because the `name=value` format inside the call parentheses is a keyword argument. Common misconception: `requests.get` is called 10 times. There is no loop or `range` statement, and the number 10 is passed to the `timeout` parameter, not used to count the number of calls. Point of Misinterpretation: You must verify which syntactic structure the number is part of. `function(..., name=value)` is a keyword argument that explicitly passes a value to the `name` parameter.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.project_context: This refers to the context of specifying a request timeout to prevent indefinite waiting during Harvest or external API calls.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.reading_goal_internal: HTTP 호출 안의 `timeout=10`을 특정 매개변수에 값을 전달하는 keyword argument로 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: A keyword argument is a syntax where values are passed in the form `parameter_name=value` when calling a function.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Check the function name and the arguments inside the parentheses; in `timeout=10`, read the left side as the parameter name and the right side as the value to be passed.
concept_explanation.key_point: The "10-second timeout" refers to how the requests library works, while the Python syntax focus is on passing keyword arguments.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: `timeout=10` It is easier to read as a variable assignment outside the function. Inside the call parentheses, it is a keyword argument.

teaching_example.code:
def fetch(path, timeout):
    return timeout

seconds = fetch("/health", timeout=5)
print(seconds)
teaching_example.walkthrough: Since the call `timeout=5` passes 5 to the `timeout` parameter, the function returns 5.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: The call begins with `requests.get(`. The URL is the first positional argument. `timeout=10` is the second argument, where the parameter name is specified explicitly.
answer_explanation.why_correct: The `name=value` format inside the call parentheses is because it is a keyword argument.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: There are no loops or `range` statements, and the number 10 is passed to the `timeout` parameter, not as the number of calls.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: You must check which grammatical structure the number belongs to.

answer_explanation.takeaway: `function(..., name=value)` is a keyword argument that explicitly passes a value to the `name` parameter.

lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.title: `for attempt in range(3)` Reading the number of retry attempts
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.reading_goal: Track the maximum number of attempts by considering both the three values produced by `range(3)` and the possibility of `break`.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.question: Looking only at `for attempt in range(3):`, what is the maximum number of times the loop body can be executed?
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.explanation: `range(3)` generates 0, 1, and 2 in sequence. Since the `for` loop enters the `body` for each value, it enters at most three times if `break` is never executed. This is because `range` provides three values, so the maximum number of cycles for the `for` loop is also three. Common source of confusion: The final value “2” in option 2 refers to the value assigned to `attempt` in the third cycle, not the number of iterations. Common Misinterpretation: You must distinguish between the value of the loop variable and the number of iterations. `for x in range(n)` iterates over n values from 0 to n-1 by default, so the body is executed at most n times.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.project_context: This refers to a context where a limited number of retries are allowed for API calls that may temporarily fail.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.reading_goal_internal: `range(3)`이 제공하는 세 값과 `break` 가능성을 함께 읽어 최대 시도 횟수를 추적한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: A `for` statement is a compound statement that retrieves values one by one from an iterable object and executes the loop body.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: For `for variable in iterable:`, first determine which values the iterable produces, then check whether the loop body contains a statement such as `break` that can terminate the loop early.
concept_explanation.key_point: Since `range(3)` returns the values 0, 1, and 2, the body will execute three times unless a `break` is present.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to think that `range(3)` generates 1, 2, and 3. However, when the start value is omitted, `range` starts at 0 and does not include the stop value of 3.

teaching_example.code:
for index in range(2):
    print(index)
teaching_example.walkthrough: `range(2)` produces 0 and 1, so the loop body runs twice and prints 0 and 1.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: `range(3)` generates 0, 1, and 2 in sequence. Since the `for` loop executes the `body` for each value, it enters the `body` up to three times—unless `break` is executed at any point.
answer_explanation.why_correct: Since `range` provides three values, the maximum number of cycles in the `for` loop is also three.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: The final value 2 refers not to the count but to the value passed to `attempt` in the third cycle.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: You must distinguish between the value of an iteration variable and the number of iterations.

answer_explanation.takeaway: `for x in range(n)` Since it iterates over n values from 0 to n-1 by default, the body is executed at most n times.

lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.title: Reading the Authorization Header Dict Assignment
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.reading_goal: Read the assignment flow where a Bearer string created with an f-string becomes a dict value and is stored in the header name.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.question: What is the string printed on the last line?
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.explanation: The token is abc123. The f-string concatenates `Bearer ` with the token value to form `Bearer abc123`. This string is stored in the Authorization key, and the final subscription reads that value. This is because the `Authorization` value in the completed dictionary on the right side of the assignment is exactly `Bearer abc123`. A common source of confusion: `abc123` is the original token value, while the value stored in the headers is a new string created by the f-string with a prefix. Point of confusion: You must consider the order in which the f-string is evaluated before the dict value is stored. The assignment first evaluates all nested expressions on the right-hand side and then stores the resulting value in the left-hand target.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.project_context: This refers to the context of configuring a token as the value of the Authorization header in an external API request.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.reading_goal_internal: f-string으로 만든 Bearer 문자열이 dict value가 되어 headers 이름에 저장되는 대입 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: An assignment is an expression that first evaluates the right-hand side and then stores the result in the left-hand side name or location.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: I interpret this to mean that the value expression inside the dict literal on the right is evaluated first, and the entire resulting dict is then stored in the name on the left.
concept_explanation.key_point: `Authorization` and `Bearer` are HTTP-authentication context; the Python syntax focus is the assignment that evaluates the dict on the right and stores it in `headers`.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: `token` It’s easy to assume that the string itself is stored in `headers` as-is. The actual value is a new string created by the f-string, including the ``Bearer `` prefix.

teaching_example.walkthrough: The key value “xyz” is inserted into an f-string to become “Key xyz,” and that string is stored as the value for the X-Api-Key key.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: `token` is `abc123`. The f-string combines `Bearer ` with the token value to create `Bearer abc123`. This string is stored under the `Authorization` key, and the final subscription reads that value.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the `Authorization` value of the completed `dict` on the right side of the assignment is exactly ``Bearer abc123``.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: `abc123` is the original token value, and the value stored in `headers` is a new string created by prepending an f-string.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: You need to consider the order of operations: the f-string is evaluated first, before the `dict` value is stored.

answer_explanation.takeaway: The `assignment` operator first evaluates all nested expressions on the right side and then stores the resulting value in the target on the left.

lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.title: Logging an ERROR-level message by calling logging.error()
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.reading_goal: When reading the `logging.error(message)` call, distinguish between the target of the call, the message passed, and the log level.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.code:
import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
logging.info("started")
logging.error("failed")
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.question: What is the log level recorded by `logging.error("failed")`?
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.explanation: `logging.error` The call name determines the log level, and ``failed`` is the message to be logged at that level. This is because ``logging.error()`` is a call in the Python logging API that logs a message at the ERROR level. A common source of confusion: `INFO` is the level used by ``logging.info("started")`` on the previous line. Source of Misreading: This occurs when the names of two consecutive `logging` calls are read in the wrong order. When reading `logging` calls, **the call name indicates the level, and the argument inside the parentheses indicates the message**.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.project_context: It distinguishes between INFO, WARNING, and ERROR in server and batch logs and links them to the code to determine issue priority.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.reading_goal_internal: `logging.error(message)` 호출에서 호출 대상과 전달된 메시지, 로그 레벨을 구분해 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: A call in the form of `object.name(...)` locates the name within an object or module and then passes arguments to execute it.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: `logging.error("failed")` This reads as: "`logging`" passes the string "`failed`" to the ``error`` call.
concept_explanation.key_point: `error` is the name of the call that selects the log level, not the message content itself.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: `logging.error()` It is easy to assume that this automatically raises a Python exception. This call simply logs an ERROR-level message.

teaching_example.code:
import logging

logging.warning("disk almost full")
teaching_example.walkthrough: Pass a string to the `warning()` call to record a WARNING-level message.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: `logging.error` The call name determines the log level, and ``failed`` is the message to be logged at that level.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because `logging.error()` is a call in the Python logging API that logs messages at the ERROR level.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: INFO is the level used by the ``logging.info("started")`` in the previous line.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is an example where the names of two consecutive logging calls were read in the wrong order.

answer_explanation.takeaway: A `logging` call is read by distinguishing **the level by the call name and the message by the argument in parentheses**.

lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.title: Saving the checkpoint state by calling `write_text()`
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.reading_goal: Read the sequence in which a JSON string is first created in a nested call and its result is passed as input to `write_text`.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.code:
import json
from pathlib import Path

state = {"last_shard": 42}
Path("checkpoint.json").write_text(json.dumps(state), encoding="utf-8")
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.question: What is the first argument actually passed to `write_text()`?
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.explanation: Python evaluates call arguments first. Therefore, `json.dumps(state)` creates a JSON string, and its return value is passed to `write_text()`. `write_text()` is a method that writes a string, and in this case, it receives the return string from the nested `json.dumps()`. Common source of confusion: The `state` dictionary itself is first passed to `json.dumps()`, and the value received by `write_text()` is the return string from that call. Point of Misinterpretation: This occurs when the order in which the inner result is passed to the outer argument in a nested call is overlooked. Nested calls should be read in the order: **inner call result → outer call argument**.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.project_context: It is linked to the checkpoint file code, which saves the progress made in processing long shards and nodes so that the process can be resumed.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.reading_goal_internal: 중첩 호출에서 JSON 문자열이 먼저 만들어지고 그 결과가 write_text의 입력으로 전달되는 순서를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `Path(...).write_text(text, encoding=...)` is a method call that writes a string to a file.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: It reads that `write_text()` inside the argument is evaluated before the outer `json.dumps(state)` to create a string.
concept_explanation.key_point: Nested calls are read in the order where the result of the inner call becomes an argument for the outer call.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that the `state` dictionary itself is written to the file as-is. First, `json.dumps()` serializes it into a string.

teaching_example.code:
import json
from pathlib import Path

state = {"page": 3}
Path("state.json").write_text(json.dumps(state), encoding="utf-8")
teaching_example.walkthrough: `json.dumps()` converts `state` into a JSON string, and `write_text()` writes that string to a file.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: Python evaluates call arguments first. Therefore, ``json.dumps(state)`` creates a JSON string, and its return value is passed to ``write_text()``.
answer_explanation.why_correct: `write_text()` is a method that writes a string, and here it receives the return string from the inner `json.dumps()`.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: The `dict` is first passed to ``json.dumps()``, and the value received by ``write_text()`` is the return string from that call.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case where, in a nested call, the order in which the inner result is passed to the outer argument is skipped.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Nested calls are read in the order of **inner call result → outer call argument**.

lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.title: Use a filtered list comprehension to exclude completed IDs.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.reading_goal: `not in` Read the sequence that creates a new list containing only the remaining values, excluding completed items where the condition is false.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.code:
all_ids = ["001", "002", "003"]
done = {"001", "002"}
pending = [id for id in all_ids if id not in done]
print(pending)
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.question: What is the list stored in `pending`?

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `x in container` checks whether the value on the left is contained within the container on the right, returning True or False.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: If there are calls on both sides, first obtain the return values of each call, and then perform a ``in`` check using those two actual values.

answer_explanation.why_correct: If you replace both `lower()` results with their actual strings, `rag` is contained in the string on the right, so the result is True.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Although the original text uses “RAG” and “rag” with different capitalization, the difference disappears because both are converted to lowercase using `lower()` before comparison.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Before evaluating `in`, first determine which strings are returned by both method calls.

lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.title: Check whether both the `score` and `evidence` conditions are satisfied using “and”
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.reading_goal: It evaluates the comparison on the left side of “and,” and when that is true, checks the comparison on the right side to determine whether both conditions are true.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.question: What is the result of the entire `and` condition in this candidate?
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.explanation: 1) Since `score` is 0.85, `0.85 >= 0.8` is True. 2) Since the left side is True, the right side is also checked. 3) Since `evidence_count` is 2, `2 >= 2` is also True. 4) Combining the two results with `and` yields True. 5) Therefore, the “promoted” branch is selected.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.project_context: It is connected to an evidence-first validation workflow that promotes KG edge candidates based on multiple criteria, such as scores and the number of supporting examples.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.reading_goal_internal: and의 왼쪽 비교부터 평가하고 참일 때 오른쪽 비교까지 확인해 두 조건이 모두 참인지 판단한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `A and B` is a logical operation where the result is true only if both A and B are truthy.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Evaluate A on the left first; if A is true, evaluate B on the right as well, and combine the two final results.
concept_explanation.key_point: Satisfying only one of the two thresholds does not make the entire condition true. **Both must be true.**
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to conclude that the entire `if` statement is true the moment the `score` condition is true. However, you must also check the `evidence` condition to the right of `and`.

teaching_example.code:

evidence = 1
ready = score >= 0.8 and evidence >= 2
print(ready)
teaching_example.walkthrough: Although the left side is True, the `evidence` condition is False, so the overall `and` result is False.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) Since `score` is 0.85, `0.85 >= 0.8` is True. 2) Since the left side is True, the right side is also checked. 3) Since `evidence_count` is 2, `2 >= 2` is also True. 4) Combining the two results with `and` yields True. 5) Therefore, the “promoted” branch is selected.
answer_explanation.why_correct: Since both conditional expressions are True, the result of `and` is also True.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Since the second condition is `>= 2` rather than `> 2`, the condition is satisfied even if evidence_count is exactly 2.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Calculate each comparison operator accurately, then combine them with “and” at the end.

answer_explanation.takeaway: `and` is read in the following order: **evaluate the left-hand condition → evaluate the right-hand condition if necessary → combine the two results**.

lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.title: Get the number of occurrences of "KEEP" using the `labels.count('KEEP')` call
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.reading_goal: Read the flow where calling the `count` method on a list returns the number of occurrences of the specified value as an integer, and that value is used in the next comparison.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.question: What value does the `labels.count("KEEP")` call itself return?

lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.reading_goal_internal: 리스트의 count 메서드 호출이 지정한 값의 등장 횟수를 정수로 반환하고 그 값이 다음 비교에 사용되는 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `list.count(value)` is a method call that counts how many times an item equal to `value` appears in a list and returns an integer.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Check the actual items in the list of call targets, count the number of items—such as the value inside the parentheses—and read that number as the result of the call.
concept_explanation.key_point: The result of a `count` call is not the `KEEP` string itself or `True`/`False`, but rather the **integer count of occurrences**.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) Checking the items in `labels` reveals KEEP, REJECT, and KEEP. 2) `count('KEEP')` counts the number of items matching "KEEP." 3) The first and third items match, for a total of 2. 4) Therefore, the return value of the method call itself is the integer 2. 5) The subsequent code compares this 2 to `>= 2`, resulting in True.
answer_explanation.why_correct: Since the string "KEEP" appears exactly twice, the return value of the `count` call is `2`.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: `True` is the result of the next step, which compares the 2 returned by `count` with `>= 2`.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Read the result of the method call separately from the result of the outer comparison expression that uses that result.

answer_explanation.takeaway: If a method call appears within an expression, **the return value of the call is evaluated first and then used in the outer operation**.

lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.title: Generate 1 value for each DONE shard using a generator expression
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.reading_goal: Read the execution sequence where the generator expression iterates through the statuses and generates a 1 only for the iterations marked as DONE, passing the result to the outer sum() function.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.code:

done = sum(1 for status in statuses if status == "DONE")
print(done)
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.question: How many times is the number `sum()`, which this generator expression passes to `1`, generated in total?
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.explanation: 1) The first status is DONE, so the condition is True, and it generates 1. 2) The second is also DONE, so it generates 1 again. 3) FAILED and PENDING have False conditions, so they do not generate any values. 4) Therefore, the generator yields two values: 1 and 1. 5) The outer `sum()` function adds these together to produce 2.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.project_context: It connects to code that aggregates the number of completed shards in large-scale LLM and data processing tasks to determine the scope of re-execution and the remaining work.
lessons/python_deep_expansion_v4.json.reading_goal_internal: generator expression이 statuses를 순회하면서 DONE인 회차에만 1을 만들어 바깥 sum()에 전달하는 실행 순서를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: A generator expression, such as `(expression for variable in iterable if condition)`, does not generate a list of values all at once, but instead generates the necessary values sequentially as they are needed.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: First, retrieve one current value from the iteration target, and if there is an if condition, check the condition. Only in iterations where the condition is true is the value of the first expression generated.
concept_explanation.key_point: The `1 for ... if ...` in this card does not output the status string as-is, but rather generates **one number 1 for each item marked as DONE**.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to assume that a value of 1 is created four times because of all the entries in `statuses`. However, a value is generated only for the iterations that pass the subsequent `if` condition.

teaching_example.code:
states = ["OK", "FAIL", "OK"]
count = sum(1 for state in states if state == "OK")
print(count)
teaching_example.walkthrough: Since 1 is generated only in the first and third iterations (which are OK), sum() returns 2.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) The first status is DONE, so the condition is True, and it generates 1. 2) The second is also DONE, so it generates 1 again. 3) FAILED and PENDING have False conditions, so they do not generate any values. 4) Therefore, the generator yields two values: 1 and 1. 5) The outer `sum()` function adds these together to produce 2.
answer_explanation.why_correct: Since the "DONE" state occurs only twice, and 1 is returned only in the run that passes the generator’s if condition, the correct answer is 2.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Although there are four items in `statuses`, the `FAILED` and `PENDING` entries do not generate the preceding `1` because the `if` condition is False.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Distinguish between the number of iterations and the number of times actual values are generated to verify the result of the `if` statement for each iteration.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Read a generator expression with a condition as **iterate → check condition → produce a value only for passing iterations**.

lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.title: Reading the Dog class and method overrides with a base class
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.reading_goal: Read the code to determine which implementation is selected when a method with the same name in a subclass is called in conjunction with the base class notation.
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.question: What is the direct reason that `pet.speak()` returns `bark`?
choices: Since `Animal` does not have a `speak()` method,
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.explanation: `Dog(Animal)` establishes an inheritance relationship, and the Dog class redefines `speak()`. Since `pet` is a Dog instance, `pet.speak()` uses Dog’s method to return `bark`. This is because when a subclass overrides a method with the same name as its parent, that implementation is selected when the subclass instance is called. A common source of confusion: Since Animal does not have a `speak()` method, the subclass also has `speak()` and returns `sound`. Point of Misinterpretation: This occurs when the body of the parent class is not examined. Inheritance code follows this sequence: **check the base class → check for overriding → select the implementation that matches the instance type**.
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.project_context: This ties into understanding the differences in behavior between base classes and subclasses in class-based app and server code, as well as in libraries.
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.reading_goal_internal: base class 표기와 subclass 내부의 같은 이름 메서드를 연결해 호출 시 어떤 구현이 선택되는지 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `class Child(Base):` This is a class definition where ``Child`` inherits from ``Base``.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: After checking the base class in parentheses, see if a method with the same name is redefined in the subclass body.
concept_explanation.key_point: Although Dog inherits from Animal, it directly redefines `speak()`, so Dog instances use Dog’s implementation.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that the parent method is always executed because it’s inherited. However, if a subclass overrides the same method, its implementation takes precedence.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Although `Bike` inherits from `Vehicle`, it overrides `kind()`, so `bike` is printed.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: `Dog(Animal)` It establishes an inheritance relationship, and the Dog class redefines ``speak()``. Since ``pet`` is a Dog instance, ``pet.speak()`` uses Dog’s methods to return ``bark``.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because when a subclass overrides a method with the same name as its parent, that implementation is selected when the subclass instance is called.

common_wrong_choice.choice: Since `Animal` does not have a `speak()` method,
common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: The `Animal` class also has a ``speak()`` method and returns a ``sound``.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case where the body of the parent class has not been checked.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Inheritance code is read as **check the base class → check if it is overridden → select the implementation that matches the instance type**.

lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.title: Understanding the structure where `@property` is applied to the method immediately below it
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.reading_goal: Read about the relationship between function decorators and decorated methods, and understand why the calculated value is accessed without parentheses.
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.question: `cfg.is_fast` Why does the calculation produce a result even when read without parentheses?
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.explanation: `@property` turns the `is_fast` method immediately below it into a property. Therefore, accessing the `cfg.is_fast` property triggers the execution of the internal function, and since the current mode is `fast`, it returns `True`. This is because the property decorator allows a method to be used as a descriptor-based property. Common misconception: Since `print` automatically calls the method, it simply outputs the passed value and does not perform property conversion. Point of Misinterpretation: This is a case where the role of the decorator was mistakenly attributed to `print`. Note that a decorator **is applied to the definition immediately below it and can subsequently change how it is used**.
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.project_context: This relates to reading code that exposes values calculated from configuration objects or model objects as if they were regular attributes.
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.reading_goal_internal: function decorator와 decorated method의 관계를 읽고 호출 괄호 없이 계산된 값을 접근하는 이유를 이해한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: A function decorator is a syntax where `@name` is written immediately above a function definition to wrap or transform that definition with different behavior.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Treat the decorator line and the `def` immediately below it as a pair, and observe how their usage changes afterward.
concept_explanation.key_point: `@property` `is_fast`, when applied, reads values from an instance in the form of attribute access, such as ``cfg.is_fast``.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that `cfg.is_fast()` must be called. The `property` executes an internal getter when the attribute is accessed.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Since `status` is a property, reading it as `user.status` will output `on`, which is the result of an internal calculation.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: `@property` This creates the ``is_fast`` method as a property. Therefore, accessing the attribute ``cfg.is_fast`` triggers the execution of the internal function, and since the current mode is `fast`, it returns `True`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because a property decorator allows methods to be accessed as descriptor-based attributes.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: `print` simply outputs the values passed to it; it does not perform property conversion.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is an example where the role of a decorator was mistakenly described as that of `print`.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Read that a **decorator is applied to the definition immediately below it and can be used differently afterward**.

lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.title: Read the execution flow where a function decorator applies a wrapper.
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.reading_goal: A decorator returns a wrapper when defining a function and tracks the flow so that subsequent calls begin with the wrapper.
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.question: In the final `run()` call, what is printed before `run`?
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.explanation: `@log_call` When applied, ``log_call`` returns ``wrapper``. Subsequent calls to ``run()`` execute the `wrapper`, which first outputs ``before`` and then calls the original `run`. This is because the function returned by the decorator is bound to the name of the decorated function. A common source of confusion: The original `run` is called later within the `wrapper` at ``fn()``. Point of Misinterpretation: This occurs when you overlook the fact that the target of the call is the wrapper after the decorator has been applied. The wrapper decorator follows this sequence: **wrapping at definition → wrapper execution begins upon call → original function call**.
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.project_context: This ties into the fundamentals of reading code from decorator-based libraries, such as FastAPI routes, click commands, and testing tools.
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.reading_goal_internal: decorator가 함수 정의 시 wrapper를 반환하고 이후 호출이 wrapper부터 시작되는 흐름을 추적한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `@decorator` is a syntax that passes the function definition immediately below it to the decorator, thereby associating the transformed function object with that name.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: First, look at what the decorator function returns, and then track which function actually starts when the decorated function is called.
concept_explanation.key_point: `log_call` Since it returns ``wrapper``, the subsequent ``run()`` begins with the wrapper behavior.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to think that a decorator is redefined every time `run()` is called. However, the decorator is applied when the function is defined, and when the function is called, the wrapped function is executed.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Since the `decorator` returns `wrapped`, when it is called, `trace` is printed first, followed by the original `save` function.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: `@log_call` When applied, ``log_call`` returns ``wrapper``. Subsequently, the call to ``run()`` executes the wrapper, which first prints ``before`` and then calls the original `run`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the function returned by the decorator is associated with the name of the decorated function.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Originally, `run` is called later within the `fn()` function in the wrapper.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is an instance where the learner failed to recognize that the target of the call is `wrapper` after the decorator was applied.

answer_explanation.takeaway: A wrapper decorator is interpreted in the following order: **wrapping upon definition → wrapper execution upon call → call to the original function**.

lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.title: Understanding the Execution Order of `with` in a Custom Context Manager
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.reading_goal: Track the order in which the `with` statement executes the context manager’s entry, body, and exit operations.
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.question: Which of the following is closest to the order of output?
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.explanation: When entering `with Timer():`, `__enter__()` runs first and prints `start`. The body then prints `work`, and when leaving the block, `__exit__()` prints `end`. This is because the context-manager protocol calls entry and exit hooks before and after the `with` block. Common wrong answer: `work → start → end`. Context entry happens before the body. Misreading point: This happens when the entry step of the `with` statement is skipped. Read `with` in the order **enter → body → exit**.
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.project_context: It relates to code that safely handles resources—such as files, database connections, locks, and sessions—which require cleanup before and after use.
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.reading_goal_internal: with statement가 context manager 진입·본문·종료 동작을 어떤 순서로 실행하는지 추적한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `with manager:` is a statement that executes its body between the entry and exit of a context manager.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Execute the actions performed upon entry, followed by the indented body, and then the actions performed upon block exit.
concept_explanation.key_point: In a custom context manager, ``__enter__`` typically handles the behavior at the start, and ``__exit__`` handles the behavior at the end.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that the body is executed first and `__enter__` comes later. However, the entry handling occurs before the body.

teaching_example.walkthrough: It is printed in the following order: “open” at the entry point, “use” in the body, and “close” at the exit point.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: When entering `with Timer():`, `__enter__()` runs first and prints “start.” Next, the main body prints “work,” and upon exiting, `__exit__()` prints “end.”
answer_explanation.why_correct: Because the context-manager protocol calls entry and exit hooks before and after the `with` block.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Context initialization occurs before the main text.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case where the entry point of the `with` statement was skipped.

answer_explanation.takeaway: "with" is read in the order **enter → body → exit**.

lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.title: Tracking from `asyncio.run(main())` to the `await` result
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.reading_goal: Track the asynchronous execution flow starting from `asyncio.run` through the `await` in `main` to the `fetch` return.
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.code:
import asyncio

async def fetch():
    return "data"

async def main():
    result = await fetch()
    print(result)

asyncio.run(main())
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.question: What is the output?
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.explanation: The `main` coroutine is executed, and since the result of ``await fetch()`` is ``data``, `result` becomes `data`. The `print` statement then outputs that value because the actual output target is `result`, which stores the return value of `fetch`. A common source of confusion: “main” is just the name of a function; it is not the value that `print` outputs. Common Misinterpretation: This occurs when the name of the called function is confused with the data flow inside the function. For async output, trace the flow as **entry call → await → return value → usage location**.
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.project_context: It relates to reading the entry point and `await` flow in code that calls asynchronous API servers, crawlers, and agent tools.
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.reading_goal_internal: asyncio.run에서 시작해 main의 await와 fetch return까지 이어지는 비동기 실행 흐름을 추적한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `asyncio.run(coro)` is a top-level asyncio helper function call used to execute a coroutine.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: It identifies which async function created the coroutine passed in parentheses and follows it all the way to the inner `await`.
concept_explanation.key_point: The output value is determined not by the name of `asyncio.run` itself, but by the actual return value of the `fetch` function awaited within `main`.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to assume that async functions execute automatically simply by being defined.

teaching_example.code:
import asyncio

async def value():
    return 3

async def main():
    result = await value()
    print(result)

asyncio.run(main())
teaching_example.walkthrough: `value` returns 3, and `main` awaits this value and then prints 3.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: Since the `main` coroutine is executed and the result of `await fetch()` is `data`, `result` becomes `data`. The `print` statement then outputs that value.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the actual output destination is `result`, which stores the return value of `fetch`.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: `main` is only a function name; it is not the value printed by `print`.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is an example of confusion between the name of the called object and the data flow within the function.

answer_explanation.takeaway: We also trace async output using the sequence **entry call → await → return value → usage location**.

lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.title: Waiting for an asynchronous HTTP response with `await client.get()`
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.reading_goal: Read the structure where the `await` statement is used to receive the `response` object upon completion of the `async HTTP client` method.
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.question: What is `await client.get(...)` waiting for?
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.explanation: `client.get` creates an async task representing an HTTP request, and `await` waits until that task completes and returns a `Response` object. This is because the result of an async HTTP GET is a `Response`. A common source of confusion: CSS rendering code does not contain CSS processing logic. Point of Misinterpretation: This occurs when the role of the HTTP client is confused with UI rendering. Asynchronous HTTP code should be read as **request call → await → response object**.
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.project_context: This relates to the basic flow of handling bulk API calls or internal asynchronous requests in FastAPI.
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.reading_goal_internal: async HTTP client method의 완료 결과를 await해 response 객체를 받는 구조를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `await expression` is an expression that waits for an awaitable operation to complete and then receives its result.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Check what the right-hand side of the `await` call does and where the return value is stored after it completes.
concept_explanation.key_point: In an async get call from an HTTP client, you must await until the network I/O is complete and the response is received.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to think `await` waits for the URL string itself. It waits for the asynchronous work created by the `get` call.

teaching_example.walkthrough: When the async result of `get` completes, it returns a `response` dictionary and returns status code 201.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: `client.get` creates an async task representing an HTTP request, and `await` waits until that task completes and returns a `Response` object.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the result of an async HTTP GET is a `response`.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: The code does not contain any CSS processing logic.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is an example of confusing the role of an HTTP client with UI rendering.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Asynchronous HTTP code follows the pattern: **request call → await → response object**.

lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.title: Reading the `body.text` attribute of the requested model instance
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.reading_goal: Understand the structure in which the model instance reads `field` as an instance attribute representing the request body.
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.question: What value is stored in `question`?
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.explanation: `Question("RAG란?")` When the object is created, a string is stored in ``self.text``. Later, ``body.text`` reads that attribute and assigns it to ``question``, because instance attribute access returns the value of the attribute stored in that object. Common source of confusion: “text`text`” is the attribute name, while the actual stored value is “`RAG란?`.” Point of misinterpretation: This occurs when the attribute name and the attribute value are confused. The model object interprets the process as **check instance → check attribute name → read stored value**.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `object.name` is an expression that reads an attribute associated with an instance.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Check what the object on the left is, and find the value of the attribute on the right stored in that instance.
concept_explanation.key_point: In the context of FastAPI/Pydantic, the request body is prepared as a model instance, and fields can be read as `body.text`. The sample code fixes this as a local object to verify only Python’s native behavior.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: `body.text` It’s easy to mistake this for a dict key lookup. However, since it uses dot notation rather than square brackets, it’s attribute access.

teaching_example.walkthrough: The `content` attribute of the `Message` instance’s body is read, and `hello` is stored in `value`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: `Question("RAG란?")` When generated, the string is stored in ``self.text``. Subsequently, ``body.text`` reads that attribute and assigns it to ``question``.
answer_explanation.why_correct: Because instance attribute access returns the attribute value stored on that object.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: `text` is the attribute name, and the actual stored value is `RAG란?`.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is an instance where the attribute name and attribute value were confused.

answer_explanation.takeaway: The model interprets the object as **check instance → check attribute name → read stored value**.

lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.title: Reading the `status_code` keyword argument of the `route` decorator
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.reading_goal: Within a decorator call, read the keyword argument names and values separately and associate them with the route response settings.
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.question: In `status_code=200`, what value is `200` passed as?
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.explanation: `status_code=200` is a keyword argument inside the `app.get()` call, so 200 is the setting value passed under the name `status_code`. In Python call syntax, `name=value` passes a value to the parameter with that name. A tempting wrong answer is `DB id`, but this code configures a route decorator rather than reading a database ID. Read `name=value` inside a call as a **setting name and supplied value pair**.
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.project_context: It is linked to a code review that configures the API server response status in the route declaration and tracks client errors.
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.reading_goal_internal: decorator 호출 안에서 keyword argument 이름과 값을 분리해 읽고 route 응답 설정과 연결한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `name=value` Values passed to a call in this format are keyword arguments.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Check what the name on the left refers to and read the actual value on the right.
concept_explanation.key_point: `status_code=200` is a route configuration value passed to the `app.get()` call, not an iteration count or a DB ID.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to mistake 200 for the function’s return value. The 200 at this location is the value of an argument passed to the call.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Since `code=202` is a named keyword argument, the value 202 is passed to the `code` parameter.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: `status_code=200``app.get()` is a keyword argument within the `` call. Therefore, 200 is a configuration value passed under the name ``status_code``.
answer_explanation.why_correct: In Python call syntax, `name=value` is a keyword argument that passes a value to the corresponding parameter name.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: This is not code that reads a DB ID; it is a route decorator configuration.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case where the calling context surrounding the number 200 was not checked.

answer_explanation.takeaway: The ``name=value`` function reads **configuration names and their corresponding values as pairs**.

lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.title: Reading the list literal passed to CORS `allow_origins`

from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware

answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the number of items in a list literal is determined by the number of values actually written inside the square brackets.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Instead of a wildcard string `*`, which represents all sources, a single specific URL is listed.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case of considering only the CORS concept without checking the actual list values.

lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.title: Reading the call to the SQLite conn.commit() method
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.reading_goal: Read that calling the `commit` method of the `connection` object after an `INSERT` operation is the step that finalizes transaction changes.
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.code:
import sqlite3

conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
conn.execute("CREATE TABLE notes(title TEXT, body TEXT)")
conn.execute(
    "INSERT INTO notes(title, body) VALUES (?, ?)",
    ("memo", "hello"),
)
conn.commit()
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.question: `conn.commit()` Which of the following best describes its role?
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.explanation: After an INSERT operation makes changes to the connection, `conn.commit()` is called. Commit finalizes the changes made by that transaction. This is because the commit method of a DB connection is the step that permanently reflects the changes from the pending transaction. Common Confusion: This is a call to a DB connection method, not a file I/O function for reading a file. Point of Misinterpretation: This occurs when the receiver `conn` and the preceding SQL context are not verified. To understand the save flow, you must read the DB code all the way through **executing changes → checking whether to commit**.
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.project_context: It is linked to the transaction flow of the server code that stores notes, progress, and curation results in the database.
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.reading_goal_internal: INSERT 실행 이후 connection 객체의 commit 메서드 호출이 transaction 변경을 확정하는 단계임을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `object.method()` calls a method belonging to a specific object.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Check the object and method names to the left of the dot, and see how that call handles the state created by the preceding code.
concept_explanation.key_point: `conn.commit()` is not a call that creates a new INSERT, but rather a step that commits database changes that have already been made.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: `execute()` Since it’s there, it’s easy to think of a commit as a simple query. Here, however, it’s the process of finalizing an INSERT change.

teaching_example.walkthrough: The receiver is `session`, and the called method is `commit`. The return value is `saved`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: After INSERT makes changes to the connection, `conn.commit()` is called. commit finalizes the changes made by that transaction.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the `commit` method of a database connection is the step that permanently applies changes made by a pending transaction.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: This is a call to a database connection method, not a file I/O function.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case where the receiver `conn` and the preceding SQL context were not checked.

answer_explanation.takeaway: To understand the save flow, you must read the DB code up to the point of **executing the changes → checking whether to commit**.

lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.title: Read the parameter-tuple argument of SQL `execute()`.
lessons/python_advanced_expansion_v5.jso.reading_goal: Note that the second positional argument of the `execute` call is a tuple of values corresponding to SQL placeholders.

source_name = "manual"
