lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.title: Creating a dependency snapshot text using `join()`
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.reading_goal: Read the process by which the string method `join()` creates a single text by inserting line breaks between each package specification in the sequence.
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.question: What is the content of `requirements_text`?
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.explanation: The list order is `fastapi, uvicorn`, and the separator is a line break. Therefore, a single line break is inserted between the two strings. This is because `join()` concatenates the sequence items using the separator to return a single string. Common mistake: `fastapi==0.115.0uvicorn==0.30.6`. Since the separator is `\n` rather than an empty string, a line break is inserted between the two items. Point of Misinterpretation: This occurs when the `separator`—the object used to call `join()`—is not checked. `separator.join(items)` is interpreted as **inserting `separator` between the items to form a single string**.
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.project_context: This connects to the process of serializing the list of package versions in the current environment into a reproducible requirements format.
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.reading_goal_internal: 문자열 메서드 `join()`이 sequence의 각 패키지 사양 사이에 줄바꿈을 넣어 하나의 requirements 텍스트를 만드는 과정을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `separator.join(strings)` is a method call that combines multiple strings into a single string by inserting a separator between them.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: First, check what the separator is, and then read it as inserting that separator between each list item in order.
concept_explanation.key_point: The meaning of “snapshot” in `pip freeze` is specific to the domain context, and the key aspect of Python syntax is the `join()` call, which concatenates lists into a single string.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to think newlines are automatically added before the first and after the last item. `join()` inserts the separator only **between** items.

teaching_example.code:
installed = ["numpy==2.0.1", "pandas==2.2.2"]
text = "\n".join(installed)
teaching_example.walkthrough: One newline appears between the two items, producing a two-line string.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: The list order is `fastapi`, then `uvicorn`, and the separator is a newline. Therefore, one newline appears between the two strings.
answer_explanation.why_correct: `join()` This is because it concatenates the sequence items using a separator to return a single string.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Since `separator` is not an empty string but ``\n``, a line break is inserted between the two items.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case of not checking the separator object on which `join` is called.

answer_explanation.takeaway: `separator.join(items)` is read as **"joins the items with the separator to form a single string"**.

lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.title: Separating Exact Version Pins Using Unpacking Substitution
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.reading_goal: Read the example of the `version pin` to understand the process of unpacking the two values resulting from splitting a string into the first two variables in the order they appear.
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.question: What is the string stored in `version` after the assignment?
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.explanation: `spec.split("==", 1)` produces `["fastapi", "0.115.0"]`. Since unpacking assignment places the two values into the left-hand variables in order, `version` is the second string. This is because unpacking assignment maps the positions of the sequence’s values to the left-hand targets on a 1:1 basis. Commonly Misunderstood Answer: `fastapi` is the first value in the split result, so it is assigned to the first variable, `name`. Point of Misinterpretation: This occurs when the order of the left-hand variables and right-hand values is reversed. Unpacking **first creates the right-hand result and then stores it in the left-hand variables in order of position**.
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.project_context: It connects to code that verifies by isolating the exact package names and versions specified in the requirements.
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.reading_goal_internal: 문자열 split 결과의 두 값을 왼쪽 두 변수에 위치 순서대로 언패킹하는 과정을 version pin 예제로 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `a, b = sequence` is an unpacking assignment that stores the values from the sequence on the right into the variables on the left in order.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: First, check what sequence the expression on the right creates, then map the first value to the first variable and the second value to the second variable.
concept_explanation.key_point: The dependency meaning of `==` is coverage, and the key Python syntax point is unpacking the two values produced by `split` into `name, version`.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to assume that Python automatically matches values based on the meaning of variable names. Unpacking, however, corresponds to positional order.

teaching_example.code:
spec = "numpy==2.0.1"
name, version = spec.split("==", 1)
teaching_example.walkthrough: In the result of `split`, the first value of `["numpy", "2.0.1"]` is assigned to `name`, and the second value is assigned to `version`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: `spec.split("==", 1)` creates `["fastapi", "0.115.0"]`. Unpacking assignment places the two values into the two left-hand variables in order, so `version` is the second string.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because "unpacking assignment" establishes a one-to-one correspondence between the positions of the sequence values and the left-hand side of the assignment.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: `fastapi` is the first value in the `split` result, so it is assigned to the first variable, `name`.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is an example where the order of the left-hand side variable and the right-hand side value has been reversed.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Unpacking **first generates the result on the right, then stores it in the variables on the left in the order they appear**.

lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.title: Reading the list of dependencies in project metadata
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.reading_goal: Read the value of the `dependencies` key from the Python dictionary that structures the dependencies of `pyproject`.
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.question: `dependencies` Which of the following is the closest equivalent to the role of [ ]?
choices: List of packages required to run the project
List of Items to Clear from Cache
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.answer: List of packages required to run the project
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.explanation: The value of the `dependencies` key is ``['fastapi', 'uvicorn']``, and both values are Python package names. This is because this field is configured to represent the project’s dependency declarations. A common source of confusion: Git branch list. Git branches and Python package metadata are separate concepts. Point of misinterpretation: This occurs when the meaning of a field in project metadata is confused with Git settings. Packaging metadata should be interpreted as **field name → value type → installation/execution meaning**.
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.project_context: It relates to the metadata required when organizing a project as an installable Python package rather than a simple collection of scripts.
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.reading_goal_internal: pyproject의 dependency 의미를 구조화한 Python dict에서 dependencies key의 value를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `mapping[key]` is a subscription that reads the value associated with a key in a dictionary.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Check which metadata field the current lookup key refers to, then inspect the type and items of the value.
concept_explanation.key_point: You can declare the packages required to install and run the project in the `dependencies` section of `pyproject.toml`.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to think of "dependencies" as a list of Git branches. It is a list of package dependencies in Python packaging.

teaching_example.code:
project = {"name": "demo", "dependencies": ["requests"]}
packages = project["dependencies"]
teaching_example.walkthrough: The `requests` list, which is the value of the `dependencies` key, is stored in `packages`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: The value of the `dependencies` key is `['fastapi', 'uvicorn']`, and both values are Python package names.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because this field is configured to represent project dependency declarations.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Git branches and Python package metadata are separate concepts.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is an instance where the meaning of a field in project metadata was confused with Git settings.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Read packaging metadata as **field name → value type → installation/execution meaning**.

lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.title: Check `sys.executable` when a `ModuleNotFoundError` occurs.
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.reading_goal: This means that `sys.executable` represents the current execution path of the Python interpreter.
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.question: What does the `sys.executable` value itself represent?
choices: The path to the interpreter executable currently running the Python process
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.answer: The path to the interpreter executable currently running the Python process
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.explanation: 1) `sys` is a module that provides information about the current Python execution environment. 2) Read the `executable` attribute after the dot. 3) This value is the path to the Python interpreter executable file that is actually running the current process. This is because `sys.executable` is path information that identifies the currently running interpreter, not a package installation command. Commonly Confused Incorrect Answer: List of installable packages. Package lists are handled by package management tools like pip and are not what the `sys.executable` attribute returns. Point of Misinterpretation: This occurs when users confuse environment information identifying the current interpreter with package management functionality. `sys.executable` is a value that identifies **which executable file is currently running Python**.
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.project_context: This ties into the workflow for checking for interpreter/venv mismatches when the FastAPI search API or packages installed in the LoRA environment cannot be found.
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.reading_goal_internal: sys 모듈의 executable attribute가 현재 실행 interpreter 경로를 제공한다는 의미를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `sys.executable` is a module attribute access that reads the `executable` attribute of an object in the `sys` module.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Distinguish between the module on the left and the attribute on the right.
concept_explanation.key_point: If an import fails after installing a package, this is useful for verifying whether the Python environment currently in use is the same as the one in which the package was installed.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that this lists all installed Python versions. It actually points to the path of the interpreter that is currently running the process.

teaching_example.code:
import os
separator = os.sep
teaching_example.walkthrough: This is similar to reading the value of the `sep` attribute in the `os` module.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) `sys` is a module that provides information about the current Python execution environment. 2) Read the `executable` attribute after the dot. 3) This value is the path to the Python interpreter executable file that is currently running the process.
answer_explanation.why_correct: `sys.executable` This is because it is not a package installation command, but rather path information that identifies the currently running interpreter.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: The list of packages is handled by package management tools such as pip and is not the return value of the `sys.executable` attribute.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is an instance where the user has confused the environment information that identifies the current interpreter with package management functionality.

answer_explanation.takeaway: `sys.executable` is a value that identifies **which executable file the currently running Python instance is**.

lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.title: Using Raw String Literals in the Windows Path
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.reading_goal: Read how string literals prefixed with `r` represent Windows backslash paths.
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.code:
from pathlib import Path

root = Path(r"D:\projects\python-reading-trainer")
lesson_dir = root / "data" / "lessons"
folder_name = lesson_dir.name
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.question: Which of the following best describes the meaning of the `r` prefix in a string?
choices: Treats the string as a raw string
It refers to a Git remote.
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.answer: Treats the string as a raw string
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.explanation: `r` The prefix is added to `D:\projects\...`, turning it into a raw string literal, which is then passed to the Path constructor. This is because Python’s raw string prefix makes it easy to represent strings that include backslashes. A common source of confusion: the string prefix “r” has nothing to do with the concept of a Git remote. Point of Misinterpretation: This occurs when the Python literal prefix is confused with terminology from other tools. Windows paths are interpreted as **string literal form → raw prefix → Path conversion**.
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.project_context: This relates to methods for minimizing backslash escape errors when handling various Windows project paths under `D:\projects` in Python.
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.reading_goal_internal: r prefix가 붙은 string literal이 Windows backslash 경로를 표현하는 방식을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `r"..."` is a raw string literal that simplifies the representation of string content by eliminating backslash escape sequences.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: The `r` prefix before a string and the entire path inside the quotes are treated as a single value.
concept_explanation.key_point: Since Windows paths contain many backslashes, using a raw string can help reduce the likelihood of confusion with escapes such as ``\n`` and ``\t``.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to assume that a raw string allows a single backslash at the end without any restrictions. However, raw strings do have syntactic constraints.

teaching_example.code:
from pathlib import Path
folder = Path(r"C:\data\new")
teaching_example.walkthrough: The backslashes in the path string are represented as raw strings and passed to `Path`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: The `r` prefix turns `D:\projects\...` into a raw string literal, which is then passed to the `Path` constructor.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because Python’s raw string prefix makes it easy to represent strings that contain backslashes.

common_wrong_choice.choice: It refers to a Git remote.
common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: The string prefix “r” is unrelated to the concept of a Git remote.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case where terminology from another tool was confused with Python literal prefixes.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Windows paths are read as **string literal → raw prefix → Path conversion**.

lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.title: Understanding the significance of setting the execution policy scope to CurrentUser
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.reading_goal: Read the state change where the `scope` key changes to `CurrentUser` in a Python mapping that structures the meanings of PowerShell options.
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.question: Which of the following matches the value and meaning of `current_scope`?
choices: CurrentUser refers to the current user scope.
"Process" refers only to the current process.
"CurrentFolder" refers only to the current folder.
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.answer: CurrentUser refers to the current user scope.
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.explanation: The `subscription assignment` replaces the `scope` value of the `policy` with `CurrentUser`. This is because the string on the right is saved directly as the new setting value. A common mistake that can be confusing: `Process`, which refers only to the current process; `Process` is the previous value before the assignment. Point of misinterpretation: cases where the state after the `assignment` is not reflected. Non-Python settings can also be read by structuring them as **setting key → new value → scope meaning**.
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.project_context: This is related to checking the PowerShell execution policy scope when the venv Activate.ps1 script fails to run on a new Windows PC.
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.reading_goal_internal: PowerShell 옵션 의미를 구조화한 Python mapping에서 scope key가 CurrentUser로 바뀌는 상태 변화를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `mapping[key] = value` is a subscription assignment that stores a new value under a specific key.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Check what the left key represents and what the new value on the right is.
concept_explanation.key_point: In PowerShell, ``-Scope CurrentUser`` means that the execution policy change applies only to the current user.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that `CurrentUser` refers only to the current folder. This setting pertains to the scope of the user account.

teaching_example.code:
settings = {"scope": "Process"}
settings["scope"] = "CurrentUser"
teaching_example.walkthrough: The scope key value changes from `Process` to `CurrentUser`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: The `subscription assignment` replaces the `scope` value of the `policy` with `CurrentUser`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the string on the right is saved directly as the new setting value.

common_wrong_choice.choice: "Process" refers only to the current process.
common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: `Process` refers to the value prior to assignment.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case where the state after the `assignment` has not been reflected.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Non-Python settings can also be structured and read as **setting key → new value → scope**.

lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.title: Reading the `parent` attribute of the `Path` returned by `resolve()`
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.reading_goal: First, determine the Path created on the left and the result of the resolve() call, then recognize that the final `.parent` is an attribute access that returns the parent path of that Path object.
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.code:
from pathlib import Path

script_file = Path("/workspace/python-reading-trainer/run_local.py")
project_root = script_file.resolve().parent
print(project_root.name)
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.question: Given the final `.parent` in the target expression, what is the value of `project_root.name`?
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.explanation: 1) The file path is `/workspace/python-reading-trainer/run_local.py`. 2) `.parent` returns the `Path` one level above the final filename. 3) The name of that path is `python-reading-trainer`.
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.project_context: It connects to a portable execution structure that locates the project folder based on the script’s location, rather than hard-coding the user-specific D: drive path.
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.reading_goal_internal: 왼쪽의 Path 생성과 resolve() 호출 결과를 먼저 구한 뒤 마지막 `.parent`가 그 Path 객체의 상위 경로를 반환하는 속성 접근임을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `object.attribute` is an expression that reads the value of an attribute held by an object.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: When dot operations occur consecutively, the result is calculated from left to right, and the final `.parent` is applied to the immediately preceding Path object.
concept_explanation.key_point: `parent` is not a method call but a Path instance attribute without parentheses.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: `.parent()` It’s easy to think of it as a function call or assume that it automatically changes the current working directory.

teaching_example.code:
from pathlib import Path
path = Path("/project/data/cards.json")
folder = path.parent
print(folder.name)
teaching_example.walkthrough: The parent directory of `cards.json` is the `data` folder, and its name is `data`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) The file path is `/workspace/python-reading-trainer/run_local.py`. 2) `.parent` returns the `Path` one level above the final filename. 3) The name of that path is `python-reading-trainer`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the parent of the file’s path is the `python-reading-trainer` folder that contains the file.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: `run_local.py` is the original filename in the `Path`, and applying `.parent` moves you to the folder containing that file.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Evaluate the chain of dots from left to right and determine to which intermediate object each attribute or method applies.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Attribute access is read as **identify the left-hand object → find the attribute name → return the attribute value**.

lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.title: Reading the `api_base` value from a nested config using an environment name
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.reading_goal: First, read the sequence where `CONFIG[env_name]` is used to obtain a sub-dictionary for the current environment, and then `['api_base']` is applied to that result to extract the URL string.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) Evaluating `env_name` returns "dev". 2) `CONFIG['dev']` is the "dev" configuration dictionary. 3) `['api_base']` is applied to that result. 4) The final value is `http://127.0.0.1:8000`.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: `dev` is the key value used for the first lookup, not the final value of the entire nested lookup.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Starting from the left, write down the intermediate results to show which dict each set of square brackets applies to.

lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.title: Expressing the README execution procedure as an ordered list literal
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.reading_goal: Read the structure, which is formed as a single list object that preserves the order of the four strings enclosed in square brackets.

lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.reading_goal_internal: 대괄호 안 네 문자열이 적힌 순서를 유지하는 하나의 list 객체로 만들어지는 구조를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: A list literal creates a new list value by placing multiple values inside square brackets, separated by commas.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Treat each quoted boundary as one string item and check the order from left to right.
concept_explanation.key_point: Since a list preserves the order of the runbook steps, the position of each item can itself represent the execution order.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that spaces within a string are split into multiple items or that lists are automatically sorted alphabetically.

teaching_example.code:
steps = ["install", "validate", "run"]
print(steps)
teaching_example.walkthrough: The list retains the exact order in which the commands were written: install, validate, run.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) The order of the list items is clone, create environment, run local server, open app URL. 2) Index 2 corresponds to the third position. 3) Therefore, the search result is run local server.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the list preserves the order in which it was created, and the 0-based index 2 corresponds to the third step.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: `create environment` is the second item, so it is at index 1.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Distinguish human counting order from Python’s zero-based indexing.

answer_explanation.takeaway: A list literal **stores values in a single list in the order they are written**.

lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.title: Compare whether the installed version matches the required version using ==
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.reading_goal: Check the current contents of the two string versions and determine whether an equality comparison returns True if they are exactly the same.
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.code:
required_version = "0.115.0"
installed_version = "0.115.0"
version_matches = installed_version == required_version
print(version_matches)
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.question: What is the result of `installed_version == required_version`?
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.explanation: 1) Check the string on the left and the string on the right. 2) Both are 0.115.0. 3) The result of the equality comparison is True.
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.project_context: It relates to the context of dependency pinning, which involves reproducing and verifying the expected versions of direct dependencies across multiple PCs and GPU servers.
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.reading_goal_internal: 두 버전 문자열의 현재 내용을 확인하고 정확히 같으면 equality 비교가 True를 만드는지 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `a == b` checks whether two values are equal and returns True or False.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: For version strings, this card checks for exact equality between the contents of the two strings, rather than comparing numerical values.
concept_explanation.key_point: In exact PIN verification, even a single character difference results in False.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that versions are similar and return `True`, or to confuse the assignment ``=`` with the comparison ``==``.

teaching_example.code:
required = "2.8.2"
installed = "2.8.2"
print(installed == required)
teaching_example.walkthrough: If two strings are exactly the same, the equality result is True.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) Check the string on the left and the string on the right. 2) Both are 0.115.0. 3) The result of the equality comparison is True.
answer_explanation.why_correct: Since the two string versions are exactly the same, the equality comparison returns True.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: 0.115.0 is the string value of the operand, and the result of the entire comparison is a Boolean.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Separate the pre-comparison operand values from the Boolean result created by `==`.

answer_explanation.takeaway: `==` is read as **checking the current values on both sides → comparing for equality → Boolean result**.

lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.title: Read the definition of the `main` function called by the package entrypoint
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.reading_goal: `def main():` Read that the indented body, which defines the function object named `main`, is executed not at the time of definition but later, when `main()` is called.
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.question: What is the most accurate description immediately after the `def main():` statement is executed?
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.explanation: 1) `def main():` is a function definition statement. 2) A function object is associated with the name “main.” 3) The function body is not executed immediately after the definition. 4) The body is executed when `main()` is called by the entry point or other code.
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.project_context: When a package is installed, this corresponds to a structure where a command such as ``py-reader-validate`` is linked to call the ``tools.validate:main`` callable.
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.reading_goal_internal: `def main():`이 main이라는 함수 객체를 정의하며 들여쓴 본문은 정의 시점이 아니라 나중에 main()을 호출할 때 실행된다는 점을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `def name():` This statement defines a function with no parameters and binds the function object to `name`.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: In the `def` header, identify the function name, and treat the indented section below the colon as the function body.
concept_explanation.key_point: For the `entrypoint` setting to point to ``tools.validate:main``, there must be a `main` callable that can be imported from that module.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to assume that validation within the function body is executed as soon as a `def` statement is encountered.

teaching_example.walkthrough: The `start` function object is defined using a `def` statement, so `callable(start)` returns `True`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) `def main():` is a function definition statement. 2) A function object is associated with the name “main.” 3) The function body is not executed immediately after the definition. 4) The body is executed when `main()` is called by the entry point or other code.
answer_explanation.why_correct: Since `def` is a statement that defines a callable function named `main`, the first explanation is correct.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: The `validate_all()` call is inside the body of `main`, so it does not execute until `main` is actually called.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Read the text by separating the point at which the function is defined from the point at which it is called.

answer_explanation.takeaway: A function definition is described as **registering the function name and body → executing the body when called later**.

lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.title: Reading default values when environment variables are omitted in an `os.getenv()` call
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.reading_goal: Pass the environment variable name as the first argument to the function call, "default" as the second argument, and read the value returned when that variable does not exist.
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.code:
import os

os.environ.pop("API_BASE_URL", None)
api_base = os.getenv("API_BASE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8000")
print(api_base)
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.question: In the current code, which lacks `API_BASE_URL`, what is the return value of the `target` call?
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.explanation: 1) API_BASE_URL does not exist. 2) os.getenv searches for the name in the environment. 3) If it is not found, it returns the second argument `http://127.0.0.1:8000`. 4) That value is stored in `api_base`.
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.project_context: This connects to a configuration flow that injects local/production API addresses and options through `.env` and the process environment without changing the code.
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.reading_goal_internal: 함수 호출의 첫 인자로 환경변수 이름, 둘째 인자로 default를 전달하고 해당 변수가 없을 때 반환되는 값을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: A function call evaluates the arguments inside the parentheses and passes them to the function, then uses the return value generated by the function as the result of the expression.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: `os.getenv(name, default)` In this case, the first argument is the name of the environment variable to search for, and the second argument is the default value to use when the variable is not found.
concept_explanation.key_point: There is a difference between a case where an environment variable exists but is an empty string and a case where it does not exist at all; the default value is used when omitted.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that the second string is always returned. If an environment variable exists, its value takes precedence.

teaching_example.code:
import os
value = os.getenv("MISSING_SETTING", "fallback")
print(value)
teaching_example.walkthrough: Assuming that MISSING_SETTING does not exist, getenv returns a fallback value.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) API_BASE_URL does not exist. 2) os.getenv searches for the name in the environment. 3) If it is not found, it returns the second argument `http://127.0.0.1:8000`. 4) That value is stored in `api_base`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the second argument of `getenv` becomes the default return value when no environment variables are present.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: If the second default argument were omitted, it could be `None`, but this call has an explicit default string.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Distinguish the role of each argument in the function call and first check whether the environment variable exists.

answer_explanation.takeaway: A function call is interpreted as **evaluating and passing arguments → applying function rules → using the return value**.

lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.title: Read the fourth step at index 3 in the reproduction setup list
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.reading_goal: Check the actual order of the `setup_steps` and note that the 0-based index 3 corresponds to the fourth step, “activate venv,” as counted by a human.
lessons/python_packaging_env_dependencie.code:
setup_steps = [
    "git clone",
    "python --version",
    "python -m venv .venv",
    "activate venv",
    "pip install -r requirements.txt",

    "start local server",
