lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.title: Unpack the dict set as `**payload` using keyword arguments
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.reading_goal: Interpret `**payload` as meaning that the model, message, and generation settings for an LLM request are passed together as keyword arguments.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.question: What is the overall purpose of unpacking the elements of `client.chat(**payload)` and passing them in `payload`?
choices: Pass the model, dialogue messages, and generation settings to the LLM together as named arguments.
Convert the `payload` dictionary into a single string and send it.
Extract the answer text from the response’s `choices`.
Only the temperature value is transmitted separately.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.answer: Pass the model, dialogue messages, and generation settings to the LLM together as named arguments.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.explanation: 1) The payload contains model, messages, and temperature. 2) `**payload` unpacks each key-value pair as keyword arguments. 3) `client.chat(...)` accepts those values as a single LLM request configuration. This explanation interprets the Python target on this card—which involves passing the model, conversation messages, and generation settings to the LLM together as named arguments—in the context of legacy/domain objectives. Common Misconception: The payload dictionary is converted into a single string and sent. This option focuses only on specific syntax or context within the code and misses the card’s core meaning. Point of misinterpretation: It’s easy to view `**` as merely a dict unpacking and overlook the fact that the payload is a request unit that bundles the model input and generation settings. The LLM request code should be read as following this flow: **construct the request payload → pass keywords via `**` → receive the response**.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.project_context: This is the context of reading code that unpacks a configuration dictionary as call arguments when passing the model name, message, and generation options to the LLM SDK.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.reading_goal_internal: `**payload`가 LLM 요청의 모델·메시지·생성 설정을 keyword argument로 묶어 전달하는 의미를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: When you prefix a dict with ``**`` in a function call, it unpacks the dict’s keys as argument names and the values as the corresponding argument values.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: `func(**settings)` As you can see, first check what key-value pairs are contained in ``settings``. Next, read that each item is passed in the form ``func(key=value, ...)``.
concept_explanation.key_point: You must interpret both the Python syntactic meaning of `**payload` and its role as the payload in an LLM request.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to view `**` merely as a dictionary unpacking and overlook the fact that the payload is a request unit that combines the model input and generation settings.

teaching_example.code:
settings = {"host": "localhost", "port": 8000}
connect(**settings)
teaching_example.walkthrough: `settings` The ``host`` and ``port`` are each unpacked as named arguments and passed as ``connect(host="localhost", port=8000)``.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) The `payload` contains `model`, `messages`, and `temperature`. 2) `**payload` unpacks each key-value pair as keyword arguments. 3) `client.chat(...)` accepts those values as a single LLM request configuration.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is an explanation that interprets the Python target on this card—which states that the model, dialogue messages, and generation settings to be sent to the LLM are passed together as named arguments—in relation to legacy/domain purposes.

common_wrong_choice.choice: Convert the `payload` dictionary into a single string and send it.
common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: This option focuses only on certain aspects of the code’s syntax or context and misses the core meaning of the card.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: It is easy to view `**` merely as a dictionary unpacking and overlook the fact that the payload is a request unit that combines the model input and generation settings.

answer_explanation.takeaway: The LLM request code follows the flow: **construct the request payload → pass keywords via `**` → receive the response**.

lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.title: Trace the nested response structure from the outside in
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.reading_goal: It follows the subscription chain—comprising a `dict` key lookup and a list index—step by step to find the final value.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.question: What is the string output by the last line, ``print(text)``?
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.explanation: `response["choices"]` is a list containing a single choice. `[0]` retrieves the first dict in that list. The `message` value in that dict is another dict, and the value of the last key, `content`, is `센서 상태를 확인하세요.` This string is stored in `text` and printed. If you apply the bracket access one step at a time from the left, the final value is exactly `센서 상태를 확인하세요.` Commonly Confused Incorrect Answer: content `content` is a key name, and the result of the bracket lookup is the value associated with that key. Common Misinterpretation: In the final `["content"]`, do not mistake the key name itself for the answer; instead, check the actual string that the key refers to. When handling nested subscriptions, you must check the data type and value one step at a time, starting from the left.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.project_context: The context involves reading code that extracts the actual response field from the nested structure of an LLM or API response.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.reading_goal_internal: dict key lookup과 list index가 이어진 subscription chain을 한 단계씩 따라가 최종 값을 찾는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: Bracket access retrieves values using position numbers in lists and keys in dictionaries. In nested data, this access may occur multiple times.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Don’t read long chains of square brackets all at once; instead, check the result data type starting from the left. If the result of `response["choices"]` is a list, the following `[0]` selects the first item in that list, and so on.
concept_explanation.key_point: Each set of brackets applies to the result of the expression immediately preceding it. Therefore, you must know what data type the previous step returns in order to accurately interpret the meaning of the next set of brackets.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: `["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]` It’s easy to view this as a single long key. In reality, it involves four steps: dict lookup → list index → dict lookup → dict lookup.

teaching_example.walkthrough: First, retrieve the `rows` list, select the first row using `[0]`, and then follow the `meta` and `score` keys in order to obtain 92.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: `response["choices"]` is a list containing a single choice. `[0]` retrieves the first dictionary in that list. The `message` value in that dictionary is another dictionary, and the value of the last key, `content`, is `센서 상태를 확인하세요.`. This string is stored in `text` and printed.
answer_explanation.why_correct: Applying the bracket accesses one step at a time from the left gives the final value exactly as `센서 상태를 확인하세요.`.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: `content` is a key name, and the result of a bracket lookup is the value associated with that key.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: In the final example `["content"]`, do not treat the key name itself as the answer; instead, verify the actual string that the key points to.

answer_explanation.takeaway: The nested subscription follows the data types and values one step at a time, starting from the left.

lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.title: Determining whether it is a system role by comparing strings
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.reading_goal: Read the expression that compares the `role` string obtained by nested subscription with `==` to produce a Boolean indicating whether it is a system message.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.code:
messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "초3 수준으로 설명하라"},
    {"role": "user", "content": "비행기는 왜 날아?"},
]
is_system = messages[0]["role"] == "system"
print(is_system)
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.question: What value is stored in `is_system` after the comparison expression is evaluated?
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.explanation: `messages[0]` is the first dict, and the `role` value in that dict is `system`. Therefore, the comparison becomes `"system" == "system"` and the result is True because the two string values are exactly equal. Common wrong answer: `"system"`. `messages[0]["role"]` produces the intermediate value `system`, but the final result of the `==` comparison is a Boolean. Misreading point: Do not stop at the subscription result; read through the outer comparison operation. A comparison expression produces True/False, not the input string itself.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.project_context: This is code that simplifies the process of verifying whether the first message in an educational LLM request is from the “system” role.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.reading_goal_internal: 중첩 subscription으로 읽어 온 role 문자열을 `==`로 비교해 system 메시지 여부를 Boolean으로 판정하는 표현식을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `==` A comparison checks whether the left-hand value and the right-hand value are the same and returns True or False.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: First calculate what value the expression on the left actually produces, then compare that value with the value on the right.
concept_explanation.key_point: Rather than the LLM concept of a “system prompt,” the crucial part in Python is the string created by ``messages[0]["role"]`` and the equality comparison in ``"system"``.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: Do not assume the first message is automatically `system`. The actual code reads the `role` string and decides from the result of the `==` comparison.

teaching_example.code:
events = [{"type": "notice"}, {"type": "error"}]
is_notice = events[0]["type"] == "notice"
print(is_notice)
teaching_example.walkthrough: Since the type value of the first `dict` is `notice` and the one on the right is also `notice`, the comparison result is True.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: `messages[0]` is the first dict, and its `role` value is `system`. Therefore, the comparison becomes `"system" == "system"` and the result is True.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the values of both strings are exactly the same.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Although the intermediate value of `messages[0]["role"]` is `system`, the final result of the `==` comparison is a Boolean.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Don’t stop at the `subscription` result; you must read all the way through to the comparison operation at the end.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Comparison expressions return True or False, not the input string itself.

lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.title: Extracting user questions using nested subscriptions
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.reading_goal: Read the expression `messages[1]["content"]`—which consists of a list index followed by a dictionary key—from left to right to find the actual user's question string.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.code:
messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "간단히 설명하라"},
    {"role": "user", "content": "비행기는 왜 날아?"},
]
question = messages[1]["content"]
print(question)
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.question: What value is extracted from `messages[1]["content"]` and stored in `question`?
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.explanation: Index 1 selects the `user` message from the second dict. Since the value of the `content` key in that dict is `Why do airplanes fly?`, that string is assigned to `question`. This is the result of applying list index access and dict key access sequentially from the left. A common source of confusion: “Explain briefly.” That value is the `비행기는 왜 날아?` of the `system` message at index 0. Point of misinterpretation: You must first confirm that index 1 refers to the second element. Consecutive `subscription` operations can be safely interpreted by counting one step at a time from the left.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.project_context: The process involves placing system instructions and user questions into the same list of messages and then extracting only the actual question strings.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.reading_goal_internal: 리스트 인덱스 접근 뒤 dict key 접근이 연속된 `messages[1]["content"]` 표현식을 왼쪽부터 읽어 실제 사용자 질문 문자열을 찾는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: Subscription is an expression that uses square brackets to specify a sequence index or dict key and retrieve an internal value.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: When brackets appear consecutively, read them step by step from left to right. First, evaluate `messages[1]`, and then apply `["content"]` to that result.
concept_explanation.key_point: The first `[1]` selects a message, and the second `["content"]` selects the content value within that message.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to mistake `[1]` for the first item. Python indices start at 0, so index 1 is the second message.

teaching_example.code:
records = [
    {"kind": "system", "text": "규칙"},
    {"kind": "user", "text": "도와줘"},
]
text = records[1]["text"]
print(text)
teaching_example.walkthrough: `records[1]` is the second dictionary, and since the `text` value of that dictionary is `도와줘`, that string is stored in `text`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: Index 1 selects the message from the second dict, `user`. Since the value of the `content` key in that dict is `비행기는 왜 날아?`, that string is assigned to `question`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: These are the results of applying list index access and dict key access, respectively, from the left.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: That value is the `content` of the system message at index 0.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: First, you must verify that index 1 corresponds to the second element.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Consecutive subscriptions can be safely read by counting one step at a time from the left.

lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.title: Filling the prompt template using the `format` method
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.reading_goal: Read the flow of the ``.format(...)`` method call, which maps named placeholders to keyword arguments to construct the final string.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.code:
template = "학년={grade} | 질문={question}"
prompt = template.format(grade=3, question="왜 비가 와?")
print(prompt)
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.question: What is the string stored in `.format(...)` after a `prompt` call?
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.explanation: The template has two placeholders, `{grade}` and `{question}`. In the `format` call, `grade=3` fills the first placeholder and `question="왜 비가 와?"` fills the second. Therefore, the final string is `학년=3 | 질문=왜 비가 와?`. This works because the keyword argument names in `format` correspond to placeholders with the same names. Common wrong answer: "학년={grade} | 질문={question}". That string is the original template before the `format` call. Misreading point: You must calculate the result of the `.format(...)` call on the right side of the assignment. `.format(name=value)` returns a new string in which a placeholder with the same name is replaced by that value.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.project_context: This code simplifies a scenario where values—such as grade level and actual questions—vary with each request by incorporating them into the same prompt structure.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.reading_goal_internal: 문자열 `.format(...)` method call이 이름 있는 placeholder와 keyword argument를 대응시켜 최종 문자열을 만드는 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: A method call uses a form such as `object.method_name(...)` to invoke functionality associated with that object.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: First, identify the target string and the placeholder names, then determine which placeholder each keyword argument in parentheses corresponds to.
concept_explanation.key_point: `grade=3` goes into `{grade}`, and `question="왜 비가 와?"` goes into `{question}`. The correspondence of names is more important than the order of arguments.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to think placeholder braces remain unchanged in the result string. When `.format(...)` succeeds, those positions are replaced with the supplied values.

teaching_example.code:
template = "이름={name} | 점수={score}"
text = template.format(name="민수", score=90)
print(text)
teaching_example.walkthrough: Since `{name}` is replaced with `민수` and `{score}` with 90, the result is `이름=민수 | 점수=90`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: The template has two placeholders, `{grade}` and `{question}`. In the `format` call, `grade=3` fills the first placeholder and `question="왜 비가 와?"` fills the second. Therefore, the final string is `학년=3 | 질문=왜 비가 와?`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the keyword argument name in the `format` function corresponds to a placeholder with the same name.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: This string is the original template before the `format` call.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: You must calculate through the result of the `.format(...)` call on the right side of the assignment.

answer_explanation.takeaway: `.format(name=value)` returns a new string in which the placeholder with the same name in the string is replaced with the corresponding value.

lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.title: Validating Required Fields in Model Responses Using `all()`
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.reading_goal: Read the sequence in which `all()` combines the various membership results generated by the generator into a single boolean.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.question: What value is stored in `valid`?
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.explanation: The generator checks whether each of the three fields contains the `data` key. Since all three results are `True`, `all()` returns `True` and is stored in `valid`. This is because `all()` returns `True` only when all the truth values passed to it are true. A common source of confusion: False: Since all three required fields exist in `data`, there is no “membership” result that is false. Point of misinterpretation: This occurs when the reader mistakenly assumes that even one field is missing or misunderstands the condition of `all()` in the opposite way. `all()` is used to combine multiple validation conditions into a single boolean value to indicate whether **all of them have been satisfied**.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.project_context: It is linked to validation code that checks whether all required fields are present before the app uses the structured response returned by the LLM.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.reading_goal_internal: generator가 만든 여러 membership 결과를 all()이 하나의 boolean으로 합치는 순서를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `all(iterable)` is a function call that returns `True` if every item in the iterable is truthy.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: I interpret this as: The presence or absence of each field within the parentheses is first determined, and then `all()` checks whether all of those results are true.
concept_explanation.key_point: The "response schema" refers to the domain context, and the focus on Python is on combining multiple validation results into a single call to `all()`.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that if just one of the required fields is present, the result is True. However, the `all()` function returns True only if all items are true.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Since both `id` and `title` are keys in the `data` dictionary, both membership results are `True`, and `all()` also returns `True`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: The generator checks whether each of the three fields contains a data key. Since all three results are True, `all()` returns True, which is stored in `valid`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because `all()` returns `True` only when all the truth values passed to it are `True`.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Since all three required fields are present in `data`, there are no false membership results.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case where the learner misread the code because even a single field was missing or misunderstood the condition of `all()` in the opposite way.

answer_explanation.takeaway: `all()` is used to combine multiple validation conditions into a single boolean value to indicate whether **all of them have passed**.

lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.target_statement: valid = all(field in data for field in required_fields)
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.focus_span: all(field in data for field in required_fields)

lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.title: Parsing Structured Model Responses with `json.loads()`
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.reading_goal: Read how the JSON string passed as a function argument is converted into a Python value.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.question: What is the data type of `parsed`?
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.explanation: `model_text` is a JSON object string enclosed in braces. When `json.loads()` parses it, a Python dict object is returned and stored in `parsed`. A JSON object maps to a Python dict in `json.loads()`. Common wrong answer: `str`. `str` is the type of `model_text` before the call; after `loads()`, the return value is a dict. Misreading point: This happens when the input type before a function call is confused with the result type after the call. `json.loads()` **parses a JSON string into a Python structure**.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.project_context: After ensuring the LLM responds in a specified JSON format, the app code connects this to the parsing stage, which handles the results as structured data.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.reading_goal_internal: 함수 호출 인자로 전달된 JSON 문자열이 어떤 Python 값으로 변환되는지 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: json.loads(text) is a function call that converts a JSON-formatted string into a Python value.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: First inspect the JSON structure of the string, then read the result of `loads` as a dict when the JSON value is an object.
concept_explanation.key_point: JSON mode is the domain context; the Python syntax focus is the input to `json.loads()` and its return value.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to assume that `loads` returns the string as-is. However, a JSON object string is converted into a Python dictionary.

teaching_example.code:
import json

text = '{"score": 3}'
parsed = json.loads(text)
teaching_example.walkthrough: The `loads()` function parses the JSON object string and returns the {"score": 3} dictionary.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: `model_text` is a JSON object string enclosed in curly braces. When `json.loads()` parses it, a Python `dict` object is returned and stored in `parsed`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the JSON object is mapped to a Python dictionary by `json.loads()`.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: `str` is the data type of `model_text` before the call, and the return value after calling `loads()` is a `dict`.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is an example where the input type before a function call and the return type after the call were not distinguished.

answer_explanation.takeaway: json.loads() **parses a JSON string into a Python structure**.

lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.title: Proceed to the fallback parser after a JSONDecodeError
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.reading_goal: Read the sequence in which a specific exception raised in `try` selects an `except` clause of the same type and leads to a fallback call.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.question: What is the value of `data["answer"]` after this code is executed?
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.explanation: Since `model_text` is not valid JSON, `loads()` raises a `JSONDecodeError`. Control flow moves to the `except` block, where `fallback_parse()` extracts the `ok` following the `=` and assigns it to `answer` in `data`. This is because the typed `except` clause matches the actual `JSONDecodeError` that occurred, causing the fallback code to execute. Common Misconception: The JSONDecodeError exception type is the cause that determines the control flow, and the final `data["answer"]` stores the fallback result. Common Misinterpretation: Confusing the exception that occurred with the final data value after the `except` block. A `typed except` allows you to **map a parsing failure to a specific recovery path**.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.project_context: This connects to code that recovers through an alternate parsing path instead of immediately stopping the app when LLM output does not match the expected JSON format.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.reading_goal_internal: try에서 발생한 특정 예외가 같은 타입의 except 절을 선택하고 fallback 호출로 이어지는 순서를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: The `except ErrorType:` clause is a branch that executes within the `try` block when an exception of that type occurs.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: It reads: "In a `try` block, the system checks the actual exception type that occurred, and if there is a matching `except` clause, it jumps to that block."
concept_explanation.key_point: Separate from the overall role of an output parser, the Python focus is the type match between `JSONDecodeError` and a typed `except`.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that the line following `json.loads()` will continue to execute. However, if an exception occurs, the rest of the `try` block is skipped, and control flows to the `except` block.

teaching_example.walkthrough: `loads()` raises `JSONDecodeError`, so the typed `except` executes and the fallback result is stored in `data`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: `model_text` is not valid JSON, so `loads()` raises `JSONDecodeError`. Control moves to the `except` block, where `fallback_parse()` extracts `ok` after `=` and stores it as `data["answer"]`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the `typed except` clause matches the actual `JSONDecodeError` that occurred, causing the fallback code to execute.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Exception types determine the control flow, and the final `data["answer"]` stores the fallback result.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is an example of confusing the exception that occurred with the final data value after the `except` block.

answer_explanation.takeaway: A typed `except` clause can **map a parsing failure to a specific recovery path**.

lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.title: If the required "answer" field is missing, reject it using an "if" statement.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.reading_goal: It determines whether `raise` is executed by applying the `not in` condition in the `if` header to the actual dict key state.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.question: What is the value of the if condition in this code?
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.explanation: The `data` contains only the `reason` key. Therefore, `answer not in data` evaluates to `True`, and the program enters the `if` block. This is because `not in` returns `True` when the key being searched for is not in the collection, and the `if` statement executes its body when the condition is `True`. Common misconception: Since the `False` answer key is actually not in `data`, the `not in` check evaluates to True. Point of confusion: This occurs when the presence of the answer key is mistakenly generalized to imply the existence of other keys. Validation of required fields follows the sequence: **check for the exact key → boolean → branching**.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.project_context: It is linked to validation code that prevents missing required fields before the LLM response is passed to the screen or a subsequent pipeline.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.reading_goal_internal: if 헤더의 not in 조건을 실제 dict key 상태에 적용해 raise가 실행되는지 판단한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: The `if condition:` statement executes the block immediately below it when `condition` is True.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: First, check the key of `data`, evaluate ``answer not in data``, and if it returns `True`, enter the block containing `raise`.
concept_explanation.key_point: Regardless of the role of output validation in the domain, the key point in Python is that the membership result determines the if branch.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: Since there are other fields in `data`, such as `reason`, it’s easy to assume that it will pass validation. However, the condition checks only whether the `answer key` exists.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Since there is no "title" key, the condition is True and the state is "missing."

answer_explanation.step_by_step: The `data` contains only the `reason` key. Therefore, `answer not in data` evaluates to `True`, and the program enters the `if` block.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because `not in` returns `True` when the key being searched for is not in the collection, and `if` executes the body of the statement when the condition is `True`.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Since the "answer key" is not actually present in the data, the "not in" check is true.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This incorrectly generalizes the existence of some other key into the existence of the `answer` key.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Validation of required fields is read in the following order: **existence of the exact key → boolean → branching**.

lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.title: Re-throwing the exception with a bare `raise` in the final retry
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.reading_goal: The bare `raise` inside the `except` block traces the flow where the current exception is propagated back to the caller after the final retry fails.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.question: What happens if the same error occurs on the third attempt?
choices: Currently, the TransientProviderError is being propagated again
Returns None as the success value.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.answer: Currently, the TransientProviderError is being propagated again
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.explanation: For attempts 0 and 1, retry continues, but on attempt 2 the condition becomes True. A bare `raise` re-raises the current `TransientProviderError`. This is written so the exception is not swallowed on the final attempt. Common wrong answer: retry forever. `range(3)` repeats only three times and raises on the final failure. Misreading point: This happens when the `for` iteration count and the final `raise` condition are not checked. Read a retry policy as **retryable error → bounded number of attempts → re-raise final failure**.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.project_context: This is linked to the resilience workflow in LLM, embedding, and search APIs, which involves limited retries for timeouts or temporary provider errors and surfaces final failures.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.reading_goal_internal: except 안의 bare raise가 마지막 retry 실패에서 현재 예외를 호출자에게 다시 전달하는 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: A bare `raise` inside an `except` block is a `reraise`, which re-raises the exception currently being handled.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: First, check the conditions under which `raise` is triggered, and determine whether a new exception is created or an existing exception is rethrown.
concept_explanation.key_point: You can retry a temporary error a few times, but if it still fails after the maximum number of attempts has been reached, the error is not hidden but is passed on to the caller.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to assume that `bare raise` automatically creates a new `RuntimeError`. Instead, it rethrows the exception currently being handled by the `except` block.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Executing a bare `raise` in the `except` block causes the original `TimeoutError` to be propagated again.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: In attempts 0 and 1, the program continues to retry, but in attempt 2, the condition becomes True. A bare `raise` statement re-triggers the current `TransientProviderError`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because it was written to `reraise` the exception rather than swallow it in the last attempt.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: `range(3)` iterates only three times and raises an exception on the last failure.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case where the number of iterations and the final `raise` condition were not checked.

answer_explanation.takeaway: The retry policy is interpreted as **errors that can be retried → limit on the number of attempts → re-raise on the last failure**.

lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.title: Calling the fallback model method after the main model fails
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.reading_goal: Read the execution sequence where, after an exception occurs in the main model, the generate method of the alternative model is called within the `except` block.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.question: What is the value of `answer`?
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.explanation: qwen raises an exception because `fail=True`, and `gpt.generate('hello')` is called in the `except` block, storing ``gpt:hello`` in `answer`. This is because the fallback method call is located in the main model’s failure branch. A common source of confusion: qwen:hello qwen.generate raises an exception before returning a valid string. Point of misinterpretation: This does not reflect the failure of the try block. The fallback process follows this sequence: **primary attempt → specific exception → backup call → identical subsequent verification**.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.project_context: It connects to a service architecture that uses Qwen, GPT, and Local Llama as backends and switches to an alternative model when a specific provider temporarily fails.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.reading_goal_internal: 주 모델 예외가 발생한 뒤 except에서 대체 모델의 generate method를 호출하는 실행 순서를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `gpt.generate(prompt)` calls the `generate` method of the `gpt` object along with the prompt argument.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Let’s look at the `except` condition that leads to this call and the variable where the return value is stored.
concept_explanation.key_point: A fallback is a pattern that provides an alternative path to prevent the entire service from immediately shutting down in the event of a failure of the primary provider.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that both models are always called simultaneously. In this structure, GPT is called only when QWEN fails.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Since the primary operation fails, control flows to the `except` block, and `Backup.run()` is called.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: qwen raises an exception by setting `fail=True`, and in the `except` block, `gpt.generate('hello')` is called, storing `gpt:hello` in `answer`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the fallback method call is located in the main model’s failure branch.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: qwen.generate raises an exception before returning a normal string.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case where the failure of the `try` call is not reflected.

answer_explanation.takeaway: "fallback" is interpreted as **primary attempt → specific exception → backup call → identical subsequent verification**.

lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.title: Treat "RateLimitError" as the error name and read "retry_after"
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.reading_goal: Explain the structure where `except-as` binds the exception object to a name, allowing attributes such as `retry_after` to be read.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.question: What is the value of `retry_after`?
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.explanation: A chat call raises a `RateLimitError` with `retry_after=4`, and the `except-as` block stores that object in `error`. The attribute lookup result is 4. This is because it reads the `retry_after` attribute of the actual exception object captured by `as error`. A common source of confusion: 30. 30 is the timeout argument for the chat call, not rate limit waiting information. Point of misreading: This occurs when the timeout value is confused with an exception attribute. API exception handling follows the sequence: **exception type → `as` binding → detailed attribute lookup**.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.project_context: This connects to the process of safely retrying when hit by a request limit from an LLM or search API, using the `retry-after` information in the exception.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.reading_goal_internal: except-as가 발생한 예외 객체를 이름에 바인딩해 retry_after 같은 attribute를 읽게 하는 구조를 해석한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `except ErrorType as error:` makes the caught exception object available under the name `error`.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Distinguish between the exception type being caught and the name following `as`, and observe how that object’s attributes are used in the `except` block.
concept_explanation.key_point: Since rate limit errors may include instructions to retry after a certain amount of time, it is helpful to read the exception object.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: `as error` It’s easy to assume that it simply converts exceptions into strings. In fact, it binds the actual exception object itself to the name.

teaching_example.walkthrough: The `BusyError` object is bound to `err`, allowing it to read `delay 3`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: The `chat` call raises a `RateLimitError` with `retry_after=4`, and the `except-as` block stores that object in `error`. The result of querying the `attribute` is 4.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because it reads the `retry_after` attribute of the actual exception object caught via `as error`.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: 30 is the timeout argument for a chat call; it is not information about the rate limit queue.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is an instance where the `timeout` value was confused with the `exception` attribute.

answer_explanation.takeaway: API exception handling is described as **exception type → as binding → retrieving detailed attributes**.

lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.title: Combining model usage and costs into a single log dictionary
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.reading_goal: Read the structure that groups the model name, number of input/output tokens, and cost value into a single dictionary literal in key/value format.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.question: `log["output_tokens"]` What is the value of ?
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.explanation: When creating a `Usage` object, 30 is stored in `output_tokens`, and the dictionary literal uses that attribute as the value for the `output_tokens` key. This is because that key is directly linked to `usage.output_tokens`. Common mistake: 120. 120 is the value of the `input_tokens` attribute. Point of confusion: This occurs when the input token and output token keys are read in reverse. An observability record must be read by **accurately matching the metric key with its actual source value**.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.project_context: It connects to operations that track LLM API, GPU, and cloud costs by feature to monitor excessive token usage and rising costs.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.reading_goal_internal: 모델 이름·입출력 token 수·비용 값을 key/value 형태로 하나의 dict literal에 모으는 구조를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `{key: value, ...}` is a dict literal that creates a single dictionary containing multiple key-value pairs.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Map each key one-to-one to the actual value or attribute it corresponds to.
concept_explanation.key_point: By keeping a cost log, you can compare which models or features consume the most tokens and costs.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that `input_tokens` and `output_tokens` have the same meaning. They are different usage metrics.

teaching_example.code:
record = {"feature": "search", "requests": 3, "cost": 0.2}
value = record["requests"]
teaching_example.walkthrough: The `dict literal` groups the three metrics into a single record, and the `requests` key is associated with 3.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: When creating a Usage object, 30 is stored in `output_tokens`, and the dictionary literal uses that attribute as the value for the `output_tokens` key.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the key is directly linked to ``usage.output_tokens``.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: 120 is the value of the `input_tokens` attribute.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case of reading the input-token key and output-token key in reverse.

answer_explanation.takeaway: An observability record is read by **accurately matching the metric key with the actual source value**.

lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.title: Separate claims regarding the success of local tool calls from those regarding downstream propagation and performance
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.reading_goal: Confirm that `**arguments` expands `query` as a keyword argument and actually calls `search_docs`, but judge that end-to-end/performance claims still do not hold because `downstream_received=False` and no performance measurement exists.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.question: When the execution result is `True 2 False`, what is the most accurate review conclusion?
choices: Although the arguments schema and local `search_docs` calls and returns have been verified, downstream propagation has failed, and since there are no performance benchmarks, end-to-end success or performance improvements have not yet been demonstrated.
Since there are 2 hits, the downstream transmission and the end-user response must also have succeeded.
Since `**arguments` are used, successful external network connectivity and improved latency are automatically guaranteed.
If `validated` is True, `search_docs` is considered an end-to-end success even if it is not actually called.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.answer: Although the arguments schema and local `search_docs` calls and returns have been verified, downstream propagation has failed, and since there are no performance benchmarks, end-to-end success or performance improvements have not yet been demonstrated.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.explanation: 1) Since the `arguments` key set is `{'query'}`, `validated` is `True`. 2) In the target `search_docs(**arguments)`, `query='cosine similarity'` is unpacked, and the actual function is called. 3) Since `hits` in `result` is 2, the local return value is also verified. 4) However, `downstream_received` is False. 5) Furthermore, since there are no Before/After metrics for latency or throughput, separate evidence is required to support the end-to-end and performance claims.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.project_context: APEX synthesizes call paths, scope, and claims vs. evidence all at once within the context of AI tool invocation.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.reading_goal_internal: `**arguments`가 query를 keyword argument로 펼쳐 search_docs를 실제 호출하는 것은 확인하되, downstream_received=False와 성능 측정 부재 때문에 end-to-end/performance 주장은 아직 성립하지 않음을 판단한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `**mapping` It unpacks the key-value pairs from the dict into keyword arguments and passes them to the actual function call. A successful local function call provides evidence only up to the boundaries of that function; it does not automatically prove subsequent passing, external processing, or performance.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Check the arguments and examine the result returned by the target call. Next, separately verify whether the downstream transmission status and performance metrics actually exist.
concept_explanation.key_point: Since `search_docs` accepts a query and returns `hits=2`, the local tool is confirmed to be running. However, since `downstream_received=False` and there is no benchmark, end-to-end success and performance improvements remain unproven.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: You should not state that simply because the `tool` function was called, everything—from network transmission and model re-reception to incorporating user responses and performance improvements—was successful.

teaching_example.walkthrough: `**args` passes the query keyword to generate local tool results—you can verify this yourself.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) Since the `arguments` key set is `{'query'}`, `validated` is `True`. 2) In the target `search_docs(**arguments)`, `query='cosine similarity'` is unpacked, and the actual function is called. 3) Since `hits` in `result` is 2, the local return value is also verified. 4) However, `downstream_received` is False. 5) Furthermore, since there are no Before/After metrics for latency or throughput, separate evidence is required to support the end-to-end and performance claims.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because observed evidence is distinguished at each system boundary, and unobserved boundaries are not assumed to be successful.

common_wrong_choice.choice: Since there are 2 hits, the downstream transmission and the end-user response must also have succeeded.
common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: `hits` is the local return value of `search_docs`, and `downstream_received` is currently explicitly set to `False`.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Break the tool pipeline into validation → local call → return → downstream delivery → user-visible result → performance.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Evidence for tool calls verifies each stage of the process: **argument validation → actual call → return value → downstream propagation → final result → performance measurement**.

reading_steps: Since the arguments key set is {'query'}, validated is True.
In `search_docs(**arguments)`, `query='cosine similarity'` is unpacked, and the actual function is called.
Since `result` has 2 hits, the local return value is also verified.
However, `downstream_received` is False.
Additionally, since there are no “Before/After” latency/throughput figures, claims regarding end-to-end and performance require separate evidence.

lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.title: If there is insufficient evidence, return a "revise/refuse" result and end the function.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.reading_goal: Read the flow where a function call following a `return` is evaluated first, its result is returned to the caller, and then the remaining normal code of the current function is not executed.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.question: When `unsupported` is True, what is the return value of ``grounded_answer(...)``?
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.explanation: 1) The `if` condition is True. 2) `revise_or_refuse` returns the string "refuse." 3) The outer `return` statement returns that value as the result of `grounded_answer`. 4) The function terminates, so the line returning the general `answer` is not executed.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.project_context: It is linked to the RAG hallucination guard, which does not allow claims unsupported by evidence to pass through but instead corrects or rejects them.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.reading_goal_internal: return 뒤 함수 호출을 먼저 평가하고 그 결과를 호출자에게 돌려준 뒤 현재 함수의 남은 정상 코드를 실행하지 않는 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `return expression` It calculates the value of the expression, returns that value to the caller, and terminates the current function execution.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: First, call `revise_or_refuse(answer)` after `return` to obtain the return value, and then the outer `return` statement sends that value as the final result.
concept_explanation.key_point: If `return` is executed in the `guard` branch, the program does not return to the normal return path for the `answer` further down in the same function.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to assume that the lines below the current function continue to execute even after calling `revise_or_refuse`.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Since `bad` is True, the `revise` function returns `fixed` and terminates immediately.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) The `if` condition is True. 2) `revise_or_refuse` returns the string "refuse." 3) The outer `return` statement returns that value as the result of `grounded_answer`. 4) The function terminates, so the line returning the general `answer` is not executed.
answer_explanation.why_correct: Since `return` is executed in the `guard` branch, the return string from `revise_or_refuse` becomes the final function result.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: The line below, which returns `draft_answer`, is reached only when `unsupported` is `False` and the code does not pass through the guard return.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This reflects the fact that the control flow of the current function ends at the point where `return` is executed.

answer_explanation.takeaway: "return" is read as **evaluate expression → return value → immediately exit the current function**.

lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.title: Reading the class header for QwenAdapter, which uses LLMAdapter as its base class
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.reading_goal: Read `LLMAdapter` inside the parentheses after the class name as the base class inherited by the new class.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.question: In `class QwenAdapter(LLMAdapter):`, what is the role of `LLMAdapter`?
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.explanation: 1) The newly defined class is QwenAdapter. 2) LLMAdapter appears within parentheses. 3) These parentheses in the class header list the base classes. 4) Therefore, QwenAdapter inherits from LLMAdapter.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.project_context: It connects to an adapter architecture that allows it to be replaced with a common generation contract regardless of the provider, such as Qwen, GPT, or a local LLM.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.reading_goal_internal: class 이름 뒤 괄호 안의 LLMAdapter가 새 클래스가 상속받는 base class라는 구조를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `class Child(Base):` This is the header that defines a new class called `Child` and specifies `Base` as its base class.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Note that the name following `class` is distinct from the `base` name in parentheses, and that the text following the colon constitutes the body of the new class.
concept_explanation.key_point: With this structure, provider adapters can inherit or override the common interface and behavior.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to mistake the LLMAdapter in parentheses for a regular function argument passed when creating a QwenAdapter.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Since "Animal" in parentheses in the `Dog` class header is the base class, the `issubclass` result is `True`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) The newly defined class is QwenAdapter. 2) LLMAdapter appears within parentheses. 3) These parentheses in the class header list the base classes. 4) Therefore, QwenAdapter inherits from LLMAdapter.
answer_explanation.why_correct: The name in parentheses in the class definition header refers to the base class to be inherited from, so “LLMAdapter” is the correct answer.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Unlike parentheses used for function calls, the parentheses in a class definition header are used to list base classes.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: First, determine whether the current context is a call or a class definition, and then interpret the meaning of the parentheses.

answer_explanation.takeaway: The header of an inheriting class is structured as **new class name → list of base classes → class body**.

lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.title: Inserting "question" and "evidence" into an f-string prompt
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.reading_goal: Read the flow of how an f-string evaluates the current value of the expression inside the curly braces and inserts it as a string at that location to construct the entire prompt.
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.code:
question = "What is RAG?"
context = "RAG retrieves evidence before generation."

prompt = f"Question: {question}\nEvidence: {context}\nRule: answer only from evidence"
print(prompt.splitlines()[0])
lessons/python_llm_api_prompt_validation.question: What is the first line of the generated `prompt`?

lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.title: Change the working directory using `os.chdir(project_root)`
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.reading_goal: Explain how the path passed as an argument in a module function call is used to change the current working directory.
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.code:
import os
from pathlib import Path

project_root = Path("demo_project")
project_root.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
os.chdir(project_root)
print(Path.cwd().name)
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.question: Which of the following best describes the role of the `os.chdir(project_root)` call?
choices: Change the current working directory to the project_root path
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.answer: Change the current working directory to the project_root path
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.explanation: `project_root` stores the path string to navigate to. ``os.chdir(project_root)`` calls the `chdir` function from the `os` module and passes that path as an argument. As a result, the current working directory changes to that path. `chdir` is a function that changes the working directory; it stands for "change directory." Common source of confusion: Deletes the `project_root` folder. This is not a deletion function but a function to change the working directory. Point of misinterpretation: Distinguish between the function name `chdir` and the role played by the path passed as an argument. ``os.chdir(path)`` does not delete a file but changes the current working directory to `path`.
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.project_context: This refers to the context of setting the working directory to the project root before executing a relative path command in an automation script.
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.reading_goal_internal: module function call에서 인자로 전달된 경로가 현재 작업 디렉터리 변경에 쓰이는 의미를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `os.chdir(path)` is a function call that changes the working directory of the current Python process to the specified path.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: After noting that `os` is the module name and `chdir` is a function within that module, check what path value is passed in the parentheses.
concept_explanation.key_point: Changing the working directory is different from moving or deleting a file. Afterward, the base location used to interpret relative paths changes.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to assume that `chdir` changes the name or contents of the `project_root` folder itself. In reality, it changes the working directory from which the current process operates.

teaching_example.code:
import os

folder = "/tmp/demo"
os.chdir(folder)
teaching_example.walkthrough: `os.chdir(folder)` instructs the system to change the current working directory to `/tmp/demo`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: project_root stores the path string to be navigated to. `os.chdir(project_root)` calls the chdir function from the os module and passes that path as an argument. As a result, the current working directory changes to that path.
answer_explanation.why_correct: `chdir` is a function that changes the working directory, as the name “change directory” implies.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: It is a function that changes the directory, not a delete function.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Distinguish between the role of the function name `chdir` and that of the passed path.

answer_explanation.takeaway: `os.chdir(path)` does not delete a file; rather, it changes the current working directory to `path`.

answer_explanation.why_correct: This explanation interprets the Python target of this card—which means “There are no tracked or untracked changes to report in the current working tree”—in the context of legacy/domain objectives.

common_wrong_choice.choice: This means there are no commits in the remote repository.
common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: This option focuses only on certain aspects of the code’s syntax or context and misses the core meaning of the card.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: `changes == []` If you view this solely as a standard list comparison, the habit of checking the before-and-after states in Git will disappear.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Before and after performing Git operations, check the **status of changes in the working tree** by verifying whether `git status --short` produces output.

lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.title: Creating multi-line strings with triple quotes
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.reading_goal: A line break within a triple-quoted string literal is treated as part of a single string value.
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.question: What is the result of `text.splitlines()`?
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.explanation: Inside the triple quotes, the word “hello” on the first line and “world” on the second line are separated by an actual line break. `splitlines()` splits the string into two items based on this line boundary. This is because triple-quoted strings preserve internal line breaks as part of the string data. A common source of confusion: ['helloworld']—there is no code that removes the line break between the two words. Point of Misinterpretation: You must verify that the line break inside the triple quotes is part of the string value. Multiple lines inside triple quotes form a single string, and the line break is included in the data.
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.project_context: The requirement to treat multi-line text as a single value, similar to PowerShell `here-strings`, has been adapted to Python’s actual multi-line string syntax.
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.reading_goal_internal: triple-quoted string literal 안의 줄바꿈을 포함해 하나의 문자열 값으로 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: Python’s triple-quote strings allow you to write text spanning multiple lines as a single string literal.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: The text is interpreted as a single string from the opening triple quotation mark to the closing triple quotation mark, and line breaks within that range are also included in the value.
concept_explanation.key_point: Even if the code spans multiple physical lines, it may be a single string literal.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to mistake the `world` on the second line for a separate Python statement. Everything up to the closing triple quotes is part of the string.

teaching_example.code:
note = """first
second"""
print(note.splitlines())
teaching_example.walkthrough: Since there are two lines inside the triple quotes, the result of `splitlines` is `['first', 'second']`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: Inside the triple quotes, the word "hello" on the first line and "world" on the second line are separated by an actual line break. The `splitlines()` function splits the string into two elements based on these line boundaries.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because triple-quoted strings preserve internal line breaks as part of the string data.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: There is no code where line breaks between words are removed.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: You must also verify whether line breaks within triple quotes are part of the string value.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Multiple lines enclosed in triple quotes form a single string, and line breaks are included in the data.

lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.title: Safely concatenate script lines into a single string using `join`
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.reading_goal: Read the flow of the `join` method call on a string, which inserts the `separator` between multiple string elements to form a single string.
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.question: What is the value output by the last line, ``print(script.count("\n"))``?
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.explanation: `script_lines` contains two elements. ``"\n".join(...)`` inserts a line break at only one point between the two elements. Therefore, the number of ``\n`` within the script is 1, and the result of the `count` operation is also 1. Since the `join` function’s `separator` is inserted between adjacent elements, if there are two elements, the `separator` appears once. A common source of confusion: This answer assumes the number of `separators` equals the number of string elements. There is only one boundary between the two elements. Point of Misinterpretation: You must distinguish whether the separator in `join` is attached to the element itself or inserted only between elements. ``separator.join(items)`` inserts the separator once at each boundary between items to form a single string.
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.project_context: This moves into a safer automation context where code lines are separated into a data structure and assembled with `join`, instead of manually managing nested multiline delimiters.
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.reading_goal_internal: separator 문자열의 join method call이 여러 문자열 원소 사이에 separator를 넣어 하나의 문자열을 만드는 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `separator.join(strings)` is a method call that combines multiple strings into a single string, separated by `separator`.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: First, identify what the separator on the left is, and then read the text as if that separator were inserted between each element in the list of strings inside the parentheses.
concept_explanation.key_point: Using `"\n"` as a separator allows you to treat each line of code as a separate string while still including line breaks in the final script.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that `join` automatically adds an extra line break at the end of a list. The `separator` is only inserted between elements.

teaching_example.code:
lines = ["alpha", "beta", "gamma"]
text = " | ".join(lines)
print(text)
teaching_example.walkthrough: The separator "` | `" appears twice between the three strings, resulting in "`alpha | beta | gamma`".

answer_explanation.step_by_step: `script_lines` contains two elements. `"\n".join(...)` inserts a newline at only one boundary between them. Therefore, `script` contains one `\n`, and the count result is also 1.
answer_explanation.why_correct: Since the separator in `join` is inserted between adjacent elements, if there are two elements, the separator is inserted once.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: This value treats the number of string elements as equal to the number of separators. With two elements, there is only one boundary between them.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: You must distinguish whether the separator in `join` is attached to the elements themselves or only appears between them.

answer_explanation.takeaway: `separator.join(items)` It inserts a separator once at each boundary between items to form a single string.

lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.title: Safely removing the previous session’s state using `pop`
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.reading_goal: Read the `key` and `default` arguments of `dict.pop` and track the state change where the corresponding item is removed from the dictionary after the call.
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.question: `state.pop("py", None)` What is the result of ``"py" in state`` after execution?
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.explanation: The initial `state` contains a `py` key. `pop` removes that key-value pair from the dictionary. Therefore, in the next membership test, `"py" in state` evaluates to False, because `dict.pop` actually removes the specified key. Common mistake: True—this answer overlooks the removal operation by only considering the state before the `pop` call. Point of confusion: You must verify whether the state of the original dictionary changes after the method call. `pop(key, default)` is a state-changing method that removes a key from the dictionary.
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.project_context: I’ve translated the scenario where session state is explicitly cleared so that values from previous automation steps do not carry over to the next execution into a Python dictionary.
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.reading_goal_internal: dict.pop의 key와 default 인자를 읽고 호출 뒤 dict에서 해당 항목이 제거되는 상태 변화를 추적한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `dict.pop(key, default)` is a method call that removes the entry and returns its value if the key exists, and returns `default` if the key does not exist.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: First, check the key to be removed; if there is a second argument, it is interpreted as the default value to use when the key is absent.
concept_explanation.key_point: When clearing an old state, specifying `default` allows the cleanup code to continue executing without raising a `KeyError`, even if the key no longer exists.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to think that `pop` simply reads the value and leaves the dictionary unchanged. However, `pop` removes the key at the same time it returns the value.

teaching_example.walkthrough: The `old` item is removed, so only the `new` item remains in the cache.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: The initial state contains the key ``py``. `pop` removes that key-value pair from the dictionary. Therefore, in the next membership test, ``"py" in state`` will evaluate to `False`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because `dict.pop` actually removes the specified key.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: This is a value for which the removal operation was missed because only the state before the `pop` call was examined.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: You must also verify whether the state of the original dictionary changes after the method call.

answer_explanation.takeaway: `pop(key, default)` is a state-changing method that removes a key from a dictionary.

lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.title: Managing the Lifecycle of Temporary Work Paths Using the `with` Statement
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.reading_goal: Read the structure in which the context manager manages the lifecycle of temporary resources in accordance with the entry and exit of the `with` block.
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.code:
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    script = Path(tmp) / "job.py"
    suffix = script.suffix
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.question: What does `with` directly refer to in this `tmp` statement?
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.explanation: `TemporaryDirectory()` is a context manager, and when entered with `with ... as tmp`, the path to the temporary directory to be used is bound to `tmp`. This is because the `as` target of the `TemporaryDirectory` context manager holds the name (path) of the created temporary directory. Commonly Confusing Incorrect Answer: The entire Python source code is the value to be written to a separate file, while `tmp` itself is the directory path. Point of misunderstanding: This occurs when the temporary workspace and the contents of the files to be placed within it are confused. `with ... as name` is **syntax that defines both the resource’s lifetime and the binding to be used within the block**.
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.project_context: This ties into a structure that manages temporary Python files and paths with clear lifecycles, rather than forcing long automation code into shell variables.
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.reading_goal_internal: context manager가 with 블록의 진입과 종료에 맞춰 임시 자원의 수명을 관리하는 구조를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `with context_manager() as name:` This sentence describes how the context is entered and ensures that the context manager’s cleanup is performed when the block ends.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Read in the following order: create a context manager → enter → bind to the `as` target → execute the body → handle block exit.
concept_explanation.key_point: A temporary Python script operates in an automation context, and the key point of this card is the structure that entrusts the lifetime of temporary resources to the ``with`` statement.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: `as tmp` It’s easy to assume that ``tmp`` is a permanent directory. However, `` is a path used within the `with` block and will be cleaned up after the block ends.

teaching_example.code:
import tempfile

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    active_inside = isinstance(tmp, str)
teaching_example.walkthrough: Within the ``tmp`` block, `` can be used as a string representing a temporary directory path, and the context manager cleans it up upon exit.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: `TemporaryDirectory()` is a context manager; when entered with `with ... as tmp`, the temporary directory path to be used is bound to `tmp`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: The ``as`` method of the `TemporaryDirectory` context manager is used to retrieve the name (path) of the temporary directory that was created.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: The source content refers to values to be written to a separate file, and ``tmp`` itself is a directory path.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case where the temporary workspace and the contents of the file within it were confused.

answer_explanation.takeaway: `with ... as name` It is **a syntax that reads resource lifetimes and bindings to be used within blocks together**.

lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.title: Convert a string to UTF-8 bytes using `encode("utf-8")`
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.reading_goal: Read the process by which the `encode` string method returns bytes according to the specified encoding rules.
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.question: `raw` What is the data type of ?
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.explanation: `text.encode("utf-8")` encodes a `str` into UTF-8 and returns `bytes`. The assignment statement stores those `bytes` in `raw`. This is because the return value of `str.encode()` is a `bytes` object represented in the specified encoding. A common source of confusion: Although the object passed to `str.encode()` is a `str`, the return value after encoding is a `bytes` object. Point of Misinterpretation: This occurs when the object type and the return type are mistakenly assumed to be the same before the method is called. `encode()` converts **strings to bytes**, while `decode()` converts **bytes to strings**.
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.project_context: It is linked to code that explicitly handles encoding when saving Korean lesson JSON, scripts, and configuration text.
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.reading_goal_internal: 문자열 메서드 encode가 지정한 인코딩 규칙으로 bytes를 반환하는 과정을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `text.encode(encoding)` is a method call that converts a string into bytes according to the specified character-encoding rules.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Check whether the call target is `str`, look at the encoding name inside the parentheses, and connect that to the fact that the return value is `bytes`.
concept_explanation.key_point: Even if the file-saving tool changes, the core of encoding is the conversion rules between text and bytes.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: `encode()` It’s easy to assume that it returns a `str`. The result is a `bytes` object.

teaching_example.code:
text = "hello"
raw = text.encode("utf-8")
teaching_example.walkthrough: Convert the string `hello` to UTF-8 bytes and store them in `raw`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: `text.encode("utf-8")` encodes a `str` into UTF-8 and returns a `bytes` object. The assignment statement stores that `bytes` object in `raw`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the return value of `str.encode()` is bytes represented in the specified encoding.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Although the call target is a `str`, the return value changes to `bytes` after encoding.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case where the object type and the return type were assumed to be the same before the method call.

answer_explanation.takeaway: `encode()` converts **strings to bytes**, while `decode()` converts **bytes to strings**.

lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.title: Interrupting an existing object using an `if membership guard`
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.reading_goal: Read the sequence where a guard `if` immediately raises an exception when the membership condition is true, blocking the later modification flow.
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.question: Does this code reach `status = "write allowed"`?
choices: It is reached only when `target` is `None`.
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.explanation: Since the membership test evaluates to True, the `raise SystemExit(...)` in the if body is executed. Since the normal execution path is interrupted after the `raise`, the subsequent assignment of `status` is not executed. This is because `raise` immediately terminates normal execution and switches to the exception flow. A common source of confusion: Since the `if` body contains a `raise` rather than a simple log statement, the normal code below does not continue. Point of misinterpretation: This occurs when the reader focuses only on the guard condition and fails to verify the control flow behavior of the body. The `overwrite` guard should be interpreted as following this flow: **check status → condition true → immediately terminate with `raise`.**

lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.title: Check for missing "not in" version markers
lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.reading_goal: Read the result of `not in`—which returns True only when the expected marker is not present in the constant string `source`—in the context of a version guard.

lessons/python_powershell_automation_rel.explanation: `expected_marker` is identical to the entire `app` string. Therefore, `marker` exists within `app`, and the result of ``not in`` is `False`. This is because ``x not in y`` is `True` only when `x` is not present in `y`. A common source of confusion: `True`—since the current `marker` actually exists within `app`, the absence condition does not hold. Point of misinterpretation: This occurs when the condition for `not in` is read in reverse. The ``not in`` in the version guard results in `mismatch=True` **only when the expected marker is absent**.

concept_explanation.common_mistake: `not` It’s easy to assume that the value is True just by seeing the word “marker,” even if there is one. ``not in`` is True **only when there is no marker**.

answer_explanation.why_correct: `x not in y` This is because it is True only when x is not inside y.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Since the marker actually exists within the app, the condition of its absence does not hold.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case of reading the true condition of `not in` backward.

answer_explanation.takeaway: The `not in` in the version guard makes `mismatch=True` **only when the expected marker is absent**.

lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.title: In the completed shard, skip execution with ``continue``.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.reading_goal: The `continue` statement skips only the remaining statements of the current iteration without terminating the entire loop.

lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.answer: Skip the current episode’s “`run_shard(shard)`” and move on to the next shard.

When `continue` is executed, the `run_shard(shard)` below is not executed in this iteration. The `for` loop retrieves the next shard and continues. This is because `continue` is defined to skip only the current iteration. Common misconception: It immediately terminates the entire `for` loop. Terminating the entire loop is the role of `break`, while `continue` moves to the next iteration. Key distinction: Understand the difference in control flow between `continue` and `break`. `continue` skips the remaining code of the current iteration and moves to the next iteration.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.project_context: This is a pipeline flow that skips already completed work after interruption/restart and processes only the remaining shards.
