concept_explanation.what_it_is: `continue` is a statement that skips the remaining code in the current iteration and moves on to the next iteration.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: continue Look for the sentence that remains at the same indentation level below and read that it will not be executed in this session.
concept_explanation.key_point: `continue` is different from `break`. It does not terminate the entire loop but moves on to the next item.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that the entire `for` loop terminates when it encounters a completed shard. That behavior is similar to a `break`, whereas `continue` moves on to the next shard.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Since only the `print` statement in the second iteration is skipped, 1 and 3 are printed.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: If the current shard is in the "completed" state, the `if` statement evaluates to `True`. If `continue` is executed, the line below—``run_shard(shard)``—will not be executed in this iteration. The `for` loop then retrieves the next shard and continues.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the definition of `continue` is that it skips only the current iteration.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: The `break` statement terminates the entire loop, while `continue` moves to the next iteration.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Distinguish between the control flow differences of `continue` and `break`.

answer_explanation.takeaway: `continue` skips the remaining code in the current iteration and moves on to the next iteration.

lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.title: Read the last completion point from the checkpoint dictionary
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.reading_goal: Understand that a checkpoint records the last completion point, allowing you to pause and resume later.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.question: What is the role of the checkpoint file that stores `checkpoint["last_done"]` in `shard_0042`?
choices: It records the progress made so that you can resume from that point after pausing.
Make sure every shard is re-run from the beginning each time.
To display only the current date,
To automatically delete completed shard files,
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.answer: It records the progress made so that you can resume from that point after pausing.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.explanation: 1) The `last_done` field in the checkpoint records the last completed shard. 2) The file remains even if the program is interrupted. 3) In the next run, this value can be read to resume from the point where the task was left off. This explanation interprets the Python target of this card—which records how far the task has been completed so it can resume from that point after an interruption—by connecting it to legacy/domain objectives. Common Misconception: It forces all shards to be re-run from the beginning every time. This option focuses only on specific syntax or contextual details of the code and misses the core meaning of the card. Point of Misinterpretation: It focuses solely on matching the string “`shard_0042`,” overlooking why the checkpoint is saved to a file. The checkpoint is a state file designed to **save the last completion point → read it upon restart → resume execution**.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.project_context: This refers to the context of reading the last completed point from a checkpoint when resuming an interrupted batch job.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.reading_goal_internal: checkpoint에 마지막 완료 지점을 기록해 중단 후 재개하는 역할을 이해한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: A `dict key lookup` is a syntax used to retrieve the value of a field with a specific name.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Find the key inside the square brackets in the checkpoint definition and read the value to its right.
concept_explanation.key_point: `last_done` The key point here is that **this value serves as the reference point for the resume**, rather than a value lookup.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: If you focus only on the `shard_0042` string, you’ll miss why checkpoints are saved as files.

teaching_example.code:

print(state["last_page"])
teaching_example.walkthrough: The value of the `last_page` key, which is 7, is printed.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) The `last_done` field in a checkpoint records the last completed shard. 2) The file remains even if the program is interrupted. 3) During the next run, this value can be read to resume execution from the point where it left off.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This explanation interprets the Python target of this card—which states that progress is recorded so that work can be resumed from that point after being interrupted—by linking it to legacy/domain objectives.

common_wrong_choice.choice: Make sure every shard is re-run from the beginning each time.
common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: This option focuses only on certain aspects of the code’s syntax or context and misses the core meaning of the card.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: If you focus only on the `shard_0042` string, you’ll miss why checkpoints are saved as files.

answer_explanation.takeaway: A checkpoint is a state file used to **save the last completion point → read it upon restart → and continue execution**.

lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.title: Expressing verified completion information using a single dict literal
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.reading_goal: Interpret the key-value pairs within the curly braces as indicating that the `marker` is a data structure that preserves both the "validated" state and the row count.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.question: What is the value of the `validated` key in this `done` marker dictionary?
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.explanation: 1) The dict literal has two keys: `validated` and `rows`. 2) The value associated with the `validated` key is the Boolean `True`. 3) The value `200` associated with the `rows` key is a different entry. 4) `done_marker['validated']` returns `True` and prints it.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.project_context: The actual "done" marker also records metadata such as the output hash, row count, and version, allowing for the distinction between a partial output and a successful completion.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.reading_goal_internal: 중괄호 안 key-value 쌍을 읽어 marker가 validated 상태와 row count를 함께 보존하는 자료 구조임을 해석한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: A dictionary literal creates a dictionary object by writing key-value pairs directly into the code in the form ``{key: value, ...}``.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Split the contents of the curly braces into pairs separated by commas, and read what each key refers to.
concept_explanation.key_point: The `validated` key points to `True`, and the `rows` key points to 200.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: There is no need to interpret the order of keys in a `dict literal` as the order of completion or priority. What matters is the meaning of each key-value pair.

teaching_example.code:
status = {"ok": True, "count": 3}
print(status["count"])
teaching_example.walkthrough: The `dict literal` creates two key-value pairs and retrieves the value 3 for the `count` key.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) The dict literal has two keys: `validated` and `rows`. 2) The value associated with the `validated` key is the Boolean `True`. 3) The value `200` associated with the `rows` key is a different entry. 4) `done_marker['validated']` returns `True` and prints it.
answer_explanation.why_correct: In a dictionary literal, the validated key is directly associated with `True`.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: 200 is the value of the `rows` key, not the value of the `validated` key.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Read each key and the value immediately to its right as a pair.

answer_explanation.takeaway: A dictionary literal is read as **identifying key-value pairs → selecting the required key → interpreting the associated value**.

lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.title: `written_rows < expected_rows` Determining Whether It Is a Partial Output
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.reading_goal: It compares the current number of lines written with the expected number of lines to determine, as a Boolean value, whether the actual result has been written incompletely.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.code:
written_rows = 57
expected_rows = 200
is_partial = written_rows < expected_rows
print(is_partial)
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.question: If only 57 lines have been written but 200 lines are expected, what does `is_partial` mean?
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.explanation: 1) The current value of `written_rows` is 57. 2) The current value of `expected_rows` is 200. 3) Evaluating ``57 < 200`` returns True. 4) That Boolean is stored in `is_partial` and printed.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.project_context: This connects to the process of detecting a partial state through count-based verification when a JSONL shard is interrupted midway or when only the file remains after bulk generation.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.reading_goal_internal: 현재 작성 행 수와 기대 행 수를 비교해 실제 결과가 아직 덜 쓰였는지 Boolean으로 판단한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `left < right` compares whether the value on the left is less than the value on the right and returns a Boolean.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Treat the two values as actual numbers and preserve the direction of the inequality.
concept_explanation.key_point: Since 57 is less than 200, the partial check returns True.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: If you omit the comparison of quantities based solely on the fact that the file exists, you may miss the "incomplete output" result.

teaching_example.code:
written = 9
expected = 10
print(written < expected)
teaching_example.walkthrough: Since 9 is less than 10, "True" is printed.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) The current value of `written_rows` is 57. 2) The current value of `expected_rows` is 200. 3) Evaluating ``57 < 200`` returns True. 4) That Boolean is stored in `is_partial` and printed.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the actual number of lines written is less than the expected number of lines.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Because 57 is less than 200, the less-than condition is true.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: It evaluates the numerical comparison itself first, before attempting to infer whether it has been completed.

answer_explanation.takeaway: The less-than comparison is read as **checking both values → applying the `<` direction → performing a Boolean calculation → linking it to the state’s meaning**.

lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.title: Use `and` to require both file existence and successful validation to create a safe skip condition
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.reading_goal: When `output_exists` on the left is True, evaluate `validation_passed` on the right as well; the whole condition is True only if both are True.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.code:
output_exists = True
validation_passed = False
skip_ready = output_exists and validation_passed
print(skip_ready)
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.question: If the file exists but validation fails, what is ``skip_ready``?
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.explanation: 1) The value of `output_exists` is True. 2) Since the left-hand side is truthy, the right-hand side, `validation_passed`, is also evaluated. 3) `validation_passed` is False. 4) The result of combining True and False is False.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.project_context: This ties into the safety principle in the “resume-safe” pipeline, which does not simply check for the presence of “output exists,” but verifies the results or the “done” marker before skipping.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.reading_goal_internal: 왼쪽 output_exists가 True일 때 오른쪽 validation_passed까지 평가하고 둘 다 True여야 전체 조건이 True가 되는 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `A and B` If A is falsy, it stops there; if A is truthy, it evaluates up to B to determine the result.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: The left-hand condition is evaluated first, and only if it is True is the right-hand condition checked.
concept_explanation.key_point: In the example, although a file exists, the validation failed, so the overall result for True and False is False.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: You should not assume that `skip_ready` is True simply because `output_exists` is True.

teaching_example.code:
exists = True
checked = True
print(exists and checked)
teaching_example.walkthrough: Since both the left and right sides are True, the overall result is True.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) The value of `output_exists` is True. 2) Since the left-hand side is truthy, the right-hand side, `validation_passed`, is also evaluated. 3) `validation_passed` is False. 4) The result of combining True and False is False.
answer_explanation.why_correct: The "and" operator evaluates to true only when both conditions are true.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: It is not enough for the file to simply exist; it must also pass the validation criteria on the right.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: In compound conditions, check the Boolean value of each operand separately.

answer_explanation.takeaway: "and guard" is interpreted as **"left evaluation → right evaluation if necessary → passes only if both are true"**.

lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.title: Read the `if` gate that writes the done marker only after validation succeeds
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.reading_goal: Read the sequence where the return value of a function call serves as an `if` condition to determine whether to execute the call to mark completion.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.question: Under what condition does `write_done_marker()` execute?
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.explanation: `validate_output()` The return value serves as the condition for the `if` statement. Only when this value is truthy will the body be executed and the `marker` function be called. This is because the `if` statement determines whether the body is executed based on the truth value of the conditional expression. A common source of confusion: If `run_job()` is simply called, there is a separate validation condition between the `run_job` call and the `marker` call. Point of misinterpretation: This occurs when only the sequential calls are considered, and the “if gate” is ignored. The completion indicator should be read in the following order: **result of the verification call → if evaluation → call to `marker` if successful**.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.project_context: This is linked to a workflow that sets a completion marker before the output verification passes for long batch jobs, preventing them from being resumed incorrectly.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.reading_goal_internal: 함수 호출 반환값이 if 조건이 되어 완료 표시 호출의 실행 여부를 결정하는 순서를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `if condition:` executes the body only when condition is truthy.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: If the condition is a function call, the result of that call is obtained first; after verifying that the result is true, a decision is made on whether to execute the body.
concept_explanation.key_point: For the `done` marker, what matters is not simply that it appears later in the sequence, but rather **whether it is located within a branch that executes only when verification succeeds**.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that a marker is always recorded whenever a validation function is called. However, if the return value is False, the body of the `if` statement is not executed.

teaching_example.walkthrough: `validate()` Since `ga` is `False`, the `if` block is skipped, and `done` is not added to ``events``.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: The return value of `validate_output()` is the `if` condition. Only when this value is truthy does execution enter the body and call the marker function.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the `if` statement determines whether to execute the body based on the truth value of the conditional expression.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: There is a separate validation condition between the `run_job` call and the `marker` call.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case where only sequential calls were considered, and the if gate was ignored.

answer_explanation.takeaway: The completion indicator is read in the following order: **verification call result → if statement → marker call on success**.

lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.title: Reading the positional arguments in `tmp.replace(output)`
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.reading_goal: Read the structure where positional arguments inside the method call parentheses are passed as the destination path for `replace`.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.code:
from pathlib import Path

tmp = Path("result.tmp")
output = Path("result.json")
tmp.replace(output)
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.question: What is the positional argument passed to `replace()` as the destination?
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.explanation: In `tmp.replace(output)`, the `tmp` before the dot is the object calling the method, and the `output` inside the parentheses is the input passed to `replace`. This is because the first expression written inside the parentheses without a name is passed as the first positional argument. Common Confusion: `tmp` is the receiver of the method call, not a positional argument inside the parentheses. Point of Misinterpretation: This occurs when the calling object and the call arguments are not distinguished. A method call should be read as **receiver.method(argument)**.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.project_context: This is linked to a saving pattern where the result is first completed in a temporary file and then replaced with the final path, thereby minimizing the exposure of incomplete files in the event of an intermediate failure.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.reading_goal_internal: 메서드 호출 괄호 안 positional argument가 replace의 목적지 경로로 전달되는 구조를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: In a function or method call, a value passed by position rather than by name is called a positional argument.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Distinguish between the call target and the expression inside the parentheses, and verify the value of each argument.
concept_explanation.key_point: In `tmp.replace(output)`, `tmp` is the caller, and `output` is the destination argument passed to `replace`.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to assume that `output` is the return value of the `replace` call. In this context, however, it is an argument passed to the method as input.

teaching_example.walkthrough: The `output` string is passed as the first positional argument to the `destination` parameter.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: `tmp.replace(output)` In the line “`tmp`,” the part before the dot is the object calling the method, and the part inside the parentheses—`output`—is the input passed to the `replace` method.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the first expression written without a name in parentheses is passed as the first positional argument.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: `tmp` is the receiver of the method call, not a positional argument inside the parentheses.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is an example where the called object and the call arguments are not distinguished.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Read method calls by breaking them down into the **receiver.method(argument)** structure.

lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.title: Reading the upsert status, which can be re-executed with the same key
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.reading_goal: Track the fact that assigning a value to a `dict` key replaces the existing key’s value, and that repeatedly assigning the same value does not change the final state.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.question: After calling `item` twice with the same `upsert(item)`, how many keys does `store` have?
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.explanation: Both calls use the same dict key because ``item['id']`` is ``A``. The second assignment does not add a new key but resets the value of the existing `A`. This is because a dictionary maintains only one entry per key, and assigning a value to an existing key updates that value. A common source of confusion: The fact that the code was executed twice does not mean that two different keys were created. Point of misinterpretation: This occurs when the number of calls is mistakenly equated with the number of dictionary keys. When reading an idempotent storage operation, track **how the key and final value change after re-execution**.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.project_context: This is linked to a structure in batch and collection tasks—which are retried after failure—that prevents the duplicate creation of the same items and ensures convergence to the same final state.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.reading_goal_internal: dict key 대입이 기존 key의 value를 교체하며 같은 값을 반복 대입하면 최종 상태가 달라지지 않는다는 점을 추적한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `mapping[key] = value` is a subscription assignment that stores a value under a specific key in a dictionary.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: First calculate the key expression, then store the right-hand value at that position. If the same key already exists, its previous value is replaced.
concept_explanation.key_point: If you repeatedly save the same item with the same ID, the item is not added repeatedly; instead, the state of the item with that key is maintained.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that since the function was called twice, two dict entries were created. However, a dict does not store duplicate keys.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Since the same dict is stored under the key `X` both times, the final number of keys is one.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: Since `item['id']` is `A` in both calls, they use the same dictionary key. The second assignment does not add a new key but resets the value of the existing `A`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because a `dict` maintains only one instance of each key; assigning a value to an existing key updates that value.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: The fact that it was executed twice does not mean that two different keys were created.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is an example where the number of calls is considered equal to the number of dict keys.

answer_explanation.takeaway: When reading an idempotent save, track **how the key and final value change after re-execution**.

lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.title: Put a failed task into the retry queue with `append()`.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.reading_goal: Track the state change where, after passing the `if` condition, the `list.append` call adds the new ID to the end of the existing queue.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.question: What is the value of `retry_queue` after the code runs?
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.explanation: Since the `failed` value of `item` is `True`, the code enters the `if` block. ``append(item_id)`` appends ``job-2`` to the end of the existing ``job-1``. ``append()`` appends a single value to the end of the existing list. A common source of confusion: `["job-2"]` `append` adds a new item after the existing items without replacing the existing list. Point of Misinterpretation: This occurs when `append` is misread as if it were assigning a new list. The retry queue should be interpreted as following the flow: **check for failure conditions → append failure ID → reprocess later**.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.project_context: This connects to the operational workflow that collects only the items that failed in the collection, conversion, and verification batch for separate retries.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.reading_goal_internal: if 조건을 통과한 뒤 list.append 호출이 기존 queue의 끝에 새 id를 추가하는 상태 변화를 추적한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `list.append(value)` is a method call that adds a single item, `value`, to the end of a list.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Check the list state and argument value before the call, then reflect the post-call state where one item has been added to the end.
concept_explanation.key_point: The purpose of a retry queue is to keep failed items in a separate list so they can be processed again later.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: `append()` It’s easy to assume that it returns a new list. However, it modifies the original list directly.

teaching_example.code:
queue = ["task-1"]
failed_id = "task-3"
queue.append(failed_id)
teaching_example.walkthrough: `task-3` is added to the end of the existing list, so the queue now contains two items.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: Since the `failed` value of `item` is `True`, the code enters the `if` block. The ``append(item_id)`` statement appends ``job-2`` to the existing ``job-1``.
answer_explanation.why_correct: `append()` This is because it adds a single value to the end of the existing list.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: `append` adds a new item to the end of an existing list without overwriting the existing items.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is an example of interpreting `append` as if it were assigning to a new list.

answer_explanation.takeaway: The retry queue follows the flow of **check for failure conditions → append failure ID → reprocess later**.

lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.title: Iterate only through `failed_ids` to selectively re-execute them
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.reading_goal: Read the flow of the for loop, which uses only the list of failures as an iterable to re-execute the code while excluding successful items.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.question: Which of the following best describes the advantage of "failed-only rerun"?
choices: Repeating successful tasks reduces time and costs.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.answer: Repeating successful tasks reduces time and costs.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.explanation: `load_failed_ids` returns only the failed items—item-03 and item-08—and the `for` loop calls `rerun` only for these two items. This is because the iteration itself is limited to the failed items. Common misconception: “It always creates more redundancy.” The goal is to reduce redundant execution of successful items. Point of misinterpretation: This occurs when selective retry and full retry are interpreted in reverse. “Selective retry” should be read as **extract the list of failures → loop only over failed items → reuse successful items**.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.project_context: This connects to an operational pattern that saves resources in long GPU batches or paid LLM calls by rerunning only failed shards or rows.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.reading_goal_internal: 실패 목록만 iterable로 사용해 성공 항목을 제외하고 재실행하는 for loop 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `for item in iterable:` This is a for statement that iterates over the body of the code, adding the values of the iterable to `item` one by one.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Check which values are contained in the collection being iterated over.
concept_explanation.key_point: "Failed-only rerun" allows you to process only the failed items without rerunning the entire batch, thereby reducing time and GPU/API costs.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to think the `for` loop automatically iterates over the entire original task list. Its current iterable is only `failed_ids`.

teaching_example.code:
failed = ["b", "d"]
rerun = []
for item in failed:
    rerun.append(item)
teaching_example.walkthrough: Since only b and d are subject to iteration, only those two values are included in `rerun`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: `load_failed_ids` returns only the failed items `item-03` and `item-08`, so the `for` loop calls `rerun` only for those two items.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because repeated input is restricted to failed items.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: The goal is to reduce redundant execution of successful items.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is an example where "selective re-execution" and "full re-execution" were interpreted incorrectly.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Read selective retry as **extract the failure list → loop over only failed items → reuse successful items**.

lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.title: Select only the “RUNNING” shards from the status table
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.reading_goal: Read the flow that filters only `RUNNING` items from shard-status records to find the pieces currently in progress.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.code:
shards = [
    {"shard_id": "0031", "total": 200, "done": 200, "status": "DONE"},
    {"shard_id": "0067", "total": 200, "done": 154, "status": "RUNNING"},

lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.question: What is the value of `running_ids`?
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.explanation: Among the two rows, only 0067 has a status of RUNNING, so the result of the comprehension is `['0067']`. This is because the filter condition `row['status'] == 'RUNNING'` is True only for 0067. A common source of confusion: ["0031", "0067"] 0031 is excluded from the filter because its status is DONE. Point of misreading: This occurs when the if filter in the comprehension is ignored. Shard monitoring follows the sequence: **status records → filter → extraction of required shard IDs**.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.project_context: It connects to an operations dashboard that allows you to quickly check the status of completed, in-progress, and failed shards when executing large-scale GPU/LLM tasks split into shards.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.reading_goal_internal: shard 상태 레코드에서 RUNNING 항목만 필터링해 현재 진행 중 조각을 찾는 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `[expression for item in items if condition]` This is a filtered list comprehension that adds only items that satisfy the condition to a new list.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Check the iteration target, the value to be inserted into the result, and the final filter condition in that order.
concept_explanation.key_point: By structuring the status by shard, you can quickly identify completed, in-progress, and failed shards.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that all shard_ids are included in the result. Only rows with a status of RUNNING remain.

teaching_example.code:
jobs = [{"id": "a", "status": "DONE"}, {"id": "b", "status": "RUNNING"}]

teaching_example.walkthrough: Since only “b” is RUNNING, “running” is ['b'].

answer_explanation.step_by_step: Of the two rows, only 0067 has a status of RUNNING, so the result of the comprehension is ``['0067']``.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the filter condition `row['status'] == 'RUNNING'` is True only in 0067.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: 0031 is excluded from the filter because its status is DONE.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case where the `if` filter in `comprehension` was ignored.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Shard monitoring is described as **state record → filter → extraction of required shard IDs**.

lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.title: Convert `done/total` and the shard ID into `progress` f-strings
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.reading_goal: Read the process by which several progress state variables are inserted into an f-string to form a single line of human-readable log.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.code:

shard_id = "0067"
message = f"DONE {done}/{total} shard={shard_id}"
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.question: What is the value of `message`?
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.explanation: The values of the three variables are inserted into the f-string in order, resulting in `DONE 154/200 shard=0067`. This is because the f-string evaluates the expression within the curly braces to its current value. A common source of confusion: DONE {done}/{total} shard={shard_id} This format represents the template as it appears before the f-string is evaluated. Point of confusion: This is the case before f-string substitution is applied. The progress log is structured as **key status value → f-string → operational message that can be read at a glance**.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.project_context: This ties into operations where progress on time-consuming tasks—such as node extraction, LoRA, and large-scale validation—is tracked via brief logs.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.reading_goal_internal: 여러 진행 상태 변수가 f-string에 삽입되어 사람이 읽기 쉬운 로그 한 줄이 되는 과정을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: An f-string is a syntax that constructs a string by inserting the current value into the `{expression}` placeholder.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Check the current value of the variable inside each set of curly braces and combine it with a literal string.
concept_explanation.key_point: For long tasks, include both the "done" and "total" counts along with the shard ID to make it easy to determine whether the task is in progress or has been paused.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: `{done}` It’s easy to assume that the same characters will be printed as-is. In f-strings, they are replaced with variable values.

teaching_example.code:
done = 3
total = 5
msg = f"DONE {done}/{total}"
teaching_example.walkthrough: "msg" becomes `DONE 3/5`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: The values of the three variables are inserted into the f-string in order, resulting in `DONE 154/200 shard=0067`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the f-string evaluates the expression within the curly braces to its current value.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: This is the template before the f-string is evaluated.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case of not applying f-string substitution.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Create the **progress log** by converting **key state values → f-strings → operational messages that are easy to read at a glance**.

lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.title: Read a `while` loop that records a heartbeat while running.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.reading_goal: Read the condition check and termination flow of the `while` loop that records the heartbeat as long as the `liveness` flag is true.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.code:
heartbeats = []

def write_heartbeat(timestamp):
    heartbeats.append(timestamp)

running = True
while running:
    write_heartbeat("10:04")
    running = False
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.question: What does `heartbeat` primarily indicate?
choices: Has the Git remote address changed?
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.explanation: While the `while` loop is executing, the heartbeat logging function is called to demonstrate that the process is running periodically. This is because a heartbeat is a typical liveness signal. A common source of confusion: Just because the correct answer is always returned does not guarantee that the process is alive or that the result is correct. Point of misinterpretation: This is a case where liveness and quality verification are confused. Operational status should be interpreted by **separating liveness signals from result verification**.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.project_context: This is linked to the operation of a watchdog or heartbeat mechanism that monitors whether a process has stopped when running long-running model inference or batch jobs on a server.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.reading_goal_internal: liveness flag가 참인 동안 heartbeat를 기록하는 while loop의 조건 검사와 종료 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `while condition:` is a while statement that repeats the body as long as `condition` is truthy.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Track the value of the condition before the loop and how that condition changes within the loop body.
concept_explanation.key_point: A heartbeat is used not to assess the quality of the results, but to verify that the process is still active and is periodically sending a signal.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that if there’s a heartbeat, the task results are always normal. Liveness and correctness are separate concepts.

teaching_example.code:
running = True
beats = []
while running:
    beats.append("alive")
    running = False
teaching_example.walkthrough: Once “alive” is recorded, “running” becomes False, and the loop ends.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: While the `while` loop is running, the `heartbeat` function is called to indicate that the process is running periodically.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because a heartbeat is a typical liveness signal.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: The fact that a process is still running does not guarantee the correctness of the result.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is an instance where "liveness" was confused with "quality verification."

answer_explanation.takeaway: Read operational state by **separating liveness signals from result validation**.

lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.title: Find the impact of changing the crash-recovery completion decision on `pending` and downstream artifacts.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.reading_goal: Based on the current behavior—where the `for` loop checks each job and leaves items not found in ``validated_done`` in the `pending` queue—we will determine which jobs are incorrectly excluded and assess the scope of that impact if the completion criterion is changed to simply the existence of a checkpoint.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.question: If a patch were made to change the current `validated_done` standard to the `checkpoint_done` standard, what would be the most significant scope of impact?
choices: Even though shard_02 has not yet completed verification, it is removed from the "pending" state and is not re-executed, which may result in missing downstream results that depend on it.
The `for` loop is automatically converted to parallel execution
The order of the `jobs` list is automatically reversed
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.answer: Even though shard_02 has not yet completed verification, it is removed from the "pending" state and is not re-executed, which may result in missing downstream results that depend on it.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.explanation: 1) Currently, the `for` loop is checking `shard_01`, `shard_02`, and `shard_03` in sequence. 2) Since `validated_done` contains only `shard_01`, `shard_02` and `shard_03` remain in `pending`. 3) Since shard_02 is also in `checkpoint_done`, changing the `authority` condition removes shard_02 from `pending`. 4) However, since shard_02 is not in `validated_done`, its actual completion has not been verified. 5) Therefore, the impact extends not only to the omission of re-executing shard_02 but also to the downstream stage that merges its output.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.project_context: This addresses a weakness in APEX where, after modifying a single line of code, the impact on surrounding calls and data was not sufficiently explained. The same line of reasoning can be applied to resume-safe pipelines, checkpoints, and cache-validity determinations.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.reading_goal_internal: for 반복이 각 job을 검사해 `validated_done`에 없는 항목을 pending에 남기는 현재 동작을 읽고, 완료 기준을 단순 checkpoint 존재로 바꾸면 어떤 job이 잘못 제외되는지와 그 영향 범위를 판단한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `for job in jobs:` iterates through the items in `jobs` one by one. In recovery logic, the actual scope of re-execution is determined not only by the loop itself but also by the “completion authority” referenced by the loop body.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: For each job, verify the difference between `validated_done` and `checkpoint_done`, and when conditions change, confirm that jobs removed from the `pending` state have actually been validated. Next, examine the downstream stages that use the output from those removed jobs.
concept_explanation.key_point: shard_02 has a checkpoint but is not included in validated_done. Therefore, while the current code leaves shard_02 as a candidate for re-execution, a patch that relies solely on checkpoints might incorrectly skip shard_02.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: Do not immediately treat the existence of a checkpoint file as proof of completion. Since it could represent partial output, a marker just before failure, or a corrupted output, it must be distinguished from actual verification completion.

teaching_example.walkthrough: "a" is excluded because it has been verified, while "b" remains in "pending" because it has not been verified. The key point is not whether the file exists, but which set of completion statuses is used as the authority.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) Currently, the `for` loop is checking `shard_01`, `shard_02`, and `shard_03` in sequence. 2) Since `validated_done` contains only `shard_01`, `shard_02` and `shard_03` remain in `pending`. 3) Since shard_02 is also in `checkpoint_done`, changing the `authority` condition removes shard_02 from `pending`. 4) However, since shard_02 is not in `validated_done`, its actual completion has not been verified. 5) Therefore, the impact extends not only to the omission of re-executing shard_02 but also to the downstream stage that merges its output.
answer_explanation.why_correct: What the patch changes is not simply the set name, but the “authority that considers it complete.” If an unverified shard is skipped, the output of that shard—as well as the aggregates and manifests that use it—may be incorrect.

common_wrong_choice.choice: The `for` loop is automatically converted to parallel execution
common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Changing the set of completions only alters the membership determination; it does not convert a regular for loop into parallel syntax.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Don’t just look at the modified lines; track the targets that are executed or skipped based on those conditions, along with their downstream consumers.

answer_explanation.takeaway: The scope of impact is traced from **modified evaluation criteria → changed execution targets → generated/missing output → downstream consumers**.

reading_steps: Currently, the `for` loop is checking `shard_01`, `shard_02`, and `shard_03` in sequence.
Since `validated_done` contains only `shard_01`, `shard_02` and `shard_03` currently remain in `pending`.
Because `checkpoint_done` also contains `shard_02`, changing the condition authority removes `shard_02` from `pending`.
However, since shard_02 is not in validated_done, its completion has not been verified.
Therefore, the scope of impact includes not only the omission of the re-execution of shard_02 but also the downstream stage where its output is combined.

lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.title: Grouping final output information into a dict literal
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.reading_goal: Read the structure where three key-value pairs within curly braces form a single manifest dictionary.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.question: What is the value of `manifest['rows']`?
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.explanation: 1) Find the `rows` key. 2) The value associated with that key is 120. 3) The square bracket lookup returns 120.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.project_context: It is connected to the audit workflow that seals the KG pack, lesson batch, and shard output into the final manifest.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.reading_goal_internal: 중괄호 안 key-value 쌍 세 개가 하나의 manifest dict가 되는 구조를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: A dict literal creates a single mapping consisting of `{key: value}` pairs.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Ensure that the key on the left of each colon corresponds exactly to the value on the right.
concept_explanation.key_point: `manifest` groups filenames, row counts, and validation statuses into the same record for tracking.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to count the number of words in an internal string as the number of items in a dictionary.

teaching_example.code:
m={"name":"a","status":"PASS"}
print(len(m))
teaching_example.walkthrough: Since there are two key-value pairs, the length is 2.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) Find the `rows` key. 2) The value associated with that key is 120. 3) The square bracket lookup returns 120.
answer_explanation.why_correct: The value of the `rows` key is stored as the integer 120.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: 3 refers only to the number of keys in the manifest; it is not the value of `rows`.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: It is easy to count the number of words in an internal string as the number of items in a dictionary.

answer_explanation.takeaway: A dictionary literal reads the key-value pairs first.

lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.title: Skip the current iteration using `continue` in the `complete` shard
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.reading_goal: `continue` skips the remaining body of the current iteration and moves to the next item.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.question: What is the shard remaining in `ran`?
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.explanation: 1) s1 is "done," so it continues. 2) s2 is not "done," so it is appended. 3) s3 is also "done," so it continues. 4) Therefore, only s2 is executed.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.project_context: It connects to the resume-safe pattern, which prevents duplicate processing of verified shards during node-pass re-execution.
lessons/python_resume_safe_pipeline_chec.reading_goal_internal: `continue`가 현재 반복의 남은 본문을 건너뛰고 다음 항목으로 이동하는 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `continue` interrupts the current iteration of the nearest loop and moves on to the next iteration.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Verify that the conditions under which `continue` is executed and the subsequent call to `run_shard` are within the same loop body.
concept_explanation.key_point: In a completed shard, `run_shard` is not called again.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to confuse `continue` with `break` because `continue` terminates the entire `for` loop.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Skip only the 2nd iteration, resulting in [1, 3].

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) s1 is "done," so it continues. 2) s2 is not "done," so it is appended. 3) s3 is also "done," so it continues. 4) Therefore, only s2 is executed.
answer_explanation.why_correct: Since completed items are skipped using `continue`, only s2 remains.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Those two are, in fact, skipped completion shards.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: It is easy to confuse `continue` with `break` because `continue` terminates the entire `for` loop.

answer_explanation.takeaway: "continue" skips the text below in the current session and moves to the next iteration.

lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.title: Comparing Function Results with Expected Values Using `assert`
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.reading_goal: Read the flow of the `assert` statement, which checks whether a condition is `True` and raises an `AssertionError` if it is `False`.
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.question: If the `assert` statement in this code passes, what is the final output?
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.explanation: `add(2, 3)` returns 5. `5 == 5` is True. The `assert` passes, and `test_add` ends. Then, `print("passed")` is executed. This is because the `assert` condition is true, so execution is not interrupted. Common misconception: Since the AssertionError comparison condition is True, an AssertionError does not occur. Point of confusion: The condition following `assert` is first evaluated as an actual value. `assert` fails when the condition is False and proceeds to the next code when it is True.
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.project_context: The context is reading unit test code to quickly verify the expected behavior of a single small function.
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.reading_goal_internal: assert statement가 조건이 True인지 검사하고 False일 때 AssertionError를 발생시키는 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `assert condition` is a verification statement that expects `condition` to be true. If it is false, an `AssertionError` is raised.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: The condition following `assert` is evaluated using the actual value to determine whether it is True or False.
concept_explanation.key_point: `assert` is not a statement that prints a value. If the condition is met, execution proceeds to the next line; if it fails, an exception is raised.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that the number 5 following `assert` will be printed. However, 5 is used only for comparing the expected value; the print statement is separate.

teaching_example.code:
def square(x):
    return x * x

assert square(4) == 16
print("ok")
teaching_example.walkthrough: Since `square(4)` is 16, the condition is True, so the `assert` is passed and `ok` is printed.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: `add(2, 3)` returns 5. `5 == 5` is True. The `assert` passes, and `test_add` ends. Afterward, `print("passed")` is executed.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the `assert` condition is true, so execution does not stop.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Since the comparison condition is True, an AssertionError is not raised.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: The condition following `assert` is evaluated first using actual values.

answer_explanation.takeaway: `assert` fails when the condition is `False` and proceeds to the next line of code when it is `True`.

lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.title: Check the status of multiple components together at `and`
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.reading_goal: and boolean operations evaluate to true when all conditions are true.
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.code:
app_ok = True
lessons_ok = True
cards_ok = True
integration_ok = app_ok and lessons_ok and cards_ok
print(integration_ok)
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.question: What is the final output when all three states are ``True``?
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.explanation: `app_ok` is True, `lessons_ok` is True, and `cards_ok` is True. When these three values are combined with `and`, the result is True because all items in the `and` condition are True. Commonly Confused Incorrect Answer: False—There are no items that are False. Point of Misinterpretation: Check the current values of the three variables one by one. ``and`` is true only when all the connected conditions are true.
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.project_context: This is the context of reading an integration test scenario where multiple components—such as app and lesson loading, and card validation—must all succeed simultaneously.
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.reading_goal_internal: and boolean operation이 여러 조건이 모두 참일 때 참으로 평가되는 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `and` is a Boolean operator that evaluates to true only when both conditions are true. Multiple conditions can be chained together.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: It checks whether each value, starting from the left, is truthy; if even one is False, the entire expression evaluates to False.
concept_explanation.key_point: In integration context, individual components can each succeed while their connection state still needs separate verification. The Python focus of this card is combining three Booleans with `and`.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that if just one of three values is True, the whole expression is True. That behavior is similar to “or,” whereas “and” requires all values to be True.

teaching_example.code:
db_ok = True
api_ok = False
print(db_ok and api_ok)
teaching_example.walkthrough: Since `api_ok` is False, the result of the entire `and` operation is False.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: `app_ok` is True, `lessons_ok` is True, and `cards_ok` is True. When these three values are combined with the `and` operator, they are all true, so the overall result is also True.
answer_explanation.why_correct: and because all items in the condition are True.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: There are no items marked as "False."
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Check the current values of the three variables one by one.

answer_explanation.takeaway: `and` is true only when all of the connected conditions are true.

lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.target_statement: integration_ok = app_ok and lessons_ok and cards_ok

lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.title: Both existing and new features must function correctly to pass the regression gate.
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.reading_goal: First evaluate the result on the left side of “and”; if it is true, then check the right side as well. The flow is such that both evaluations must be true for the entire gate to be true.
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.code:
old_cards_ok = True
new_cards_ok = True
regression_ok = old_cards_ok and new_cards_ok
print(regression_ok)
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.question: What is `regression_ok` when both the existing card and the new card validation are True?
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.explanation: 1) `old_cards_ok` is True. 2) Since the left side is truthy, the right side, `new_cards_ok`, is also evaluated. 3) `new_cards_ok` is also True. 4) The result of True and True is True.
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.project_context: After adding a new lesson, this is linked to regression testing, which re-verifies the existing rules for card loading, correct answers, and references.
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.reading_goal_internal: and의 왼쪽 결과를 먼저 평가하고 참일 때 오른쪽까지 확인해 두 검증이 모두 참이어야 전체 gate가 참이 되는 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `A and B` does not evaluate the right-hand side if A is falsy; if A is truthy, it evaluates B as well to determine the final result.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Start by reviewing the verification results on the left, and when they are True, check the verification results on the right.
concept_explanation.key_point: Since both values are True, `regression_ok` is also True.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: I don’t believe that regression tests will pass just because new features are implemented. Maintaining existing features is also necessary.

teaching_example.code:
old_ok = True
new_ok = False
print(old_ok and new_ok)
teaching_example.walkthrough: Since the right-hand side is False, the overall result is False.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) `old_cards_ok` is True. 2) Since the left side is truthy, the right side, `new_cards_ok`, is also evaluated. 3) `new_cards_ok` is also True. 4) The result of True and True is True.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because both operands of “and” are True.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Currently, none of the two verification results are False.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Check the verification values for existing and new features, respectively.

answer_explanation.takeaway: The quality gate is interpreted as **check left → check right if necessary → pass only when all are true**.

lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.title: Pass two key state values to the `smoke_check(...)` function call to perform a quick initial check
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.reading_goal: Read the call sequence where the two argument values are evaluated first and passed to the function parameters, and the function returns whether the test passes or fails.
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.code:
def smoke_check(core_ready, screen_rendered):
    return core_ready and screen_rendered

core_ready = True

print(smoke_check(core_ready, screen_rendered))
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.question: What is the return value of `smoke_check` when both key conditions are True?
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.explanation: 1) The current values of `core_ready` and `screen_rendered` are both `True`. 2) These two values are passed to the corresponding function parameters in order. 3) The function body evaluates `True` and `True`. 4) `return` returns `True` to the caller.
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.project_context: In an actual smoke test, we briefly check not only the responses from key files but also basic product flows, such as minimal rendering and console errors.
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.reading_goal_internal: 두 argument 값을 먼저 평가해 함수 parameter에 전달하고 함수가 기본 통과 여부를 반환하는 호출 순서를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: A function call evaluates the arguments and passes them to the function, then receives the return value as the result of the call after the body is executed.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Read in the following order: function name, current values of each argument, parameter binding, and return value.
concept_explanation.key_point: Since both conditions are True, the function returns True.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: You should not assume that this local model performs actual HTTP requests or browser rendering. It is a training model that combines previously observed state values.

teaching_example.walkthrough: When True and False are passed as parameters, the function returns False.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) The current values of `core_ready` and `screen_rendered` are both `True`. 2) These two values are passed to the corresponding function parameters in order. 3) The function body evaluates `True` and `True`. 4) `return` returns `True` to the caller.
answer_explanation.why_correct: Both input states are true, so the function’s `and` result is True.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Since both inputs are currently True, there are no failure conditions.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Distinguish, in order, between the values passed to the function and the results of calculations performed within the function.

answer_explanation.takeaway: A function call proceeds as follows: **argument evaluation → parameter binding → body execution → return value reception**.

lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.title: `actual == expected` Compare the actual output to the approved "golden" standard to verify they match
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.reading_goal: After checking the current values of both data structures, the flow checks for equality; if the contents match, it returns True.
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.code:
expected = ["A", "B"]
actual = ["A", "B"]
matches_golden = actual == expected
print(matches_golden)
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.question: What is the result of comparing the actual and expected values?
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.explanation: 1) `expected` is a list containing two strings, A and B. 2) `actual` also contains the same two strings, A and B, in the same order. 3) `==` compares the equality of the values in the two lists. 4) Since the contents are the same, `True` is returned.
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.project_context: We modeled the core comparison operations of golden-file testing—which compares generated results or manifest formats against approved standards—as in-memory values.
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.reading_goal_internal: 양쪽 자료구조의 현재 값을 확인한 뒤 equality 비교가 내용이 같으면 True를 만드는 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `left == right` It compares whether the two values are equal and returns a Boolean.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: First, we unpack the actual values of `expected` and `actual` to check whether they have the same structure and values.
concept_explanation.key_point: Since the two lists contain the same two strings in the same order, the equality result is True.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: If the "golden" result differs, you should not automatically assume that the actual code contains a bug. If the requirements have changed, the "golden" result itself may need to be updated.

teaching_example.code:
expected = [1, 2]
actual = [1, 3]
print(actual == expected)
teaching_example.walkthrough: Since the second item is different, the result of the equality comparison is False.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) `expected` is a list containing two strings, A and B. 2) `actual` also contains the same two strings, A and B, in the same order. 3) `==` compares the equality of the values in the two lists. 4) Since the contents are the same, `True` is returned.
answer_explanation.why_correct: The two lists have the same length, order, and item values.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: That list consists of operand values, and the final result of the equality expression is a Boolean.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Distinguish between the value being compared and the comparison expression from the newly created Boolean.

answer_explanation.takeaway: "equality" is read as **check left-hand value → check right-hand value → compare for equality → Boolean result**.

lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.title: Comparing current output and saved snapshots using ==
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.reading_goal: It determines whether snapshot regression has occurred by comparing the actual values of the two rendering strings using equality.
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.question: What value is stored in `matches_snapshot`?
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.explanation: The two strings have the same “button” structure, but their internal text differs: “`Retry`” and “`Save`.” Therefore, the comparison ``==`` returns `False`, because string equality returns `True` only when all character sequences are identical. Common misconception: True. Even if the tags are the same, the internal string values are different, so the entire strings are not identical. Point of confusion: This occurs when users confuse similar structures with values that are exactly the same. A snapshot comparison **exactly compares the current value with the reference value to check for differences**.
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.project_context: It is linked to regression tests that compare the output to previously approved results to check for any unintended changes in the rendering structure.
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.reading_goal_internal: 두 rendering 문자열의 실제 값을 equality로 비교해 snapshot regression 여부를 판단한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `left == right` compares whether two values are equal and returns a boolean.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Check the actual values of the current output and the expected output, respectively, and then compare them to see if they are exactly the same.
concept_explanation.key_point: The domain objective of the snapshot test is change detection, and the direct result of Python syntax is a True/False equality check.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that strings are True if they look almost the same. `==` returns True only if the actual values are exactly the same.

teaching_example.code:
current = "<button>Save</button>"
saved = "<button>Save</button>"
matches = current == saved
teaching_example.walkthrough: Since the two strings are exactly the same, ``matches`` is True.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: The two strings have the same button structure, but their internal text differs: “`Retry`” and “`Save`.” Therefore, the comparison ``==`` returns `False`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because string equality returns True only when all character sequences are identical.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Even if the tags are the same, the entire strings are not identical because their internal string values differ.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is an example of confusing something with a similar structure with something that has exactly the same value.

answer_explanation.takeaway: A snapshot comparison **accurately compares the current value with the reference value to check for any differences**.

lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.title: Reading the `choices` field from the fixture dictionary
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.reading_goal: Reads the value of the key specified in the test fixture dictionary via a subscription.
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.question: What value is stored in `choices`?
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.explanation: `fixture_card['choices']` It retrieves the `choices` key. Since the associated value is ``['A', 'B']``, that list is stored in the left-hand variable. This is because a dictionary lookup returns the value associated with the key. A common source of confusion: A. A is the value of the ``answer`` key, but the key being looked up here is `choices`. Common misreading: This occurs when you fail to verify the actual key inside the square brackets among the fixture’s various fields. When reading fixture data, you must **accurately match the key inside the square brackets with its associated value**.
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.project_context: This connects to a workflow that reliably checks validation and rendering results by reusing the same card structure across multiple tests.
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.reading_goal_internal: 테스트용 fixture dict에서 지정한 key의 value를 subscription으로 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `mapping[key]` is a subscription that reads the value associated with the given key in a dict.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: After accurately verifying the key inside the square brackets, find the value for that key in the dict.
concept_explanation.key_point: A fixture is a test context, and the focus of the Python grammar is on reading specific fields from prepared test data.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to think the key string `choices` itself is the result. Subscription returns the value associated with that key.

teaching_example.code:
fixture = {"id": "T1", "expected": 3}
expected = fixture["expected"]
teaching_example.walkthrough: The value 3 of the "expected key" is stored in a variable.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: `fixture_card['choices']` It looks up the `choices` key. Since the associated value is ``['A', 'B']``, that list is stored in the variable on the left.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because a `dict` subscription returns the value associated with the key.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: A is the value of the `answer` key, and the currently selected key is `choices`.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case where the actual bracket key was not checked among the various fields of the fixture.

answer_explanation.takeaway: When reading fixture data, **make sure to accurately match the keys inside the square brackets with their corresponding values**.

lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.title: Using `assert` to check if `actual` and `expected` are the same
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.reading_goal: It evaluates the actual Boolean value of the expression following `assert` to determine whether the test passes.
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.code:
lesson_cards = [None] * 923
expected = 923
actual = len(lesson_cards)
assert actual == expected
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.question: What does this `assert` statement directly check for?
choices: whether the actual and expected values match
whether to increase the number of lesson_cards to 923
Is the data type of `actual` a list?
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.answer: whether the actual and expected values match
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.explanation: An assertion (`actual == expected`) is followed by a comparison expression. Therefore, this statement checks whether the values of `actual` and `expected` are the same. This is because an assertion is a statement that verifies the truth value of the expression that follows it. A common source of confusion: The equality operator ``==`` was used instead of the assignment operator ``=``, which would imply that `expected` is being assigned to `actual`. Point of misinterpretation: This is a case where the roles of ``==`` and ``=`` were confused. `assert` is **not a statement that changes a condition, but a statement that verifies whether a condition is true**.
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.project_context: It is linked to a test flow that automatically verifies whether the rewritten result—such as the number of cards, a set of IDs, or output values—meets the expected contract.
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.reading_goal_internal: assert 뒤 비교식의 실제 boolean 값을 계산해 테스트가 통과하는지 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: The `assert condition` statement checks whether `condition` is truthy; if it is falsy, it raises an `AssertionError`.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: It actually calculates the value of the condition behind the `assert` before evaluating the `assert` itself.
concept_explanation.key_point: Don’t assume it’s correct just by looking at the variable names “expected” and “actual”; you must verify the result of the comparison between the two values.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to think that `assert` makes two values equal. However, `assert` does not modify any values; it only checks the condition.

teaching_example.code:
expected = 4
actual = 5
assert actual == expected
teaching_example.walkthrough: Since `5 == 4` is False, this assert raises an AssertionError.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: An `actual == expected` comparison follows `assert`. Therefore, this statement checks whether the values of `actual` and `expected` are the same.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because `assert` is a statement that verifies the truth value of the expression that follows it.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: The equality operator `==` was used instead of the assignment operator `=`.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is an example of confusion between the roles of `==` and `=`.

answer_explanation.takeaway: `assert` is **a statement that verifies whether a condition is true, not one that changes the condition**.

lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.title: Use `in` to check if a specific situation is included in the list of edge cases
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.reading_goal: Use a membership test to verify whether a specific string value actually exists in a list.
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.question: What value is stored in `has_broken_json`?
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.explanation: If you look at the `cases` list, you’ll see “`broken_json`” at the end. Since the same string exists, ``in`` returns `True`. This is because the membership test returns `True` if the value being searched for exists in the collection. A common source of confusion: `False`, where `broken_json` is explicitly listed as an actual list item. Common misreading: This occurs when the list is not checked all the way to the end. Even for edge cases, the list must be **checked one by one to verify whether the actual value is included**.
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.project_context: This ties into the process of explicitly including edge cases—such as empty inputs, duplicates, and corrupted JSON—as well as valid cards in the regression test list.
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.reading_goal_internal: 리스트에 특정 문자열 값이 실제로 존재하는지 membership test로 확인한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `value in collection` checks whether the collection contains the same value and returns a Boolean.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Check the value to be found on the left and compare it with the actual items in the collection.
concept_explanation.key_point: Apart from the “edge case” test category, Python only checks whether a string value is actually contained.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to assume that strings with similar meanings are True. The `in` operator checks for values that are exactly the same as the actual elements in a collection.

teaching_example.code:
cases = ["empty", "duplicate"]
has_timeout = "timeout" in cases
teaching_example.walkthrough: Since there is no "timeout" string, the result is False.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: If you look at the `cases` list, `broken_json` is at the end. Since the same string exists, `in` returns True.
answer_explanation.why_correct: The membership test returns True if the value being searched for exists in the collection.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: `broken_json` is explicitly defined as an actual list item.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case where the list was not reviewed in its entirety.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Read the list of edge cases by **checking each one to see if it includes the actual values**.

lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.title: Defining a FakeLLM test double instead of the actual API
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.reading_goal: Read the structure that defines a fake class with a `generate` method similar to the actual provider, allowing testing without an external API.
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.question: What is the main reason for using `FakeLLM`?
choices: To test the call flow without incurring actual LLM API costs,
To avoid ever disclosing actual API keys,
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.answer: To test the call flow without incurring actual LLM API costs,
lessons/python_tests_regression_quality_.explanation: Since the FakeLLM object returns a fixed response to `generate` calls, no actual API requests are required at all. This is because the purpose of a test double is to replace external dependencies and reliably test the target code flow. A common source of confusion: It is designed to allow testing without actual provider credentials, precisely to avoid exposing real API keys. Point of Misinterpretation: This occurs when the roles of the fake and the actual provider calls are reversed. A test double is defined as **the same interface + controlled results + elimination of external dependencies**.
