lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.project_context: This relates to a context where simple verification conditions are used to check whether the uniqueness rule of a `set` is maintained in code that requires duplicate removal.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.reading_goal_internal: add 호출 뒤 실제 set 길이를 구하고 오른쪽 정수 1과 같은지 비교해 Boolean을 만드는 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `a == b` compares whether two values are equal; if they are, it returns True; if they are not, it returns False.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: First, we retrieve the current value of `len(tags)`, then compare that integer with the number 1 to the right.
concept_explanation.key_point: Since a set does not allow duplicate elements, `len(tags)` remains 1 even after adding `python` again.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to assume that “add” refers to two saves and therefore interpret the length as 2.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Even if you add the same x again, the number of elements in the set remains 1, so the equality test returns True.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) Initially, `tags` contains one Python element. 2) Although the same Python element is added again, no duplicate elements are created in the set. 3) Therefore, `len(tags)` is 1. 4) The comparison `1 == 1` evaluates to `True`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: Since the length of the set remains 1 even after adding duplicates, the result of the equality comparison is True.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: 2 is a value resulting from a misunderstanding of `add` as simple cumulative storage, and a `set` does not retain duplicate elements.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: It is easy to assume that “add” refers to two saves and therefore interpret the length as 2.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Read a comparison as **calculate the actual values on both sides → test their relationship → produce a Boolean result**.

lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.title: Expand the two sets using * and merge them into a single new set
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.reading_goal: Read the flow where the elements of `left` and `right` are spread out into a new set, and duplicate `ai`s are reduced to a single instance.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.question: What are the unique combinations of values included in `combined`?
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.explanation: 1) Expand “python” and “ai” on the left. 2) Expand “ai” and “web” on the right. 3) Only one instance of “ai” is retained. 4) The three unique values—“python,” “ai,” and “web”—remain.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.project_context: This relates to situations where sets of tags or concepts from multiple sources are combined.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.reading_goal_internal: left와 right의 원소가 새 set에 각각 펼쳐지고 중복 ai는 한 번만 남는 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `*iterable` is star unpacking: it expands the iterable's values one by one inside the surrounding collection expression.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: `{*left, *right}` It reads that elements from `left` and `right` are added to a new set.
concept_explanation.key_point: A set does not allow duplicate elements with the same value.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to assume that `*left` inserts the left set itself as a single element or that the order of elements in the resulting set is fixed.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Three unique values—x, y, and z—remain, so the length is 3.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) Expand “python” and “ai” on the left. 2) Expand “ai” and “web” on the right. 3) Only one instance of “ai” is retained. 4) The three unique values—“python,” “ai,” and “web”—remain.
answer_explanation.why_correct: After expanding all elements of the two inputs, the set’s deduplication rule is applied.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: The set that contains only "ai" is the intersection.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: It is easy to assume that `*left` inserts the left set itself as a single element or that the order of elements in the resulting set is fixed.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Star unpacking is read in the following order: unpack elements → apply the outer collection’s rules → construct the result.

lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.title: Use set comprehension to retain only the values present in the set on the right
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.reading_goal: Read the flow of the code: iterate through `left` and add only elements that also exist in `right` to a new set.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.question: What value remains in `common`?
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.explanation: 1) Each element of `left` is treated as an `item`. 2) `python` is excluded because it is not present in `right`. 3) `ai` is present in `right` as well, so it satisfies the condition. 4) Only `ai` is added to `common`.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.project_context: This ties into the process of filtering to identify the common ground between the concepts learned and those required by the problem.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.reading_goal_internal: left를 순회해 right에도 있는 원소만 새 set에 넣는 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: A set comprehension, in the form `{expression for item in iterable...}`, creates a new set from the results of an iteration.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: It takes items one by one from `left` and adds the preceding item to the result only if it passes the subsequent `if` condition.
concept_explanation.key_point: "Python" is excluded, leaving only "AI" on both sides.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to overlook the `if` condition and assume that all values in `left` are included, or that `web`—which appears only in `right`—is also included.

teaching_example.walkthrough: When iterating through `a`, only the `y` values that also appear in `b` are added to `common`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) Each element of `left` is treated as an `item`. 2) `python` is excluded because it is not present in `right`. 3) `ai` is present in `right` as well, so it satisfies the condition. 4) Only `ai` is added to `common`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: There is only one value, "ai," that is common to both sets.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: "python" is not on the right.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: It’s easy to overlook the `if` condition and assume that all values in `left` are included, or that `web`—which appears only in `right`—is also included.

answer_explanation.takeaway: "comprehension" is read in the following order: selecting iterated values → checking conditions → adding values that pass the check.

lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.target_statement: common = {item for item in left if item in right}
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.focus_span: {item for item in left if item in right}

lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.title: Check whether "learned" is an element not present in "needed" using "not in"
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.reading_goal: It reads the condition where, if the current item is not in `needed`, the result is `True` and remains in the set difference.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.question: When `item` is `print`, what is the result of `item not in needed`?
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.explanation: 1) The current item is `print`. 2) `needed` contains only `if` and `for`. 3) `print` cannot be found in `needed`. 4) The result of `not in` is `True`.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.project_context: This ties into identifying the gap between what has already been learned and what is currently needed.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.reading_goal_internal: 현재 item이 needed에 없으면 True가 되어 차집합 결과에 남는 조건을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `value not in collection` Returns True when the left-hand value is not in the right-hand collection.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: It checks the actual string of `item` against the elements of `needed` to see if any match.
concept_explanation.key_point: "print" is not listed under "needed," but "if" and "for" are.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to misinterpret “not in” as a deletion command or to read the set difference direction in the opposite direction.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Since `a` is not in `used`, it is `True`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) The current item is `print`. 2) `needed` contains only `if` and `for`. 3) `print` cannot be found in `needed`. 4) The result of `not in` is `True`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: Since `print` is not present in `needed`, the result is `True`.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: For the expression to evaluate to `False`, `print` must be in `needed`.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: It is easy to misinterpret “not in” as a deletion command or to read the set difference direction in the opposite direction.

answer_explanation.takeaway: "not in" is interpreted as: check the left-hand value → search the right-hand collection → return True if not found.

lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.title: Passing the `dict keys view` as an argument to the `set` constructor
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.reading_goal: Read the sequence where the inner `data.keys()` creates a key view and passes the result to the `set` constructor.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.question: What values are included in the set created by `set(data.keys())`?
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.explanation: 1) First, call `data.keys()`. 2) Obtain the key views `a` and `b`. 3) Pass those views to the `set` constructor. 4) `a` and `b` become elements of the set.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.project_context: This relates to patterns such as checking for field existence or creating a set of keys that have already been seen.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.reading_goal_internal: 안쪽 data.keys()가 key view를 만들고 그 결과를 set 생성자에 전달하는 순서를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `set(iterable)` is a constructor call that creates a new set whose elements are the items in the iterable.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Starting with the inner `data.keys()`, it evaluates the keys `a` and `b` and passes them as input to the set.
concept_explanation.key_point: The new set contains keys a and b, not values 1 and 2.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to assume that `set(data.keys())` returns a value or adds the entire dictionary as a single element.

teaching_example.walkthrough: `keys()` returns `x` and `y`, and `set()` creates a set with these two keys as elements.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) First, call `data.keys()`. 2) Obtain the key views `a` and `b`. 3) Pass those views to the `set` constructor. 4) `a` and `b` become elements of the set.
answer_explanation.why_correct: Because the result of `keys()` is the input to `set()`, `a` and `b` become elements.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Lessons 1 and 2 are values, and values() was not called.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: It is easy to assume that `set(data.keys())` returns a value or adds the entire dictionary as a single element.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Nested calls are read in the following order: inner return value → outer argument passing → outer result.

lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.title: Reading the score value directly using the key name "Mina"
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.reading_goal: Read the flow within the square brackets: Mina is a dict key, and it returns the associated score of 90.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.question: What is the result of `scores["Mina"]`?
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.explanation: 1) `scores` is a dictionary that uses names as keys. 2) The lookup key is `Mina`. 3) The value associated with `Mina` is 90. 4) The result of the lookup, 90, is stored.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.project_context: It is linked to name-based lookups, such as individual student scores or user-specific settings.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.reading_goal_internal: 대괄호 안 Mina가 dict key이며 연결된 점수 90을 반환하는 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `mapping[key]` returns the value associated with that key in the dictionary.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Search for keys—such as "Mina" in square brackets—within the key-value pairs of `scores`.
concept_explanation.key_point: A dict can find a value directly by key name rather than by position number.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: Since this is the first item, it’s easy to assume it should be read as a list index, such as `scores[0]`.

teaching_example.code:
ages={"Jin":14,"Mina":13}
print(ages["Mina"])
teaching_example.walkthrough: It returns the value 13 for the `Mina` key.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) `scores` is a dictionary that uses names as keys. 2) The lookup key is `Mina`. 3) The value associated with `Mina` is 90. 4) The result of the lookup, 90, is stored.
answer_explanation.why_correct: The value associated with the "Mina" key is 90.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: "Mina" is the lookup key, and the result is the value.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Since this is the first item, it’s easy to assume it should be read as a list index, such as `scores[0]`.

answer_explanation.takeaway: A `dict lookup` is described as: check the key → find the matching key → return the value.

lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.title: Reading the second value of a coordinate tuple as index 1
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.reading_goal: Read the flow where the 0-based index corresponds to the order of values in the tuple, so that `point[1]` returns the second coordinate, 20.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.question: What is the result of point[1]?
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.explanation: 1) The first element, 10, has an index of 0. 2) The second element, 20, has an index of 1. 3) point[1] selects the second element. 4) The value 20 is stored in y.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.project_context: It is associated with tuples that have a fixed meaning related to position, such as coordinates or ranges.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.reading_goal_internal: tuple의 값 순서에 0-based index를 대응해 point[1]이 두 번째 좌표 20을 반환하는 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `sequence[index]` returns a single item at the specified position in an ordered data structure.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Prepend 0 and 1 to the two elements of `point` from the left, then find the value at index 1.
concept_explanation.key_point: In a tuple, it is the position—not the key name—that matters, and indexing starts at 0.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to map the first human-counted position to index 1 and therefore misread `point[1]` as 10.

teaching_example.code:
size=(640,480)
print(size[1])
teaching_example.walkthrough: Index 1 points to the second element, 480.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) The first element, 10, has an index of 0. 2) The second element, 20, has an index of 1. 3) point[1] selects the second element. 4) The value 20 is stored in y.
answer_explanation.why_correct: In a 0-based index, 1 refers to the second value, 20.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: 10 is the first element at index 0.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: It is easy to map the first human-counted position to index 1 and therefore misread `point[1]` as 10.

answer_explanation.takeaway: A tuple index is read as: check the element’s order → map to a 0-based position → return the value.

lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.title: Convert the strings inside the curly braces into set literals
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.reading_goal: Read the structure where values inside curly braces without colons form a set rather than a key-value dictionary.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.question: What data structure is created by {"python", "ai"}?
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.explanation: 1) There are two strings inside curly braces. 2) There is no colon between the two values. 3) The values are listed with commas, so this is a set literal. 4) `tags` contains two unique string elements.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.project_context: It is associated with a set of values—such as tags, IDs, and visited nodes—where duplication must be avoided.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.reading_goal_internal: 콜론 없는 중괄호 안 값들이 key-value dict가 아니라 set을 만든다는 구조를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: A set literal is an expression in the form `{value1, value2,...}` that directly creates a set of unique elements.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: First, check if there is a colon inside the curly braces; if values are listed with commas and no colon, read them as a set.
concept_explanation.key_point: A set is suitable for a collection of unique values that does not store the same value more than once.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to assume that braces always mean a dict, or to read set elements as if they had fixed list-like positions.

teaching_example.code:
skills={"python","sql"}
print("python" in skills)
teaching_example.walkthrough: When two strings are provided without a colon, a set is created.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) There are two strings inside curly braces. 2) There is no colon between the two values. 3) The values are listed with commas, so this is a set literal. 4) `tags` contains two unique string elements.
answer_explanation.why_correct: A non-empty brace expression that lists values without colons is a set literal.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: If it's a `dict`, there must be a colon between the key and the value.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: It is easy to assume that braces always mean a dict, or to read set elements as if they had fixed list-like positions.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Curly-bracket expressions are read in the following order: presence or absence of a colon → value structure → distinction between set and dict.

lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.title: Read a missing grade key using get() to retrieve the default value of 0
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.reading_goal: Read the flow where the first argument of `get` is used as a lookup key, and if the key does not exist, the second argument (0) is returned.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.question: What is the return value of `user.get("grade", 0)` when `grade` is not present?
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.explanation: 1) The only key for `user` is `name`. 2) It looks for the first argument, the `grade` key. 3) Since there is no `grade`, there is no actual value. 4) It returns the second default value, 0.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.project_context: It connects to external data or settings that may be missing certain fields, ensuring they are read safely.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a2_.reading_goal_internal: get의 첫 인자를 조회 key로 찾고 key가 없을 때 두 번째 인자 0이 반환되는 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: The `get(key, default)` method of `dict` returns the actual value if the key exists, and the default value if it does not.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Check the target of the call, `user`, find the first argument, `grade`, and then, depending on whether it exists, select either the actual value or the default value.
concept_explanation.key_point: If `grade` is missing, it returns 0 without raising a `KeyError`, unlike when using square brackets.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that if the default value 0 is stored as a new key in a dict, or if the key doesn’t exist, the `get` function will raise an error.

teaching_example.code:
settings={"mode":"dark"}
print(settings.get("font_size",14))
teaching_example.walkthrough: Since `font_size` is missing, the default value of 14 is returned.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) The only key for `user` is `name`. 2) It looks for the first argument, the `grade` key. 3) Since there is no `grade`, there is no actual value. 4) It returns the second default value, 0.
answer_explanation.why_correct: If the key is not found, `get` returns the second argument, `default`.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: `get` returns the default value specified for a missing key.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: It’s easy to assume that if the default value 0 is stored as a new key in a dict, or if the key doesn’t exist, the `get` function will raise an error.

answer_explanation.takeaway: "dict.get" is interpreted as: search for a key → if found, return the value; if not found, return the default value.

lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.title: Reading a `while` loop that iterates from 0 to 2 while re-evaluating the condition
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.reading_goal: Read the loop structure where `while` re-evaluates `i < 3` before the start of each iteration and executes the body only when it is True.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.code:
i = 0
while i < 3:
    print(i)
    i = i + 1
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.question: Which of the following is the correct output order?
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.explanation: 1) At `i=0`, the condition is True, so 0 is printed and `i` becomes 1. 2) At `i=1`, 1 is printed and `i` becomes 2. 3) At `i=2`, 2 is printed and `i` becomes 3. 4) `3 < 3` is False, so the loop ends.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.project_context: It is linked to the basic structure of an iterative process that terminates based on current state conditions.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.reading_goal_internal: while이 매 반복 시작 전에 i < 3을 다시 검사하고 True일 때만 본문을 실행하는 순환 구조를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `while condition:` It repeats the body as long as the condition is truthy and re-evaluates the condition before each iteration.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: It repeats the sequence: check initial i → check condition → execute body → update i → check condition again.
concept_explanation.key_point: When `i` becomes 3, the program terminates because the next condition, `3 < 3`, evaluates to False.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to miscount the number of iterations by checking a condition only once or by omitting the line that updates `i`.

teaching_example.code:
i=1
while i < 3:
    print(i)
    i=i+1
teaching_example.walkthrough: In Lessons 1 and 2, the code runs and terminates at `i=3`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) At `i=0`, the condition is True, so 0 is printed and `i` becomes 1. 2) At `i=1`, 1 is printed and `i` becomes 2. 3) At `i=2`, 2 is printed and `i` becomes 3. 4) `3 < 3` is False, so the loop ends.
answer_explanation.why_correct: The condition is True only in the three iterations where i is 0, 1, or 2.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: The first iteration is 0, and when i=3, the condition is already False.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: It is easy to miscount the number of iterations by checking a condition only once or by omitting the line that updates `i`.

answer_explanation.takeaway: The `while` loop repeatedly traces the flow: current value → condition → body → update → next condition.

lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.title: Determine whether the comparison 5 < 3 evaluates to False before entering the `while` loop
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.reading_goal: The flow is such that the values on both sides of the comparison expression are determined before the body, and since the result of the first condition is False, entry into the body is blocked.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.code:
i = 5
while i < 3:
    print(i)
    i = i + 1
print(i < 3)
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.question: What is the result of `i < 3` when the `while` loop is first reached?
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.explanation: 1) The current value of i is 5. 2) The value on the right is 3. 3) Since 5 is not less than 3, the comparison returns False. 4) The body of the function is never executed.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.project_context: This relates to reading comprehension exercises that involve identifying code blocks that do not execute because their conditions are not met from the start.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.reading_goal_internal: while 본문보다 먼저 비교식 양쪽 값을 확정하고 첫 조건 결과가 False라 본문 진입이 막히는 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `a < b` compares whether the left value is smaller than the right and returns a Boolean.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: First, compare the current value of `i` (5) with the value on the right (3) to determine whether 5 < 3 is true or false.
concept_explanation.key_point: Since the `while` loop evaluates the condition before the body, if the first comparison is `False`, the body will not be executed at all.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to assume that a program is executed at least once simply because `print` appears in the text.

teaching_example.code:
n=4
print(n < 2)
teaching_example.walkthrough: 4 is not less than 2, so the result is False.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) The current value of i is 5. 2) The value on the right is 3. 3) Since 5 is not less than 3, the comparison returns False. 4) The body of the function is never executed.
answer_explanation.why_correct: Since 5 < 3 is not true, the result is False.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: The comparison asks whether 5 is less than 3.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: It is easy to assume that a program is executed at least once simply because `print` appears in the text.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Conditional loops are read in the following order: operand value → comparison result → whether to enter the body.

lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.title: Updating the cumulative sum with `total += i` inside the `while` loop
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.reading_goal: Track the state changes for each iteration by adding the current value of `i` to the existing `total` and storing the result back in `total`.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.code:
i = 1
total = 0
while i <= 3:
    total += i
    i += 1
print(total)
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.question: What is the value of `total` after the third accumulation is complete?
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.explanation: 1) Initially, `total` is 0 and `i` is 1. 2) After the first iteration, `total` becomes 1. 3) After the second, `total` becomes 3. 4) After the third, `total` becomes 6.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.project_context: It is linked to iterative calculations such as total score, total cost, and cumulative throughput.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.reading_goal_internal: 각 반복의 현재 i를 기존 total에 더해 다시 total에 저장하는 상태 변화를 회차별로 추적한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `x += y` is an augmented assignment that adds y to the current value of x and stores the result back in x.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: In each iteration, check the current value of `total` and the current value of `i`, then update `total` with the result of the addition.
concept_explanation.key_point: `total` accumulates from 0 to 1 to 3 to 6, and `i` increments separately by 1.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to interpret `total += i` as a statement that simply outputs `total` and `i`, or to read it as a single variable that updates both `i` and `total`.

teaching_example.code:
i = 1
total = 0
while i <= 2:
    total += i
    i += 1
print(total)
teaching_example.walkthrough: `total` changes from 0 to 1 to 3, resulting in a final value of 3.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) Initially, `total` is 0 and `i` is 1. 2) After the first iteration, `total` becomes 1. 3) After the second, `total` becomes 3. 4) After the third, `total` becomes 6.
answer_explanation.why_correct: 1, 2, and 3 are added to the current total in sequence, resulting in a final cumulative value of 6.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: 3 is the intermediate total after the second iteration, and the third accumulation (where i=3) remains.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: It is easy to interpret `total += i` as a statement that simply outputs `total` and `i`, or to read it as a single variable that updates both `i` and `total`.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Cumulative assignment is read in the following order: **check the existing value → add the value on the right → store the new value in the same variable**.

lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.title: Reading the item at index i from items[i] using a `while` loop
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.reading_goal: On each iteration, check which list position the current value of `i` points to and trace the flow from `a` to the next value `b`.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.code:
items = ["a", "b"]
i = 0
while i < len(items):
    print(items[i])
    i += 1
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.question: What is the value of `items[i]` in the second iteration?
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.explanation: 1) In the first iteration, since i = 0, items[0] is a. 2) At the end of the body, i becomes 1. 3) Since the condition for the second iteration is True, the program enters the body. 4) items[1] is b.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.project_context: It relates to code that iterates through a list of files or a list of cards based on an index.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.reading_goal_internal: 각 반복에서 i의 현재 값이 list의 어느 위치를 가리키는지 확인해 a 다음 b를 읽는 흐름을 추적한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `sequence[index]` returns a single item at the specified 0-based position in an ordered data structure.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: First, check the current value of `i`, then use that number as the index for `items`.
concept_explanation.key_point: If i = 0, a is selected; if i = 1, b is selected.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to assume that `i` itself is printed or to interpret index 1 as the first item.

teaching_example.code:
items = ["x", "y"]
i = 0
while i < len(items):
    print(items[i])
    i += 1
teaching_example.walkthrough: It reads x when i=0 and y when i=1.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) In the first iteration, since i = 0, items[0] is a. 2) At the end of the body, i becomes 1. 3) Since the condition for the second iteration is True, the program enters the body. 4) items[1] is b.
answer_explanation.why_correct: The current index in the second iteration is 1, and the value at index 1 in the list is b.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: 1 is the index value used for lookup, and the result of the subscription is the item b at that position.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: It is easy to assume that `i` itself is printed or to interpret index 1 as the first item.

answer_explanation.takeaway: The index is read in the following order: **current index value → sequence position → return the corresponding item**.

lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.title: Check whether the current `i` in `countdown` is greater than 0
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.reading_goal: At the start of each iteration, the flow is determined by comparing the current value of `i` with 0 to decide whether to execute the body of the code.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.code:
i = 3
while i > 0:
    print(i)
    i -= 1
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.question: What is the result of `i > 0` after `i` becomes 0?
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.explanation: 1) The condition for i is True at 3, 2, and 1. 2) After each iteration, i decreases by 1. 3) Eventually, i becomes 0. 4) Since 0 > 0 is False, the loop ends.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.project_context: It is linked to iterations that decrease, such as the number of retries, remaining attempts, and a countdown.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.reading_goal_internal: 각 회차 시작 시 현재 i와 0을 비교해 본문 실행 여부가 정해지는 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `a > b` checks whether the left-hand value is greater than the right-hand value and returns a Boolean.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Currently, every time the value of `i` changes from 3 to 2 to 1 to 0, the program re-evaluates whether it is greater than 0.
concept_explanation.key_point: When `i=1`, `0 > 0` is True, but when `i=0`, it is False.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to misread the text as “0 is printed once” or to interpret `>` as `>=`.

teaching_example.code:
i = 2
while i > 0:
    print(i)
    i -= 1
teaching_example.walkthrough: Since 2>0 and 1>0 are True, but 0>0 is False, only 2 and 1 are printed.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) The condition for i is True at 3, 2, and 1. 2) After each iteration, i decreases by 1. 3) Eventually, i becomes 0. 4) Since 0 > 0 is False, the loop ends.
answer_explanation.why_correct: Since 0 is not greater than 0, the result of the greater-than comparison is False.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Since the condition is a strict `>=` rather than `>`, it is not true for the value 0.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: It is easy to misread the text as “0 is printed once” or to interpret `>` as `>=`.

answer_explanation.takeaway: The loop condition is read as **current operand value → comparison operator → Boolean → whether to enter the body**.

lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.title: When n is 3, use a `break` to immediately terminate the nearest `for` loop
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.reading_goal: Read the flow where, the moment the current iteration value becomes 3, the `break` statement is executed, causing neither the `print` statement in that iteration nor the subsequent value 4 to be executed.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.question: What is the actual order of the values printed due to the `break` statement?
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.explanation: 1) When n=1, the condition is False, so 1 is printed. 2) When n=2, the condition is also False, so 2 is printed. 3) When n=3, the condition becomes True, so the `break` statement is executed. 4) The loop ends, so the `print(3)` statement and the n=4 iteration are not executed.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.project_context: When the search encounters the first termination condition, it is connected to a flow that stops without needing to check further.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.reading_goal_internal: 현재 반복값이 3이 되는 순간 break가 실행되어 그 회차의 아래 print와 이후 값 4가 모두 실행되지 않는 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `break` terminates the entire nearest loop as soon as it is executed.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: As the loop iterates through the values in order, when it encounters a condition that actually triggers a `break`, the loop terminates at that point.
concept_explanation.key_point: On the `n=3` iteration, `break` executes before `print`, so 3 is not printed either.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to think `break` behaves like `continue` and skips only the current iteration, or to think it prints 3 and then stops.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Only `n=1` is printed, and the `break` statement at `n=2` terminates the entire loop.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) When n=1, the condition is False, so 1 is printed. 2) When n=2, the condition is also False, so 2 is printed. 3) When n=3, the condition becomes True, so the `break` statement is executed. 4) The loop ends, so the `print(3)` statement and the n=4 iteration are not executed.
answer_explanation.why_correct: Since the `break` statement executes before the `print` statement for `n=3`, it terminates the loop, so only 1 and 2 are printed.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: In case n=3, the `break` statement is executed first, so the `print` statement below it is not reached.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: It is easy to think `break` behaves like `continue` and skips only the current iteration, or to think it prints 3 and then stops.

answer_explanation.takeaway: "break" is interpreted as **condition met → break executed → nearest loop terminated immediately**.

lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.title: Reassign the first matched word to `found` and save the result
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.reading_goal: Read the state change that occurs when the initial empty string in `found` is replaced with the first matching word, “apple,” and is retained after the `break`.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.code:
words = ["cat", "apple", "ant"]
found = ""
for word in words:
    if word.startswith("a"):
        found = word
        break
print(found)
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.question: What value is stored in `found` when `found = word` is executed for the first time?
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.explanation: 1) Since “cat” does not start with “a,” the assignment is skipped. 2) The next word is “apple,” and the condition is True. 3) “found = word” is executed, so “found” is set to “apple.” 4) “break” is executed immediately, so the program does not proceed to “ant.”
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.project_context: It is linked to a search pattern that stores the first item in the list that satisfies the condition in the result variable.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.reading_goal_internal: found의 초기 빈 문자열이 첫 일치 단어 apple을 만났을 때 새 값으로 교체되고 break 뒤 유지되는 상태 변화를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: Reassignment is the operation of assigning a new value to a name that already has a value associated with it, so that the name subsequently refers to the new value.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: After checking the previous value of `found` and the current value of the word on the right, assign the value and update what `found` points to.
concept_explanation.key_point: Immediately after storing `apple`, the `break` statement is executed, so it does not change back to `ant`.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to assume that `found` either continues to hold the initial empty string or is updated to the last match after checking up to the subsequent `ant`.

teaching_example.code:
words = ["x", "yes", "yard"]
found = ""
for word in words:
    if word.startswith("y"):
        found = word
        break
print(found)
teaching_example.walkthrough: After the first "y" word, "yes," is stored in `found`, `yard` is not checked due to the `break`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) Since “cat” does not start with “a,” the assignment is skipped. 2) The next word is “apple,” and the condition is True. 3) “found = word” is executed, so “found” is set to “apple.” 4) “break” is executed immediately, so the program does not proceed to “ant.”
answer_explanation.why_correct: Since the word "apple" satisfies the first condition, its value is reassigned to `found`.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Since the loop ends with a `break` immediately after `apple` is stored, the `ant` iteration is not executed.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: It is easy to assume that `found` either continues to hold the initial empty string or is updated to the last match after checking up to the subsequent `ant`.

answer_explanation.takeaway: "reassignment" is interpreted as **checking the previous value → evaluating the current value on the right → binding the name to the new value**.

lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.title: Skip the remaining body of the code using `continue` on even iterations
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.reading_goal: In iterations where the even condition is True, the `continue` statement is executed, skipping the `print` statement in the current iteration and moving on to the next `n`.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.question: What is the actual order in which the values are output?
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.explanation: 1) Since n=1 is not an even number, it prints 1. 2) Since n=2 is even, `continue` skips the `print` statement. 3) Since n=3 is not even, it prints 3. 4) Since n=4 is even, it skips the `print` statement again.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.project_context: This ties into the pattern of quickly skipping items that are not to be processed in a filtering loop.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.reading_goal_internal: 짝수 조건이 True인 회차에서는 continue가 실행되어 현재 반복의 아래 print를 건너뛰고 다음 n으로 이동하는 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `continue` skips the remainder of the current iteration and moves to the next iteration of the nearest loop.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: It reads that for each n, the condition is checked, and if `continue` is executed, the statements in the same iteration below it are not executed.
concept_explanation.key_point: In steps 2 and 4, `print` is not executed; output is generated only in steps 1 and 3.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to misinterpret “continue” as ending the entire loop like “break,” or to read it as printing an even number and then proceeding to the next iteration.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Only in the n=2 iteration is the print statement skipped, so 1 and 3 are printed.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) Since n=1 is not an even number, it prints 1. 2) Since n=2 is even, `continue` skips the `print` statement. 3) Since n=3 is not even, it prints 3. 4) Since n=4 is even, it skips the `print` statement again.
answer_explanation.why_correct: Since `continue` skips only the `print` statements on even-numbered iterations, only the odd-numbered ones (1 and 3) are printed.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: In lines 2 and 4, `continue` is executed immediately, so the `print` statement below it is not reached.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: It is easy to misinterpret “continue” as ending the entire loop like “break,” or to read it as printing an even number and then proceeding to the next iteration.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Read `continue` as **condition satisfied → skip the remaining code in the current iteration → move to the next iteration value**.

lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.title: Checking if `item` is an empty string using `==`
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.reading_goal: In each iteration, it reads a Boolean that determines whether to execute `continue` by comparing the current string of `item` with an empty string literal.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.question: In the "Empty String" session, what is the result of `item == ""`?
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.explanation: 1) The `item` in the second iteration is an empty string. 2) The right-hand operand is also an empty string literal. 3) The two strings are exactly the same. 4) The `==` comparison evaluates to `True`, so `continue` is executed.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.project_context: It is linked to conditions that identify empty values during input validation or log processing.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.reading_goal_internal: 각 반복에서 item의 현재 문자열과 빈 문자열 literal을 비교해 continue 실행 여부를 결정하는 Boolean을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `a == b` compares whether two values are equal; if they are, it returns True; if they are not, it returns False.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Check the actual string of the current item and compare it to see if it is exactly the same as the empty string on the right.
concept_explanation.key_point: Only the middle item, `"" == ""`, evaluates to True, so the program skips to the next line using `continue`.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to mistake an empty string for a single space or to select the string itself as the answer instead of the result of the equality comparison.

teaching_example.walkthrough: It returns False for `x` and True for an empty string.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) The `item` in the second iteration is an empty string. 2) The right-hand operand is also an empty string literal. 3) The two strings are exactly the same. 4) The `==` comparison evaluates to `True`, so `continue` is executed.
answer_explanation.why_correct: Since both values are empty strings, the equality comparison evaluates to True.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Since the current `item` and the literal on the right are both empty strings, they are not different from each other.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: It is easy to mistake an empty string for a single space or to select the string itself as the answer instead of the result of the equality comparison.

answer_explanation.takeaway: "comparison" is read as **check current values on both sides → examine the relationship → Boolean result**.

lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.title: Reading the flow of a `while True` loop where an internal `break` serves as the actual exit point
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.reading_goal: The `while` header itself is always true, but when the `break` condition inside the body is satisfied, the entire loop terminates.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.question: What is the actual output sequence of this loop?
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.explanation: 1) At `i=0`, since the `break` condition is `False`, it prints 0 and sets `i` to 1. 2) The program enters the `while True` loop again. 3) When `i = 1`, the condition is still False, so it prints 1 and increments `i` to 2. 4) When `i = 2`, the `break` statement is executed, ending the loop before `print` is called.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.project_context: It is associated with loops—such as service loops or retry loops—that have termination conditions within the body rather than external conditions.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.reading_goal_internal: while 헤더 자체는 항상 참이지만 본문 안 break 조건이 충족되면 반복문 전체가 종료되는 제어 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `while True:` Although it appears to loop indefinitely based on the header conditions alone, you can terminate it within the body using a control statement such as `break`.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: After verifying that the header is always True, be sure to look for both state changes and break conditions within the body to determine whether the program might terminate.
concept_explanation.key_point: When `i` becomes 2, `break` executes before `print`, so 2 is not printed.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to jump to the conclusion that this is an infinite loop just by looking at the text, or to assume that 2 will be printed first even if there’s a `break` statement.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Although the header is always True, the `break` statement is executed at `i=1`, so only 0 is printed and the program terminates.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) At `i=0`, since the `break` condition is `False`, it prints 0 and sets `i` to 1. 2) The program enters the `while True` loop again. 3) When `i = 1`, the condition is still False, so it prints 1 and increments `i` to 2. 4) When `i = 2`, the `break` statement is executed, ending the loop before `print` is called.
answer_explanation.why_correct: Since the inner `break` terminates the loop at `i=2`, only 0 and 1 are printed.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Although the header is always True, the actual `break` statement is executed when `i` becomes 2 in the body of the code.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: It’s easy to jump to the conclusion that this is an infinite loop just by looking at the text, or to assume that 2 will be printed first even if there’s a `break` statement.

answer_explanation.takeaway: With `while True`, also inspect **state updates → internal termination condition → whether `break` executes**.

lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.title: continue: Read the sequence where `i + 1` is calculated first before the `continue` statement
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.reading_goal: Read the evaluation sequence where, in each while iteration, the increment expression executes before the continue condition, causing i to change to 1, 2, and 3.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.question: In the second session, what value does the increment expression `i + 1` produce?
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.explanation: 1) After the first iteration, i is 1. 2) At the start of the second iteration, i is currently 1. 3) The expression `i + 1` is evaluated, resulting in 2. 4) After that 2 is stored in i, the if condition evaluates to True, and `continue` is executed.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.project_context: In a `while` loop containing `continue`, this helps you assess the risk of an infinite loop without missing the `update` location.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.reading_goal_internal: 각 while 회차에서 증가식이 continue 조건보다 먼저 실행되어 i가 1,2,3으로 바뀌는 평가 순서를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `a + b` is an arithmetic expression that adds the current values of the two operands to produce a new value.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: It currently reads as: First, i is added to the integer 1 to create a new value, which is then stored in i, and then the if statement and continue are executed.
concept_explanation.key_point: Even in the iteration where `i` becomes 2, since the increment itself has already ended, `i` will not remain at 2 during the next condition check.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to think `continue` also cancels an increment that already occurred above it, or to misread the increment as appearing after `continue`.

teaching_example.walkthrough: In the first iteration, `i` is first set to 1, then `continue` is executed, and in the next iteration, it starts with `i = 1`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) After the first iteration, i is 1. 2) At the start of the second iteration, i is currently 1. 3) The expression `i + 1` is evaluated, resulting in 2. 4) After that 2 is stored in i, the if condition evaluates to True, and `continue` is executed.
answer_explanation.why_correct: The increment expression for the second iteration adds 1 to the current value of 1, resulting in 2.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: 1 is the previous value of `i` before the increment expression is evaluated; it is not the result of the calculation `+ 1`.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: It is easy to think `continue` also cancels an increment that already occurred above it, or to misread the increment as appearing after `continue`.

answer_explanation.takeaway: If an arithmetic operation appears on the right side of an assignment, read it in the following order: **check current value → calculate arithmetic result → assign → next control statement**.

lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.title: Obtaining a new list in ascending order by calling the `sorted(nums)` function
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.reading_goal: Examine the current elements of `nums` and follow the flow of the `sorted` function as it returns a new list arranged in ascending order.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.code:
nums = [3, 1, 2]
result = sorted(nums)
print(result)
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.question: `sorted(nums)` What is the return value of this function?
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.explanation: 1) The values in `nums` are 3, 1, and 2. 2) Pass `nums` to the `sorted` function. 3) Sort the numbers in ascending order to produce the sequence 1, 2, 3. 4) Return a new list [1, 2, 3].
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.project_context: It relates to code that sorts data requiring a specific order, such as rankings, scores, and filenames.
lessons/python_foundation_level3_v95_a3_.reading_goal_internal: nums의 현재 원소를 확인하고 sorted 함수가 오름차순으로 배치한 새 list를 반환하는 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `sorted(iterable)` is a function call that returns a new list with the items in the iterable sorted.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Check the values in the input iterable, apply the default sorting rules, and then read the order of the new list that is returned.
concept_explanation.key_point: Even if the original `nums` is [3,1,2], the return value of `sorted(nums)` is [1,2,3].
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to assume that `sorted` is equivalent to `list.sort()`, which returns `None`, or that it returns the original order unchanged.

teaching_example.code:
values = [2, 1, 3]
result = sorted(values)
print(result)
teaching_example.walkthrough: `sorted` returns a new list [1,2,3], which is stored in `result`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) The values in `nums` are 3, 1, and 2. 2) Pass `nums` to the `sorted` function. 3) Sort the numbers in ascending order to produce the sequence 1, 2, 3. 4) Return a new list [1, 2, 3].
answer_explanation.why_correct: `sorted` returns a new list in which the numbers are sorted in ascending order by default.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: "None" is an option that is often confused with the return value of `list.sort()` (which operates in-place), whereas `sorted` returns a new list.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: It is easy to assume that `sorted` is equivalent to `list.sort()`, which returns `None`, or that it returns the original order unchanged.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Read a function call in the order **check the input values → apply the function rule → check the return value → pass it to the next code**.
